title: Colts' 3 Biggest Disappointments Through Five Weeks of 2026
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts entered 2026 betting heavily on internal growth. Five games in, a few of those bets have already become major concerns.
There is still plenty of season left, but these three have fallen well short of expectations so far.
After what looked like a breakout 2025 season, Laiatu Latu was supposed to take another step toward becoming one of the NFL's premier young edge rushers.
Instead, he has been nearly invisible for long stretches.
Latu finished last season with 8.5 sacks, 45 tackles and three interceptions across 16 starts. Through five games this year, he has just one sack and 14 total pressures, while earning a 58.8 pass-rush grade from PFF.
That grade ranks 72nd among 106 qualified edge defenders.
Indianapolis desperately needs more from Latu because this pass rush has been the worst in football.
The Colts own a 23.7% pressure rate through five weeks, according to Next Gen Stats, making them the only defense in the NFL below 30%. Latu is playing plenty of snaps, and he is supposed to be the guy leading the charge in turning this pass rush around.
Simply put, Indianapolis needs him to start wrecking games.
This one is less about how Pierce has played and more about the fact that he simply has not been available.
Indianapolis handed Pierce a four-year, $114 million extension in March after he posted a career-high 1,003 receiving yards in 2025. Shortly after signing, he underwent surgery on the left heel/ankle issue that had bothered him since 2024.
The expectation was that he would be ready for Week 1, and technically, he was.
Pierce caught four passes for 61 yards against Baltimore, then aggravated the heel against Kansas City after one catch for 11 yards. He has been on injured reserve ever since.
The Colts invested heavily in Pierce because his ability to stretch the field is what helps open up this entire offense, particularly for Jonathan Taylor.
Through five weeks, Indianapolis has barely gotten to use it.
The Colts made a pretty significant gamble this offseason when they traded Zaire Franklin to Green Bay and elected to address their linebacker room primarily through the draft.
Through five weeks, that gamble has not paid off.
Second-round pick CJ Allen played just 11 defensive snaps through the first four games before finally seeing 24 against Pittsburgh. Bryce Boettcher has played roughly 80-plus defensive snaps, but his PFF grade sits in the mid-40s.
That lack of immediate impact is hard to ignore considering how badly this defense needed help at linebacker.
Third-round safety A.J. Haulcy has played considerably more, but his start has been rough, particularly in coverage. Still, there have been some flashes of the player Indianapolis believed it was drafting.
There is still plenty of time for this rookie class to turn things around, but the early returns have been anything but encouraging.
And for a general manager in Chris Ballard who entered this season desperately needing results, this rookie group has not given him much help yet.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Rookie Class Rankings After Week 5: Colts Need More from First-Year Players
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts needed an impactful draft class to help elevate their roster ahead of a 2026 season with plenty riding on it. But so far, the returns have been minimal.
In Justin Melo of Sports Illustrated’s recent rankings of all the NFL rookie classes through five weeks, Indianapolis ranked 29th out of 32 teams, receiving a “D” grade, the result of a change in strategy.
Colts general manager Chris Ballard altered his approach to the draft this time around. Instead of taking elite athletes with promising developmental traits and hoping the coaching staff can polish them out, Ballard went for older, more experienced players instead.
The initial indications from the rookie class were good. There were plenty of flashes in preseason and all eight draft picks made the roster, further reinforcing the belief that these rookies could make an instant impact.
Instead, the results so far have been underwhelming. Let’s take a look at each player selected and work out why things haven’t gone to plan so far.
The Colts drafted CJ Allen 53rd overall with the goal of making him the heart of their defense at MIKE linebacker.
Allen differed from some of Chris Ballard's previous linebacker selections in that he wasn't an elite athlete, instead relying on his instincts and football IQ to make plays. He also arrived in Indianapolis with plenty of experience, having appeared in 38 games during his career at Georgia.
The vision of Allen becoming the man in the middle didn't last long, however. The rookie dealt with multiple injuries during training camp that kept him sidelined for much of the summer. Indianapolis subsequently leaned more heavily on veteran Akeem Davis-Gaither, leaving Allen with a difficult path to playing time.
Through five games, Allen has appeared in just three, logging only 35 total snaps. Melo noted that the Colts haven't trusted Allen to play WILL linebacker, and his limited involvement reflects the challenges he's faced earning a role in the defense.
Allen's situation illustrates one of the concerns surrounding Indianapolis' draft class. The Colts targeted experienced prospects with the expectation that they could contribute immediately, yet they've hardly let their second-round pick see the field. His training camp injuries provide important context, but until he earns a larger role and shows what he can do with it, the Colts will struggle to realize the immediate return they envisioned when they drafted him.
The Colts selected A.J. Haulcy 78th overall in the third round, hoping to add an experienced, physical presence to their secondary who could contribute early in his NFL career.
Haulcy came to Indianapolis after a productive season at LSU, where he earned First-Team All-SEC honors after recording 88 tackles and three interceptions in 2025. His experience across three college programs, combined with his ability to make plays against the run and in coverage, gave the Colts reason to believe he could compete for a significant role immediately.
Unlike Allen, Haulcy hasn't had to wait for an opportunity. The rookie has played in all five games, recording 21 combined tackles and two pass breakups. However, his involvement hasn't consistently translated into the kind of dependable play the Colts need from their secondary.
Melo specifically pointed to Haulcy's struggles in coverage, citing a 37.4 PFF coverage grade through the first four weeks. While the rookie has shown an ability to contribute as a tackler, his early coverage performance has been a concern, particularly for a defense counting on him to handle significant responsibilities in the back end.
The Colts have given their third-round pick an opportunity to establish himself, but the early returns have left plenty of room for improvement. Indianapolis drafted Haulcy with the expectation that his experience would help him adjust quickly to the NFL. If he's going to justify that investment, he must become more reliable in coverage and turn his substantial playing time into more consistent production.
The Colts selected Jalen Farmer 113th overall in the fourth round, hoping to add depth and a potential long-term starter to their interior offensive line. Farmer started 24 games at right guard during his final two seasons at Kentucky, continuing the trend of adding experienced prospects who could eventually compete for a starting role.
However, Farmer has yet to establish himself in the Colts' offensive line rotation. Cracking the starting lineup as a rookie was always a long shot for Farmer, as Indianapolis has one of the best starting offensive lines in football. Through five games, Farmer has played just three offensive snaps, with most of his involvement coming on special teams.
While his limited opportunities make it difficult to evaluate his development, his lack of involvement is another example of a rookie class that has yet to provide the immediate contributions Indianapolis envisioned.
The Colts selected Bryce Boettcher 135th overall in the fourth round, adding another experienced linebacker to a position group they wanted to strengthen. Boettcher arrived from Oregon after recording 136 tackles in his final collegiate season, bringing the production and experience Indianapolis hoped would translate to the NFL.
Unlike fellow rookie CJ Allen, Boettcher has found a way onto the field. He has appeared in all five games, recording 20 tackles while earning a larger role on defense.
Boettcher has at least received opportunities to contribute, but the Colts need more consistency from their fourth-round pick if he's to be a part of the future. With Indianapolis still searching for answers at linebacker, if Boettcher is going to establish himself as a dependable part of the defense, he must maintain consistency for the remainder of the year.
The Colts selected George Gumbs Jr. 156th overall in the fifth round, betting on his athletic traits and long-term potential as a pass rusher. In other words, Gumbs was the most Ballard-esque pick of the class. Gumbs recorded 6.5 tackles for loss and 2.5 sacks in his final season at Florida, but his limited starting experience made him more of a developmental prospect than a ready-made contributor.
Through five games, Gumbs has played just 11 defensive snaps, recording two tackles in his NFL debut against Pittsburgh. His limited role isn't particularly surprising given his draft position and developmental profile, but it reinforces the challenge facing Indianapolis' rookie class. The Colts targeted experienced prospects to help immediately, yet Gumbs remains a long-term project who hasn't contributed much so far.
The Colts selected Caden Curry 214th overall in the sixth round, adding another defensive end with experience at a major college program. Curry finished his Ohio State career with 12.5 sacks, showing the pass-rushing ability that made him an intriguing late-round addition.
Curry made a strong impression during the preseason, but that impact hasn't carried over to the regular season. Through five games, Curry has played just 43 defensive snaps with no sacks, though he has contributed regularly on special teams.
With Arden Key now on injured reserve, Curry has an opportunity to earn a larger role. The Colts need to see whether his preseason flashes can translate into more consistent production when given the chance. If there's something to build on there, Curry could be a piece the Cols chose to build around going forward.
The Colts selected Seth McGowan 237th overall in the seventh round, adding an experienced running back to a backfield led by Jonathan Taylor. McGowan rushed for 725 yards and 12 touchdowns in his final season at Kentucky, giving Indianapolis another option behind its star running back.
Through five games, McGowan has arguably been the most effective rookie in the class. He's recorded 61 rushing yards and 10 receiving yards while contributing on kickoff returns. While his role remains limited, he's found ways to maximize…

title: Colts Week 5 Stock Report: 3 Risers, 3 Fallers After Loss to Steelers
full_text:
Spencer Shrader scored 16 of the Indianapolis Colts' 22 points on Sunday. That's massive for Shrader, but it's a pretty ugly reflection of where this offense is right now.
While Tyler Warren continued to establish himself as a legitimate offensive weapon, the defense had another afternoon to forget in Pittsburgh.
There weren't many bright spots in this 34-22 loss, but a few players managed to separate themselves from the rest.
Here's whose stock is rising and falling after Week 5.
It’s clear why Shane Steichen keeps finding ways to get Warren the ball.
The second-year TE led Indianapolis with seven catches for 83 yards, including a physical 29-yard gain, and scored the Colts' only touchdown on a one-yard run.
With Jonathan Taylor held to 45 yards on 15 carries, Warren was practically the engine of this offense. His versatility and nose for the end zone are becoming impossible to ignore.
I don't know how much more you can ask from this guy.
Shrader drilled all five field-goal attempts, including kicks from 57 and 56 yards, accounting for 16 of Indianapolis' 22 points and tying a franchise record.
He's now a perfect 16-for-16 on field goals this season. Every time the offense stalled, Shrader made sure the Colts walked away with something.
After his ugly showing in London, Gardner needed a bounce-back performance. He delivered.
Gardner allowed just one catch for nine yards against Pittsburgh and earned a 68.2 defensive grade, via PFF.
He was outspoken about his effort last week, and you could tell making a statement mattered to him. This looked much more like the cornerback Indianapolis traded for.
There's really no way to sugarcoat this one. Davis-Gaither struggled in both run defense and coverage.
He finished with seven tackles and a tackle for loss, but his 38.5 overall grade, via PFF, was the lowest on the team.
Missed tackles and receptions allowed made for a rough afternoon, and for the guy wearing the green dot, Indianapolis needs a whole lot more.
Buckner finished with six tackles, a sack and a tackle for loss. But those numbers don't tell the whole story.
He posted one of the Colts' lowest run-defense grades Sunday, and his season-long mark sits at 49.8, via PFF.
After an impressive start to the season, this felt like a step back from someone Indianapolis needs anchoring its defensive front.
Latu didn't record a tackle against Pittsburgh, and while he batted down two passes, he was once again ineffective rushing the passer.
Through five games, the former first-round pick has just one sack and 14 pressures. After 8.5 sacks last season, I expected him to take another step forward.
Instead, we're once again questioning whether Chris Ballard got enough out of a premium edge-rusher draft pick.
At 2-3, the Colts head home to face Tennessee with plenty to clean up. The offense needs to start finishing drives, and the defense desperately needs more players to step up.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts Week 5 Report Card: More Questions Than Answers
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts had plenty of chances to walk out of Pittsburgh with their third straight victory, but once again, this team couldn't get out of its own way.
The offense looked mediocre, and Sunday made one thing painfully clear: when Jonathan Taylor gets bottled up, this version of the Colts offense simply does not have enough firepower to make up for it.
Defensively, things were even worse. The Colts struggled to generate pressure on Aaron Rodgers, leaving an already vulnerable secondary exposed throughout the afternoon.
Long story short, this defense took a massive step backward. Here are my Week 5 grades for every position.
Daniel Jones finally put an end to his turnover streak, finishing 24-of-44 for 267 yards with no interceptions or lost fumbles.
That is a big step forward for a quarterback who couldn't seem to stop giving the ball away through the first four weeks, but the rest of his performance was uninspiring.
Jones completed just 54.5% of his passes, averaged 6.1 yards per attempt and finished with a 72.8 passer rating.
The ball security was encouraging, but Jones still missed too many open receivers. It's a step in the right direction, but he still has a long way to go.
Jonathan Taylor simply could not get anything going against Pittsburgh's defensive front.
He finished with 45 yards on 15 carries, averaging just 3.0 yards per attempt, with 20 of those yards coming on one run. Take away that one carry, and Taylor managed just 25 yards on his other 14 attempts.
Sunday made one thing painfully clear: if Taylor gets bottled up, this version of Indianapolis' offense is in serious trouble.
This team is really missing Alec Pierce right about now.
Six Colts wide receivers were targeted and combined for just 126 receiving yards. Without Pierce stretching defenses vertically, Indianapolis desperately needs someone else to provide some juice.
Daniel Jones certainly missed some opportunities, but this group struggled to create separation and provided almost no explosiveness in the passing game.
This was undoubtedly Indianapolis' best offensive position group on Sunday.
Tyler Warren led the way with seven receptions on nine targets for 83 yards, while also scoring the Colts' only touchdown on a one-yard run.
All three tight ends combined for 10 receptions on 12 targets for 101 receiving yards, with Mo Alie-Cox and Drew Ogletree making the most of their limited opportunities.
The pass blocking from this group was not particularly good, but Warren continues to prove why Indianapolis invested its first-round pick in him.
The Colts' offensive line held up reasonably well in pass protection, but the run blocking was a completely different story.
Quenton Nelson was once again the clear standout, earning an 81.9 run blocking grade from PFF, but the rest of the unit struggled to create running lanes.
The Colts finished with just 66 rushing yards as a team, and when this offense relies so heavily on Jonathan Taylor, that kind of performance up front simply is not going to cut it.
One sack and seven total pressures simply was not enough against Aaron Rodgers, but the bigger concern was how badly this unit struggled against the run.
Jaylen Warren rushed for 101 yards and added another 87 through the air, while Indianapolis' defensive linemen averaged a 54.2 run-defense grade, via PFF.
Rodgers was quick and decisive, but this defensive front has consistently struggled to generate pressure, making life extremely difficult for an already vulnerable secondary.
This group had another rough afternoon, especially against the run.
Starters Akeem Davis-Gaither and Austin Ajiake posted PFF run-defense grades of 46.7 and 49.4, respectively, while Bryce Boettcher finished at 42.7 and missed a tackle on Warren's 80-yard receiving touchdown.
Ajiake was solid in coverage, but the rest of the group struggled. Davis-Gaither finished with a 43.7 coverage grade, which seems like it might be becoming a theme.
This group took a massive step backward after showing signs of improvement over the previous two weeks.
Rodgers finished with 235 passing yards, three touchdowns and a 125.0 passer rating, while Indianapolis' four cornerbacks averaged a 54.12 coverage grade, via PFF.
Granted, it is difficult to cover receivers when the defensive front cant pressure the quarterback, but this group still has to be better.
AJ Haulcy had a decent afternoon, but Cam Bynum continues to have a disappointing start to the season after showing so much potential in 2025.
The two starting safeties combined for an average PFF coverage grade of 61.45, and neither provided enough support against the run.
This group has shown it can play better, but Sunday's performance was another step in the wrong direction.
Spencer Shrader is the truth.
He went 5-for-5 on field goals, including makes from 57 and 56 yards, tying the Colts’ franchise record for field goals made in a single game.
The kickoff coverage needs work, but Shrader continues to look like the real deal.
The Colts have now dropped to 2-3, and Sunday's loss exposed some of the same problems that plagued this team during the first two weeks of the season.
Indianapolis has shown it can compete when both sides of the ball play complementary football. The problem is getting them to do it consistently.

title: Colts Week 5 Snap Analysis: Two Young Defenders Get Their Shot
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts suffered a 34-22 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday, falling to 2-3 on the season. It was a frustrating afternoon for a team that entered the game looking to build momentum, with missed opportunities on offense and defensive breakdowns contributing to the defeat.
As Indianapolis looks to regroup ahead of its next matchup, the Week 5 snap counts provide telling insight into how the coaching staff deployed its personnel and where some of the team's current roles stand.
Here's a breakdown of three developments from Sunday's loss worth monitoring.
CJ Allen’s Role Begins to Grow
After barely seeing the field through the first four games, CJ Allen finally got an extended opportunity against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
The Colts' second-round pick played a career-high 24 defensive snaps in Sunday's 34-22 loss, more than doubling his defensive workload from the first four weeks combined. Allen was mostly solid in his increased role, recording three tackles, although he did allow a short touchdown catch by Pat Freiermuth.
Allen played more than fellow rookie linebacker Bryce Boettcher, an indication of the progress he's made over the last few weeks despite limited playing time The increased workload was an encouraging step, as Allen had struggled to find his place in Indianapolis' linebacker rotation.
It's just one game and only a glimpse into what the future could be like for Allen, but his performance gives the Colts something to build on as they continue to look for answers at linebacker.
High Count, Low Impact for Laquon Treadwell
With the Colts shorthanded at wide receiver, Laquon Treadwell continued to see plenty of playing time against the Steelers. The veteran wideout played 57 offensive snaps, second-most on the team, but didn't do much with the opportunity.
Treadwell was targeted eight times on Sunday. He finished with two catches for 34 yards. He struggled to consistently connect with Daniel Jones as the Colts' passing game failed to find much rhythm.
Indianapolis was already without Alec Pierce and using a hampered Keenan Allen, meaning Treadwell had to step up. Instead but his limited impact played a role in a flat air attack
Treadwell's playing time will remain elevated as long as the Colts are dealing with injuries at receiver. But going forward, he'll need to involve himself much more.
Opportunity for Jaylahn Tuimoloau
With Arden Key sidelined by a hamstring injury, Jaylahn Tuimoloau took on alarger role on Sunday. The second-year defensive end made the most of the increased playing time, recording 49 snaps, more than any Colts edge defender other than Laiatu Latu.
Tuimoloau didn't record a sack, but he showed some encouraging flashes as a pass rusher. After spending much of his rookie season on the bench, the former second-round pick is beginning to earn more opportunities in Indianapolis' defensive rotation.
With Key expected to miss several weeks, Tuimoloau has a chance to build on Sunday's performance and make a case for a more consistent role. If he can continue to show promise as a pass rusher, he could give the Colts another option on the edge even after Key returns.

title: Six Most Revealing Quotes After Colts’ Disappointing Loss to Steelers
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts had opportunities to leave Pittsburgh with a win on Sunday. Instead, they left with a 34-22 loss to the Steelers and a list of issues that need to be addressed heading into Week 6.
Indianapolis moved the ball between the 20-yard lines but struggled to turn those drives into touchdowns. Meanwhile, the defense gave up two explosive touchdowns while tackling problems persisted.
After the game, head coach Shane Steichen, quarterback Daniel Jones and running back Jonathan Taylor offered insight into what went wrong and what the Colts need to improve. Here are six of the most important quotes from Indianapolis' Week 5 loss and what they reveal about the team moving forward.
Steichen Sounds Off on Red-Zone Woes
The Colts' red zone struggles were arguably the difference maker between a win and a loss. Indianapolis scored a touchdown on only one of its three trips inside Pittsburgh's 20-yard line, settling for field goals on two other possessions. Those missed opportunities proved costly in a 34-22 loss.
Following the game, head coach Shane Steichen acknowledged that the Colts needed to improve in those situations, including in the way he managed the offense.
“We’ve to do a better job. I’ve got to do a better job of calling plays. We’ve got to do a better job of executing. Credit Pittsburgh in those situations, but we've got to do a better job overall and get it cleaned up so we can score touchdowns down there.”
Steichen's willingness to include his own playcalling in the problem is notable. The Colts had entered Week 5 with one of the league's more productive red-zone offenses, converting 75% of their trips into touchdowns through the first four weeks. Against Pittsburgh, however, they failed to finish drives even when they had opportunities from close range.
The coach did not place the blame solely on execution or the Steelers' defense. By acknowledging his own role, Steichen made clear that the solution must involve both better decisions from the sideline and better execution on the field, not one or the other.
The red zone offense will be an area to watch in Week 6. The Colts don't have a red zone problem, at least not yet, and Sunday's performance showed how quickly stalled drives can quickly turn into a larger issue.
Colts' Offense Asking Too Much of Spencer Shrader
Spencer Shrader did everything Indianapolis could have asked of him against Pittsburgh. The kicker connected on all five field-goal attempts, tying a franchise record for field goals made in a game. Yet his production could not compensate for an offense that repeatedly failed to reach the end zone.
Running back Jonathan Taylor recognized the value of Shrader's performance but also emphasized that the offense must do more to support its special teams.
“That's definitely a lot to put on [Spencer] Shrader. We know, obviously, he's been playing amazing. But that's not something you want to keep putting on him...We want to play complementary football. Special teams has been doing a great job, like we just talked about with Shrader, but offense has to do their part as well.”
Taylor's comments reinforce the point Steichen made about the red zone, but they also offer a different perspective. The running back praised Shrader while acknowledging that the offense cannot continue asking its kicker to bail them out.
That admission carries additional weight after a difficult afternoon for Taylor himself. He finished with 45 rushing yards on 15 carries, averaging just 3.0 yards per attempt.
The Colts need more consistent production from their offense, particularly when drives reach scoring territory. Shrader has shown he can deliver points, but Indianapolis can't rely on field goals to win games
Pierce's Absence Looms Large
It's been rough sledding for the Colts' passing game without Alec Pierce, whose ability to stretch the field gives Indy a dimension that is difficult to replicate. With Pierce unavailable, quarterback Daniel Jones was asked about the team's ability to generate downfield opportunities.
Jones acknowledged that Pierce brings a special skill set while emphasizing that the offense must find other ways to threaten defenses vertically.
“He's one of the best in the league getting the ball down the field. So, yeah, (we've) got to find ways to do it and find opportunities. The red zone stuff, go back and look at the tape and see where we may have had opportunities to get the ball down the field.”
Jones finished with 267 passing yards, completing 24 of 44 attempts. He did not throw a touchdown, however, and Indianapolis struggled to convert yardage to points.
Pierce's absence does not explain every problem from Sunday, particularly the failures in the red zone. Still, Jones' comments suggest the Colts' passing attack is capped without their primary deep-ball option.
It's on the coaching staff and Jones to identify new ways to create down the field.
Jones Wants Downs More Involved
Josh Downs' involvement is another question for an Indianapolis passing game that looked sloppy on Sunday. Downs finished with just three catches for 47 yards.
Jones was asked about the receiver's role and the challenges of getting him the ball, acknowledging that defenses are particularly aware of Downs on third down. But he also took responsibility for finding ways to get the receiver more involved.
"I think they're certainly aware of him, particularly on third down," Jones said. "So, I think that's another thing that I'll go back and look at where I can be better, and where there may be opportunities to get him the ball.”
Jones' response is useful because he did not suggest that Downs' limited production was solely the result of defensive attention and is instead an opportunity for Jones to self-evaluate and figure out how to get more out of Downs.
Indianapolis needs answers when defenses hone in on their top receiving threat. That could mean finding Downs in different situations, adjusting how the offense creates opportunities or making better use of the openings that are available.
Jones' comments are not an admission of a major disconnect between him and Downs. They do, however, identify a matchup the Colts need to evaluate as they look to make their passing game more productive.
Colts Have a Tackling Problem
The offensive struggles were not the Colts' only concern in Pittsburgh. Indianapolis was also plagued by horrendous tackling problems, which helped Steelers' running back Jaylen Warren score twice on big plays.
After the game, Steichen was asked about the recurring tackling issues and acknowledged that the team needed to take a closer look at the problem.
“It's something we've got to look at hard for sure," he said. "We do tackling drills every day in practice, individuals. We've just got to hammer it home.”
Steichen's response, particularly the detail about tackling being emphasized in every practice, raises concerns. The coach did not offer a specific explanation for the missed tackles, instead emphasizing the need to reinforce fundamentals, and doesn't seem to have any idea of how to move forward.
With another divisional game approaching, improving the defense's ability to finish plays will be just as important as cleaning up the offensive mistakes.
Colts' Ground Game Hits a Wall
The Colts' inability to establish a consistent ground game added another challenge to an offense that struggled to finish drives. Taylor managed just 45 rushing yards on 15 carries, and Indianapolis finished with 66 rushing yards as a team.
With Pittsburgh limiting the ground attack, Jones was asked how the offense adjusts when the run game is not producing the results Indianapolis wants. His answer pointed to a broader responsibility for the entire unit.
“There are games like that," he said "Sometimes the run is working and the pass isn't working as well. Sometimes it's the other way around. So, we've got to be able to handle whatever kind of game it is and find ways to get in the end zone.”

title: Jaguars Injury Report: Updates on Eric Murray, While Rookies Get Dinged Up
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are hoping to get healthier by Sunday.
The Jaguars are facing a number of injury issues before their Week 6 battle with the Houston Texans, and that was even before Wednesday's injury report was released to start the week.
The Jaguars had two players miss Wednesday's practice with long snapper Ross Matiscik (shoulder) and cornerback Montaric Brown (hamstring). The Jaguars signed new long snapper Jacob Bobenmoyer to the practice squad this week to give them a chance to have a full-time option at the position after Matiscik got hurt early in last week's game against the Eagles.
Brown missed Week 4 with a hamstring injury before returning last week against the Eagles. Brown played just six snaps last week , however, before leaving the game, making it clear that he is still not 100%. As things stand today, it would appear the Jaguars are on track to miss Brown when they line up against the Texans on Sunday.
As for those who were limited on Sunday, the Jaguars had Tight end Nate Boerkircher (back), right tackle Cole Van Lanen (knee), rookie guard Emmanuel Pregnon (toe), cornerback Jarrian Jones (elbow), cornerback Jourdan Lewis (hamstring), cornerback Jaylon Jones (hamstring) and safety Eric Murray (concussion).
Jones, Lewis, and Jaylon Jones were all limited last week, so not big updates there. Murray was also limited for most of last week's practices, though he did miss Sunday's game against the Eagles following a sustained concussion in Week 4 against the Cincinnati Bengals. The Jaguars started Rayuan Lane in his place, while former practice squad safety Kaevon Merriweather also got a big boost in playing time.
“Yeah, I think we'll see today and tomorrow, be able to see him run around a little bit, see what that looks like, hopeful. But he hasn't been able to do a ton since last week," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said before practice on Wednesday from the United Kingdom.
"Eric just brings a calming confidence. Obviously, the communication being at a premium, it helps take some stuff off Antonio [S Antonio Johnson] as well, which I thought Antonio really stepped up last week and had one of his best games as a Jaguar in terms of just the playmaking, but also the communication and getting us right back there. It's great to have Eric. He's a competitor, he's physical, he brings a standard to everything that we do in the back end, and obviously he's playing against his former team.”
On top of the Murray injury, the Jaguars also saw two rookies added to the injury report in tight end Nate Boerkircher (back) and offensive lineman Emmanuel Pregnon (toe). Boerkircher and Pregnon have each been critical to the Jaguars' success on the running game and in 12 personnel this season, with Pregnon starting all five games at left guard and Boerkircher serving as a significant addition to the rushing attack.
Against a physical, edge-setting defense like the Texans, the Jaguars need as many maulers as they can get. These are two key players to watch this week.

title: 3 Critical Questions Facing Jaguars Against the Texans in Week 5: Are Walker Little, Cole Van Lanen Ready?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have a big, big week ahead of them.
The Jaguars open their AFC South slate in Week 6 against the Houston Texans , and it gives them a chance to put the Texans four games back entering the bye week. If the Jaguars don't succeed, though, they are opening the door wide open for the Texans to crawl back into the thick of things.
So, what are the most critical questions facing the Jaguars after their latest win? We break it down below.
The players with the biggest challenges on Sunday are clearly Jaguars offensive tackles Walker Little and Cole Van Lanen. The Texans pose one of the NFL's best pass-rush duos with Will Anderson Jr., who had three sacks a week ago, and Danielle Hunter. The question now is whether the Jaguars will be ready for the challenge of the best edge rushers they have played to date.
According to Next GenStats, "Anderson Jr. has recorded 7.5 sacks this season, the most in the NFL, and is the only edge rusher with at least five pressures in every game this season. Anderson has also recorded 12 run stops this season, tied for the second-most among edge rushers. He is the first edge rusher since Lorenzo Alexander in 2016 with at least seven sacks and 10 run stops through Week 5 .Danielle Hunter has been chipped 49 times this season, the most among edge rushers, yet has generated 21 pressures (10th most) with three resulting in turnovers, also the most in the league."
The Texans' pass-rushing duo is the top reason the Jaguars did not sweep the Texans a year ago. Now, the Jaguars will need to prevent them from setting a tone early and disrupting the Jaguars' passing game and offense in general.
While CJ Stroud's pure numbers may not be eye-popping, it is clear that he is playing good football right now. He is doing it despite the Texans once again having a woeful running game. This should be the type of game that the Jaguars' run defense is able to dominate like they have in recent weeks, forcing the game into Stroud's hands. Stroud and Nico Collins are the Texans' two best players on offense so they would likely have done that anyways, but shutting down the Texans against the run is how the Jaguars can build their advantages against the pass with longer down-and-distances.
According to NextGenStats, "The Texans have averaged 3.2 yards per designed run this season, the fewest in the NFL, and have posted a 30.4% success rate on designed runs, the second lowest.
 The Jaguars have allowed 2.9 yards per designed run this season, the fewest in the NFL and the fewest by any team through Week 5 since the 2023 Seahawks (2.7), and have allowed a first down on 15.6% of designed runs, the lowest rate."
In short, the Jaguars don't allow anything on the ground, and the Texans can't run the ball worth a lick. The Texans' running game did run the ball for 130 yards in Week 10 last year, though, which amounted to the second-most rushing yards an Anthony Campanile has allowed and the second-highest EPA/Rush. The Jaguars need to make sure this doesn't repeat.
If there is one single player in the NFL who has terrorized the Jaguars over the years, it is Houston Texans wide receiver Nico Collins. In nine career games against the Jaguars, Collins has caught 51 passes for 734 yards and three touchdowns. But over the last two years is when a bulk of that production has happened, with Collins caught 35 passes for 520 yards (14.85 yards per catch) and two of those touchdowns. That averages out to 8.75 catches and 130 yards per game against the Jaguars over the last two seasons.
So, what do the Jaguars do against the Texans and Collins this time? It seems unlikely the Jaguars will be with Montaric Brown against the Texans, which means Travis Hunter and Jarrian Jones will be the two corners tasked with slowing down Collins. The Jaguars do not really follow their cornerbacks, which means Collins will get reps against each. According to NextGenStats, "Travis Hunter has lined up at field cornerback on 75.2% of his 234 defensive snaps this season, while Jarrian Jones has lined up at boundary cornerback on 65.3% of his snaps."
While it is easy to say "Hunter should follow Collins" on paper, that doesn't mean it is quite as easy to execute. I think the Jaguars will simply ask for Hunter and Jones to play their games and match up to Collins with the best of their ability, just like they have against each top receivers they have played this season.

title: 3 Most Important Things Jaguars' Liam Coen Said About Week 6's Texans Matchup
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The AFC South race is about to heat up.
The Jacksonville Jaguars will kick off the first of six AFC South games this season in Week 6, facing the Houston Texans in the second of their pair of London games. The Texans have long been seen as the greatest theat to the Jaguars in the AFC South, and this battle comes a year after the Jaguars posted their best record against the AFC South in franchise history in 2025 (5-1). The Jaguars split the season series against the Texans last year, and each of their last five games have been decided by one score.
“We had two really tight games against them. Obviously, have a have a tough feeling in our stomachs from the last time we played against these guys," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Wednesday from the United Kingdom. "Know that every time that you line up against this team, it's going to be a fight. It's going to be a brawl. That's what's great about football, that's what's great about rivalries, is that you have a level of respect for each other."
So, what are the most important things Coen had to say about the battle in his first remarks on Houston on Wednesday? We break it down below.
The Texans' 1-4 start certainly was not expected by anybody considering most picked the Texans to win the AFC South entering the year. It has instead been the Jaguars who have opened the season on fire with a 4-1 start that, frankly, should be 5-0 were it not for a blown second-half in Denver. The Jaguars are higher across the board in rankings and metrics, but the Jaguars know they can not take this game lightly.
Two of the the five worst games of the Coen-era in terms of offensive EPA/Play came against the Texans last year: the Week 3 17-10 win is the fourth-worst, while the 36-29 loss to the Texans in Week 10 was the worst offensive performance. The mix things up, the Texans now have head coach DeMeco Ryans calling plays on defense instead of defensive coordinator Matt Burke. They had a great game with that set-up against a bad Tennesee Titans team, but it remains to be seen just how much has changed.
“No, it was similar. I mean, they kind of do what they do in a lot of ways. Have historically played a little bit more man coverage against us at times, to kind of take some of the air out, I think, and not give as much free access and challenge us a little bit on the perimeter," Coen said Wednesday. "He calls what they call, what they do. Their whole deal is built on the front, the rush, the way that they fly around and play and their run defense is really good this year right now. They've got a group of guys that have some confidence. Records don't mean anything. We know that in this league and we understand what this team is, what they're about, how they're going to come in and play us. So, this is going to be a test of physical strain, fight, and that's what it's going to be."
Whether the Jaguars' offensive line can hold up against the Texans' front will likely be the biggest storyline of the week, but Coen's comments make it clear that the battle on the outside may be just as important.
It remains to be seen just how large of a role the Texans envision for their new weapon after the Marvin Harrison Jr. trade over the weekend. The Jaguars traded for Jakobi Meyers mid-week last season and he was able to play that Sunday against the Texans, though, so perhaps Harrison will play in some kind of capacity. Harrison was disappointing in Arizona after being a top-five selection, but the Texans are clearly expecting plenty out of him after what they sent to Arizona.
So, how do the Jaguars prepare for a player who has not yet taken a snap for the Texans? Coen addressed that Wednesday, noting that the study has already been done on Harrison and how he may be used in Houston, though there will still be the element of the unknown until the ball actually gets snapped.
“We showed some of Marvin's clips today in terms of what he's been able to do in Arizona, maybe what areas of the field they may try to use him. It's probably going to be hard to get him into a full game plan, but shoot, we did it with Jakobi [WR Jakobi Meyers] last year, and I know Marvin's smart and he works hard," Coen said.
"So, I would imagine that he's going to be a part of their game plan and C.J. and him have a lot of chemistry and history together. There's some unknown to truly how they'll use him, but their system, they kind of run what they do, and they put the guys in positions to make plays and I think Marvin will probably be no different that way.”
The Jaguars have frequently seen Nico Collins have major days against their secondary, and slowing him down has to be the first priority. But the Jaguars can also not overlook Harrison and the impact he might have on the Texans' offense out of the gate.
The Jaguars had some absolutely brutal moments in the red-zone last week. The Jaguars went 0-for-3 on converting red-zone trips to touchdowns, which included two different trips where they had the ball on the Eagles' one-yard line on first down and didn't score. They got outright stopped on the first of those two drives, but the second one included a comedy of errors as false starts and a delay of game doomed the Jaguars before a fourth-down turnover on downs.
It remains to be seen if the Jaguars will run into the same problems on Sunday that they did against the Eagles considering most were self-inflicted. But the Jaguars will have to ensure their operation is much cleaner tis week when the stakes are even higher. Coen noted Wednesday that part of the solution falls on him as a play-caller.
“That was probably one of the louder atmospheres I've been in a while, especially in those critical moments, to where, hey guys, I can help you out with my play call," Coen said.
"Maybe shorten it up, trim the verbiage or call something a little bit more simplified down there where it was in that end zone specifically that got loud, and some of those critical downs. So, I showed the players and coaches a ton of clips of the TV copy, different versions of it to show them, look, we broke the huddle with eight seconds. That's not giving you a chance. That's not giving you guys the best chance to succeed, and that's directly on me."

title: What the Jaguars' Week 5 Win Changed About Its Trade Deadline Plans
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- When it comes to the needs facing each NFL squad entering Week 1, few things are written down in stone.
The early-season results can change what a team needs week-to-week, whether because of unexpected winning or losing streaks, injuries, or star players becoming available. Such is the case for the Jacksonville Jaguars in the wake of Week 5 with several weeks to go before the trade deadline.
So, how did the Jaguars' Week 5 win over the Philadelphia Eagles impact the Jaguars and their potential trade deadline plans? We break it down below.
The biggest concern facing the Jaguars right now is undoubtedly the left tackle situation after the injury to Anton Harrison. The Jaguars' starting left tackle was placed on injured reserve Tuesday after being carted off the field with a knee injury in the third-quarter of Week 5, and it still remains to be seen whether is out for a few weeks or out for the entire season. The answer to that question could be what ultimately sets the tone for the Jaguars' trade deadline plans.
“We'll just figure it out when we get back. You guys saw last night that when we get back, he'll have a little procedure; see what it looks like in there. Don't have any new news on what it could really look like until we get in there," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Wednesday.
The Jaguars are set to start Walker Little at left tackle against the Houston Texans in Week 6's battle in London, and that easily could be the Jaguars' plan moving forward. But if Little struggles and Harrison is out for the season, the Jaguars might find it worth it to examine the offensive tackle market. This would not have been even close to being a thought before Harrison's injury, but the onus is now on Little (and Cole Van Lanen) to make sure the Jaguars don't have to go that route.
It still feels unlikely that the Jaguars would make a move considering the depth they have with backup offensive linemen Wyatt Milum, Daniel Faalele, and eventually Patrick Mekari, but this is one spot that now at least deserves some consideration when it comes to the trade deadline plans. The Jaguars' offensive line has been up-and-down throughout the 2026 season so far, and we will see starting in Week 6 how the unit responds to Harrison's injury.
"Anytime you lose a player for a game, it's always a challenge, but I have a lot of confidence in Walker [OL Walker Little] and Cole [OL Cole Van Lanen] to go in there. And these guys have played these guys so many times and have had success against them and know what they're in for in terms of the battle and next man up mentality," Coen said.
The next spot to watch is, of course, Brian Thomas Jr. It did not make much sense for the Jaguars to consider moving Thomas in the offseason, but things have changed since then. We already knew that Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers were likely to be ahead of him on the depth chart, but the Jaguars have now also added rookie wide receiver Josh Cameron to the mix and Cameron has out-produced Thomas through five games despite playing a much smaller role.
With Cameron now in place and thriving, perhaps the Jaguars reconsider. Sunday was the first game in Thomas' career that he did not register a catch, and he has just three catches over the last three games. He has become a smaller and smaller part of the offense as the season has gone on, but that does not mean he doesn't offer plenty of value on the trade market if the Jaguars deem him a player they want to move on from.
The Marvin Harrison Jr. trade offers a good baseline for any potential Thomas trade, too. Until we see Thomas as a sustained piece of the Jaguars' offense for an extended period of time, his name is going to continue to come up when it comes to potential trade deadline plans. Thomas is a talented player, but his lack of production mixed with the Jaguars' depth at wide receiver makes this something to watch for the second year in a row.

title: Week 6 NFL Power Rankings Roundup: Jaguars Take Over the Consensus Top-5
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are 4-1 entering arguably their biggest week of the season so far, which gives them more and more room to keep rising.
After their 19-17 win over the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5, the Jaguars are currently tied with the Buffalo Bills and the Baltimore Ravens for the second-best record in the AFC, behind only the 4-0 Kansas City Chiefs. So after their latest win, where do the Jaguars land in the latest power rankings across the NFL? We break it down below.
The only team ranked ahead of the Jaguars are the 49ers, which makes a ton of sense. The Jaguars are clearly a better overall team than the Minnesota Vikings, while the Chiefs are just one spot behind the Jaguars. Jacksonville and the 49ers have been the two best teams this year on a snap-to-snap basis.
These are the rankings the Jaguars have climbed the highest in since Week 1. A win against the Texans in London and entering the bye week with a 5-1 record would likely go a long way to not just keeping the Jaguars in the top-5 for the long-term, but also help them rise higher and higher. The Texans were their preseason AFC South darlings, and the Jaguars can make them eat those words with a win in Week 6 against their AFC South rivals.
I get that the Vikings are undefeated, and they do have a special defense right now. But their offense is still miles away from the Jaguars' offense, and that has to be factored in somehow and in some fashion. The Jaguars' offense has gotten in its own way in the last two weeks, but it is a much better unit right now than Minnesota's is.
The Jaguars have a rightful place in the top-5 here, though the analysis on Liam Coen's fourth down attempts seems off. Coen did not go on multiple red-zone fourth downs last week because of "analytics." His long-snapper was hurt, which led to the Jaguars having to approach each red-zone series with a different outlook.
Three of the four teams ahead of the Jaguars this week are the NFL's three final undefeated teams with the Kansas City Chiefs, San Francisco 49ers, and Minnesota Vikings. The only other team ranked ahead of the Jaguars is the Buffalo Bills on the heels of their overtime win against the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night. The Bills and Josh Allen beat the Jaguars in the wild card a year ago, but the Bills lost to a Patriots team a few weeks ago who the Jaguars destroyed.
The top two undefeated teams are understandably ranked ahead of the Jaguars, but then so are the Seattle Seahawks and Baltimore Ravens. The Jaguars will get their battle with the Ravens later in the season, while the Seahawks lost a close game to the 49ers but also lost to a bad Washington Commanders team earlier in the season. It feels like they should be behind the Jaguars right now.
This is the only ranking that has seen the Jaguars take a step back this week. Part of that is likely due to the fact the Jaguars did not play their best football against the Eagles last week. But it also had the Ravens leapfrogging the Jaguars after their unlikely overtime Sunday Night Football win against the Falcons without Lamar Jackson.
The only two teams above the Jaguars here are the undefeated 49ers and Chiefs. The Jaguars are slotted one spot ahead of the Buffalo Bills, which seems fair. The Bills did beat the Jaguars in the Wild Card last year with mostly the same squads, so it would also be fair to give the Bills an edge. But right now, the Jaguars seem to have played better team football week-to-week

title: 3 Overreactions to Jaguars' Week 5 Win Over Eagles: The London Impact
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are ready to turn the page to an important Week 6 contest with the Houston Texans, but there is a chance for one final look at Week 5 and what it could mean moving forward.
The Jaguars managed to squeak out a 19-17 win over the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5, but it was a last-second win that nearly became a brutal loss for Liam Coen's squad.
So, what overreactions from the Week 5 win over the Eagles actually have some merit to them? We break it down below.
Listen, everyone understands why the Jaguars are playing two games in London this season. And if the Jaguars play multiple games there in 2027 while their "home" games are played in Orlando, people will understand that to. But the Eagles contest was the latest example of why the Jaguars should be ready to dump the annual London trips once their new stadium is complete and ready to host fans for the 2028 season.
This was an Eagles home game if it was anything else. London trips are already tough enough with the way they disrupt the Jaguars' weekly routine and force such a long trip overseas. But this game was a very real example of how it can disrupt the Jaguars even further, with the Jaguars having several red-zone trips seemingly impacted by the loud Eagles crowd. London was already a chore, but this week it worked against the Jaguars and created a negative impact inside the game.
It is hard to be surprised by anything that Josh Cameron does anymore. The sixth-round rookie looked very impressive in the offseason program ... and then he did the same thing in training camp. He made a nice play for his first touchdown catch in Week 1 ... and then he just kept making plays. It has not been a flash in the pan in any regard, and it feels like it might be time to start increasing his role in the offense.
“He's been awesome. I think he's really stood out since training camp when we got really competitive. Got a chance to see him go up and make some crazy catches and win some one-on-ones. Obviously, the physical ability is there, but the way he plays, if you watch the tape, he attacks," Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence said last week.
"Whether it's run game, pass game, every route, he's running it to win. Every time he has a chance to block someone, he's trying to put them in the ground. There's so many examples where you watch him play and that's how you want our guys to play. And I think our guys do play that way, but he's just another great example of that. I'm just happy for him. He's always in the right spot, knows what to do. He works extremely hard, has earned every opportunity, and is just taking it and running with it. He's been awesome for us.”
As things stand today, Cameron ranks fourth amongst Jaguars in receivers in total routes and snaps, but it feels like there could be more and more ways to get him on the field. He has impressed with a limited snap-share, and it is time to see if he can continue that production on a down-to-down basis.
The Jaguars are certainly facing some injury issues as they enter Week 6, but one injury that could quietly be a big deal is cornerback Montaric Brown. He missed the Week 4 game against the Cincinnati Bengals due to a hamstring injury, but managed to return in Week 5 against the Eagles. Brown played just six snaps against the Eagles, though, and it is fair to say that he is clearly still working his way back.
Sunday is a key game for the Jaguars, but they badly need Brown at 100%. They are better off letting him sit this game out and then use the extra week from the bye week to try to get right, because it could end up paying dividends down the road. Brown is a good player who is dealing with a tough injury, and the Jaguars should give him a bit of a runway.

title: 3 Observations on Jaguars' Post-Eagles Roster Moves: Anton Harrison and Kaevon Merriweather Impacts
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars made a couple of roster moves Tuesday, each of which could have a profound impact on the next few weeks of the season.
Along with the signing of long snapper Jacob Bobenmoyer to the practice squad, the Jaguars also signed safety Kaevon Merriweather to the active roster of the practice squad, as well as placed left tackle Anton Harrison on injured reserve.
So, what do we make of each move and what it means moving forward, especially in the wake of the latest Anton Harrison update ? We break it down below.
Between this move and last week's usage at the safety position, the Jaguars are making it fairly clear where they stand on the safety pecking order. Until it changes during a game, it certainly appears the Jaguars' answer during Eric Murray's time out is for Rayuan Lane and Merriweather to be the No. 2 and No. 3 safeties behind Antonio Johnson, leaving third-round rookie Jalen Huskey on the sidelines. This was how the Jaguars approached Week 5, with Huskey logging zero snaps on defense as a result.
"But it'd be great to get Eric [S Eric Murray] back, hopefully, but if not, have a lot of confidence. I thought Kaevon [Merriweather] had a great week of practice, and did some nice things in the game," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Monday. "I thought Ray [S Rayuan Lane III] did some nice things in the game. There's communication that's always going to exist when you have to play with some other guys. They stepped up, helped us win the game.”
We have a smaller sample size with Merriweather than with Lane, but this will be a situation to watch moving forward if Murray continues to miss time. But as things stand today, it is clear how the dust has settled.
The Jaguars' injured reserve list sure is growing longer. The Jaguars have now placed two key players on injured reserve in back-to-back weeks with Harrison and second-year safety Caleb Ransaw a week ago, with second-year defensive end BJ Green II also being placed on injured reserve after Week 1. This follows the Jaguars placing offensive lineman Patrick Mekari and defensive end Zach Durfee on injured reserve ahead of the start of the season.
Outside of Durfee, these are all critical players the Jaguars were set to lean on in some fashion this year, whether it be as starters or top depth options. The Jaguars have been mostly healthy, but the injuries have piled up over the last few weeks, and now so is the injured reserve list as a result of them.
With Harrison out for the next four games at least, the earliest he could return is in Week 11 against the New York Giants (if he is able to return at all). It is pretty clear that the Jaguars are set to place Walekr Little back in the left tackle spot that he once occupied, with Little playing quite well against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5 during the second-half. But what about the swing tackle spot that Little used to hold?
Second-year offensive lineman Wyatt Milum is set to likely to step into the swing tackle role for the next couple of weeks. The Jaguars could also start having offensive lineman Daniel Faalele active and could turn to him as a swing option, while Mekari gives them another option once he comes of the injured reserve.

title: Jaguars Report Card: Grades From Eagles Win Vary From Concerning to Gold Stars
full_text:
In the NFL, all that really matters at the end of the day is the result, and the Jaguars got the one they were looking for in their 19-17 win over the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5.
But which Jaguars position groups shined during the last-second win, and which position groups played a big role in the game being so close to begin with? We break it down with this week's report cards.
Trevor Lawrence was certainly fired up at points during Sunday's game, and it is not hard to see why. For the second week in a row, penalties set Lawrence and the Jaguars up with far too many 2nd- and 3rd-and-longs, which made the offense feel very stop-and-go at times. They did move the ball well largely thanks to Lawrence, though, and he was once again made a handful of throws that it feels like only he is completing. The interception was a bad throw while under pressure, and Lawrence did hold onto the ball a bit too long a few times, but overall this felt like a productive outing from the Jaguars' franchise quarterback.
Despite not getting a lot of efficient production from the running game on Sunday, it still felt like a strong outing from Bhayshul Tuten. He broke a lot of tackles to turn big losses into, at least, neutral plays. It feels like had the Jaguars trust him a bit more in the red-zone, he could have made a difference when it came to converting those trips into touchdowns. Chris Rodriguez Jr. did not do much with his limited touches, though, and it felt like the worst rushing performance of the year as a whole for the team.
Parjer Washington continued to do big, big things for the wide receiver room. Washington was one of the most important pieces of the Jaguars' win over the Eagles thanks to both his touchdowns, while the Jaguars were able to get production out of Jakobi Meyers and Josh Cameron when giving them targets. The only real negative plays were the few targets that Brian Thomas Jr. was not able to come down with.
It was a very productive day from the tight end room, with the Jaguars' duo of Brenton Strange and Nate Boerkircher combining for nine catches for 88 yards on 10 targets. There were a few small miscues, such as a few missed blocks from Boerkircher, a drop from Strange, and Strange leaving his feet near the goal-line. But overall, the Jaguars have gotten much more out of the tight end group as a whole than they did at this same time last season.
The Jaguars did see Walker Little step up i n a big way against the Eagles, pitching a shutout as a pass-blocker in the second-half. Little has often been far underrated amongst circles that discuss the Jaguars, and they will need him now with Anton Harrison injured. Jalen Carter did Jalen Carter things to the Jaguars, but penalties and the lack of production in the run game are what ultimately pull this score down. Carter is an elite player, but eventually the Jaguars' offensive line needs to prove that they can slow down those types of talents.
The Jaguars' defensive line had its best game of the season on Sunday, hands down. Not only did the Jaguars limit the Eagles in the running game completely, but they also sent their pass-rush at Jalen Hurts in waves. The Jaguars disrupted the Eagles' passing game and got Hurts to rush throws or make passes off-platform, with Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker making especially big impacts as pass-rushers. It took a team effort, too, with a number of depth players and blitzers at defensive back and linebacker chipping in, but the defensive line led the way.
I thought the #Jaguars dominated the Eagles OL up front, and that's what all the evidence says. 23 pressures (2nd-most in Week 5) and 54.8% pressure rate (2nd-most.) Both season highs despite Jalen Hurts having the second-quickest time to throw this week pic.twitter.com/OYkc4Pk2jk
Ventrell Miller is genuinely getting better each week. Miller had another stellar performance on Sunday, making several impressive stops both downhill against the run and in the flats as a tackler in space in coverage. Dennis Gardeck and Foyesade Oluokun also made impacts against the run and in the pass-rush, and this is a position group that is simply playing good football right now. Miller looks like a truly ascending player in Anthony Campanile's defense, and this was one of his best games yet.
There were some good things from the cornerback room; Jarrian Jones had a very effective outing, Jourdan Lewis and Antonio Johnson produced against the run and on blitzes, and as a whole the Jaguars tackled well in the back-end. But a 3rd-and-long pass-interference on Travis Hunter that eventually led to a touchdown dings them, as does some of the miscues such as the explosive 62-yard touchdown allowed to Darius Cooper in the first-half.
The only thing that keeps this from being an A+ is the fact that the Jaguars did miss an extra point and did allow a bit too much yardage on returns. But at the same time ... come on. Heath Farwell's unit returned a kick for a touchdown before a flag nullified it, then Ameer Abdullah set up Cam Little for his game-winning 57-yard field goal. The Jaguars had the better special teams unit on Sunday, and it is a big reason they won.
This felt like one of the oddest Jaguars games from a management and game-plan standpoint in some time. I do not blame Liam Coen for going for it on fourth downs due to the snap issues with Davon Hamilton and high snaps, but Coen also allowed an extra point attempt that looked like it was missed largely due to the snap. Why not be consistent? Coen also said Monday he took responsibility for a delay of game in the red-zone. Throwing the ball on second down on the four-minute drive was also an odd choice. As for the defense, I thought Anthony Campanile made great adjustments in second-half, but the first-half plan of man-blitzes was always a bad idea against Jalen Hurts, and he made them pay for it.

title: Jack Kiser Has Officially Become the New Jaguars Regime's First Draft Bust
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' new era officially has their first draft miss.
The Jaguars saw former linebacker Jack Kiser get claimed on waivers on Monday by the Cincinnati Bengals, reuniting the former Jaguars fourth-rounder with his former Notre Dame defensive coordinator Al Golden. And as a result, the Jaguars have their first draft bust of the Liam Coen/James Gladstone/Tony Boselli era.
The Jaguars drafted Kiser with the No. 107th pick in the fourth-round of the 2025 NFL Draft, tacking Kiser just a few picks after they took running back Bhayshul Tuten at No. 104 overall. But while Tuten has turned into a key piece of what the Jaguars do a year later, Kiser never quite was able to get the same footing during his short time with the Jaguars.
Kiser was a reserve for the Jaguars as a rookie, with the former Notre Dame linebacker appear in 14 games as a backup last season. He recorded 14 tackles as a rookie, playing 43 snaps on defense and 193 snaps (53%) on special teams. But Kiser was dealt a tough blow at the start of training camp in his sophmore season, going down with a knee injury during team drills on the first day of practice.
Kiser never practiced for the Jaguars again during camp, and the Jaguars ended up waiving him after camp before signing him to the practice squad. Kiser was eventually elevated from the practice squad and signed back to the active roster earlier this season, but he never ended up appearing in a game for the Jaguars this season.
The Jaguars then waived him for a second time this weekend as they made a slew of roster moves before their Week 5 game against the Philadelphia Eagles, with the Jaguars instead signing fellow 2025 draftee Jalen McLeod from the practice squad to the active roster.
No matter what Kiser ends up doing for the Bengals, this can now be classified as the new Jaguars regime's first miss. He is the first of 19 draft picks over the last two seasons to play for a new team, and the Jaguars essentially picked McLeod over him this weekend. The Jaguars also picked veteran backup linebacker Jahlani Tavai over Kiser at the end of training camp, and that stance clearly hasn't changed.
Kiser was dealt a tough hand with injuries, but the fact the Jaguars never seemed to entertain the idea of him battling for a starting spot with Ventrell Miller and Branson Combs after the departure of Devin Lloyd in free agency indicated that this was a pick they felt comfortable moving on from after a season. It is better to pull the plug on a pick too early as opposed to too late, but this was an even tougher miss considering stud Buffalo Bills defensive tackle Deone Walker was taken just a few picks later.
The Jaguars do not seem to have any other 2025 picks in danger of falling into the same category as Kiser anytime soon. McLeod was in the same boat as Kiser just a few weeks ago, but he has impressed in a big way on special teams and has seemed to at least carved out a role there for now. The returns on third-rounders Caleb Ransaw and Wyatt Milum has yet to be there, but they are not close to being off the roster outright like Kiser.
He will not be the last draft pick the Jaguars miss on, but for the new regime he is officially their first.

title: Anton Harrison Injury Update: Latest On Jaguars' Blindside Protector
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are facing their biggest injury concern of their 2026 season.
The Jaguars saw left tackle Anton Harrison get carted off the field during the third-quarter of Week 5's win over the Philadelphia Eagle s, and the latest status update has provided a best -- and a worst -- case scenario.
NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported Tuesday morning that Harrison will undergo arthroscopic knee surgery, during which a doctor will determine exactly how long the talented and valuable offensive tackle will be out. According to Rapoport, "Depending on what the surgeon sees during the procedure, Anton Harrison is either out 3-5 weeks (likely IR) or 3-4 months (out for the regular season).
"
#Jaguars starting LT Anton Harrison, starter since 2023, is expected to undergo arthroscopic knee surgery when he returns from London, per me and @JFowlerESPN . During the surgery, the doctor will determine how long Trevor Lawrence’s blindside protector is out — weeks or months. pic.twitter.com/euMcFlKvBa
It is hard to call this either good news or bad news, it really just depends on what the medical team determines when it comes to the severity of his knee injury. There are other examples of players sustaining the injury, such as Myles Garrett earlier this season. Garrett is on injured-reserve but is expected to return for the Los Angeles Rams at some point this season. But until there is a final determination on his status, it is tough to say how one should feel.
The fact that Harrison at least has a chance to potentially return is at least some solace. The Jaguars play a tough Houston Texans team this week before a Week 7 bye. Harrison will clearly miss this week, and if he is placed on injured reserve this week the soonest he would be able to return would be Week 11 against the New York Giants on the road.
Not having Harrison on hand against the Texans is clearly not ideal, though the Jaguars did see backup left tackle Walker Little step up along with the rest of the offensive line against the Eagles when Harrison was injured.
"Walker [OL Walker Little] stepping in, obviously, those guys fighting through. Just playing hard. It's hard in there, and they're playing a good group. And I felt like they just stuck with it. I thought protection-wise, for the most part of the day, I didn't think it was too bad," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Monday.
"We held on on the ball a little bit long on a few when we did get the strip sacks and I thought we just settled down a little bit more in the second half as a group, and they played hard. They played their tails off. That's a damn good front. It's one of the bigger fronts that we'll see.  Obviously, will have a huge challenge again this week with another good front."
If the Jaguars can get Harrison back within the next month and a half or so, they could have him back on the field for a critical second-half stretch to secure the AFC South over the Texans. But if he is out for the season, then the Jaguars have the depth to sustain the hit, but will still clearly feel the loss of their talented left tackle.

title: Chiefs Preaching 'Trust' Despite Unproven WR Options After Losing Tyquan Thornton
full_text:
With the NFL trade deadline still weeks away but a need at the wide receiver position being present right now, the Kansas City Chiefs find themselves in a strange spot. Coming out of a Week 5 bye, Andy Reid's team hasn't made any major additions to boost the ceiling of the room.
Perhaps the acquisition of Justin Watson can elevate the floor, but there's ample reason to be skeptical of such a prospect. The club whiffed on or simply didn't express enough interest in moving for new Houston Texans pass catcher Marvin Harrison Jr., so the in-house options will be rolled with until the next domino falls.
With no Tyquan Thornton on the field for the foreseeable future, who should Kansas City turn to as a long-term replacement? Is it one player or multiple? Speaking to the media on Wednesday, Reid expressed that he has faith in each person on the depth chart.
"That's the way things worked out for Tyquan," Reid said. "He was having a very good year, and I'm sad to see what happened to him because of that. And he's a great kid on top of all that. But one man's loss is another man's opportunity to jump in and do that. Whoever that might be that's got the call, if they make the play, then that's a positive. But I have trust in all the guys, and Xavier (Worthy) is still in there, too. He's coming off a couple of good catches the last couple of games."
Subtracting Thornton from the equation leaves KC with Worthy, Rashee Rice, first-year man Cyrus Allen, second-year man Jalen Royals, Nikko Remigio and Watson as the main non-tight end targets. Complicating things is that Rice suffered a hamstring injury early in Week 4's win over the Las Vegas Raiders and isn't practicing right after the bye . That leaves his status for Week 6 in question, thus underscoring how dire things could be for the Chiefs.
Can a cast of some shaky vets and the intriguing-but-quiet rookie get the job done versus the Los Angeles Chargers this weekend? Quarterback Patrick Mahomes echoed the same sentiment as Reid, saying his message to the Chiefs' wideouts is nothing but belief.
"It's that they're ready," Mahomes said. "They've put in the work. Obviously, we've had guys in front of them with Tyquan going out there playing great football. They've had to put in the work at practice, and they've been doing that and doing that. Now their number gets called, and they're going to step up to the role and do their job. I'm excited for them. We'll put them in positions to succeed. I have a lot of trust in those guys — a lot of confidence in them — so we'll just continue to push it forward."
Through four games, Worthy is tied for the team lead in targets with 22. He tops the wideout collective with 14 receptions, although both Thornton (219) and Rice (190) who have more yards. Royals' stat line is just three catches for 17 yards; Allen has two targets but no receptions on all of 10 offensive snaps.
If Kansas City has a high-scoring offensive output without Thornton and potentially minus Rice, it'll have to stem from someone like Worthy and perhaps an unsung hero stepping up. With the expectation and standard set at practice, Mahomes thinks the depth is prepared.
"It's going to make it easier for them," Mahomes said. "When you're kind of getting thrown in, you never know which position you're going to be at and what route you're going to be on. It's hard. That's part of playing in the NFL, you don't get those reps that you necessarily would've had in college and high school and stuff like that."

title: Josh Simmons Returns to Practice, Rashee Rice's Status Uncertain for Week 6
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs announced a mixed bag of injury news on Wednesday, as two key offensive starters entered Week 6 with injury uncertainty.
Beginning his Wednesday media availability, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid provided an update on wide receiver Rashee Rice (hamstring) and left tackle Josh Simmons (back).
"As far as the injuries go, Rashee will be the only one that doesn't go today," Reid said. "Everybody else is scheduled to do something."
Reid's statement means that Simmons will return to practice in some capacity on Wednesday, marking his first return to the field since mid-August, when he suffered a back injury late in training camp .
On September 30, Reid explained that Simmons has been dealing with a bulging disc in his lower back, which had "kind of hindered the strength of his leg," according to Reid.
On Wednesday, Reid clarified that Simmons still has some hurdles to clear before fully returning.
"We're just gonna ease him back in," Reid said. "Ease him into practice. He's gonna practice, but it'll be on a limited basis."
In Simmons' absence, undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson has played left tackle, while veteran Jaylon Moore has remained on the right side. Reid was asked what the plan would be at right tackle when Simmons returns.
"I haven't even gone there," Reid said. "I'm just glad that [Simmons] is having a chance to come back, for sure. You start dealing with backs, you've got to ease it back in if you can get back in at all, so we'll just see how he does. So I haven't really even gone there. I know [Simmons] has wanted to get back out there, and this is the first step of that."
Rice exited the Chiefs' Week 4 matchup with the Las Vegas Raiders due to a hamstring injury that ultimately sidelined him for the rest of the game.
On Wednesday, Reid was asked if he anticipated Rice returning to practice later this week
"We'll see how it goes," Reid said. "He's actually feeling pretty good as he goes here, so we'll see. Those things, you start dealing with hamstrings, and it could be a week, could be two weeks, you don't know, but I know he's eager to get back in."
The Chiefs are already dealing with one serious injury in the receiver room, as Tyquan Thornton has been placed on injured reserve due to his season-threatening ankle dislocation that he suffered later in the Chiefs' win over the Raiders. As Thornton was placed on IR, the team reunited with veteran receiver Justin Watson , who signed to Kansas City's practice squad.
