title: Rams Make Flurry of Roster Moves as Kicker Blake Grupe Headlines Three Additions
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams announced a handful of roster moves on Wednesday morning. While it was previously r eported that the Rams were signing kicker Blake Grupe off the New York Jets' practice squad, the team made the move official on Wednesday. Additionally, the Rams also signed edge rusher Garrett Nelson and cornerback Damarion Williams. In corresponding moves, the Rams officially released Harrison Mevis from the active roster and outside linebacker Jamie Sheriff from the practice squad.
Given the Rams' struggles on special teams , Grupe is the most significant of the three additions. Grupe has made 81.9 percent of field goals in his career and has made 96-of-98 extra points. Throughout his career, Grupe has made 18 field goals of 40+ yards and 19 field goals of 50+ yards, with a career-long of 60 yards last season against the Seahawks.
“This guy has experience,” said head coach Sean McVay on Tuesday. “He did a great job for Indy last year. He has kicked in a lot of big-time professional settings. We felt like he was the best guy available that had real game experience.”
Grupe competed for the Colts' kicking job this offseason, but Indianapolis ultimately went with Spencer Shrader. While Grupe was steady in training camp, he had two misses during the preseason. The Rams will hope Grupe can add some stability to the position.
Among the other signings was edge rusher Garrett Nelson. Nelson was an undrafted free agent signing out of Nebraska by the Miami Dolphins in 2023. Nelson spent time on the Seahawks ' practice squad earlier this year and was most recently with the Saints. During the preseason with the Saints, Nelson had six pressures and two sacks.
Nelson also played in the UFL for two years as part of the San Antonio Brahmas. With the Brahmas, Nelson had 27 tackles, four tackles for loss, and 2.5 sacks in 19 games played. The Rams have done well developing edge rushers in the past, most recently with Wesley Bailey.
Additionally, the Rams signed cornerback Damarion Williams to give them some depth on the practice squad. Williams was a fourth-round pick by the Baltimore Ravens in 2022. Given Jaylen Watson’s injuries, the Rams need some cornerback depth. Williams spent time with the Seahawks in 2024 and has also been with the Buccaneers over the last two years.
Williams is a smaller cornerback at 5-foot-10 and 180 pounds, with arms measuring less than 30 inches. However, he may bring some special teams value. He played 134 special teams snaps in 2022 as a rookie, but has not played much since.
While Grupe is the most significant addition given the Rams' ongoing special teams struggles, Nelson and Williams provide much-needed depth at two positions impacted by injuries. Neither is likely to make an immediate impact on defense, but both will have an opportunity to develop on the practice squad.

title: Sean McVay Shares Significant Blame for Rams' Disappointing 2-3 Start
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams haven’t started the season in the way that many have expected. Very few would have predicted the Rams to start the season 2-3. If you were to ask anybody what the reasons are for that start, most would point to special teams . While special teams have certainly played a large role, it may be time to look deeper and start pointing a finger at the head coach, Sean McVay.
Now, this isn’t to say that McVay should be on the hot seat or that the Rams should consider firing him. Let’s make that abundantly clear. For whatever role that McVay has had in the Rams’ 2-3 start, he’s still one of the best head coaches in the NFL. The Rams would not be able to do better than McVay.
At the same time, McVay has played a much larger role in the Rams’ 2-3 start than some would like to believe. For once, when McVay points the finger at himself in press conferences, he might actually be right.
Coming into the season, the Rams were scheduled to play Week 1 in Melbourne, Australia against the San Francisco 49ers. Leading up to the game, the Rams sent players and team personnel to Australia before deciding to arrive just over 24 hours before kickoff.
The Rams were criticized for this decision by the media, especially as the 49ers arrived almost a week before the game. While I didn’t have the same resources as the Rams, the data that I gathered from traveling to Australia showed how much of a negative impact that can have on the body. My sleep efficiency in the early days of arriving in Australia dropped almost 30 percentage points.
Yes, it was the same plan that the Rams had taken the previous year when they went to London. However, the Rams spent that week in Baltimore and took a seven-hour flight to London the day before. That’s almost the equivalent of the Rams going from the West Coast to the East Coast. A flight from Los Angeles to Melbourne is almost double what their trip from Baltimore to London was.
The Rams came out sluggish against the 49ers and crashed out by the second half. They allowed 20 unanswered points on their way to a 27-7 loss. Throughout the week and after the game, McVay was adamant that it wasn’t because of the travel plans. With that said, it was clear throughout the game that the Rams were out of sync and lacked cohesiveness.
Following the win over the Giants a week later, McVay finally seemed to admit the misjudgment in the team's travel plans. “Sometimes you win, sometimes you learn. Sometimes you have a dumb ass coach that makes travel plans that put you in a bad spot,” said McVay.
After beating the New York Giants, the Rams headed to Denver to take on a vulnerable Broncos team. The Rams came out hot and took a 16-0 lead into the half. Despite the Rams leading that game by multiple scores, Matthew Stafford came out of it with 55 passing attempts.
McVay seemed to lose control of the game-script. While McVay is typically great with second-half adjustments, he was getting outcoached by adjustments that the Broncos had made. Neither of the Rams’ offensive drives in the third quarter lasted more than five plays. The Rams had minus-six net yards in the third quarter as the Broncos tied the game.
Against the Broncos, the Rams averaged 0.13 EPA per rush with a 47.8 percent success rate and still threw the ball over 50 times as if they had been trailing, not leading by more than 10 points for much of the game. The Rams had a +9.3 pass rate over expected, whic was the fourth-highest for the week.
The only teams ahead of them were the Bengals, Seahawks, and Packers. The Bengals trailed the Steelers for much of their game while the Seahawks and Packers trailed by double digits in their losses. Despite having a lead, McVay let the game-script get away from him.
After a relatively quiet first half against the Bills, the Rams’ offense went into full-on attack mode in the second half, scoring touchdowns on four of their five possessions, including their last three. The Rams trailed by a touchdown late, needing to go 63 yards in just over 1:30 with one timeout. It took 1:29 and the Rams didn’t even use their timeout before they were in the end zone.
When the defense got a turnover in overtime, it seemed like almost a guarantee that the Rams would win the game given how the offense had moved the ball. Early in the drive, they did just that. With 21-yard completions to Davis Allen and Puka Nacua, the Rams were at the 35-yard line.
That’s when McVay got conservative . The Rams threw an incomplete pass from under center before McVay called a screen pass to Nacua and then a run on 3rd-and-5. It was as if he was content with a 48-yard field goal despite having a kicker that had struggled from range. Inside of 45 yards, Mevis had been solid. It was beyond 45 yards where he became more inconsistent.
For the Rams to feel comfortable about a field goal, they likely needed another 10-15 yards. Instead, McVay called a run on 3rd-and-5 that picked up zero yards. Mevis was called on for a field goal that would be blocked.
While it was Mevis who got cut on Tuesday morning, McVay deserves just as much of the blame for that sequence. McVay took the ball out of his MVP quarterback’s hands and instead put the game in the hands of his special teams unit that has consistently come up short this season. After the game, McVay was disgusted with the play call to run on third down.
“I wish I would have had a better play call and gone forward, got it a lot tighter. I'm sick right now with myself,” said McVay. “I'll be regretting kicking that and not having a better call to be able to go forward on third down and go to fourth or whatever it was. That's on me.”
Going into the game, Mevis had been 4-for-6 in his career from beyond 45 yards. He was just 1-for-3 from 48 yards out. By comparison, he had been 19-for-20 from inside of 45 yards. Everything in that moment said that the Rams needed to get closer. On Tuesday, McVay further explained his thought process behind calling a run in that spot.
“I had a thought of something on a third down and five. Then we had a little bit of time to think about it. Didn't want to leave us susceptible to maybe getting a penalty that moved us back,” McVay explained. “I certainly felt like that was the right decision based on some different things. Maybe it wouldn't have been the same call if I didn't have time to, if you want to say, overthink or have a couple of different things that talk to you out of it.”
It’s understandable that McVay wouldn’t want to take a penalty or a negative play in that spot. However, McVay treated the game as if it was over, when it wasn’t. Had the Rams had the ball at the 20-yard line instead of the 30, a run may have made more sense. Running into the middle of the Bills’ defensive line when the offense had a 39.1 percent rushing success rate was a questionable decision.
For much of the McVay era, the Rams have been one of the more disciplined teams in the NFL. In 2016 under Jeff Fisher, the Rams were the fifth-most penalized team. When McVay took over in 2017, they were the 13th-most penalized team. By 2020, the Rams were the third-least penalized team in the league. Last year, they were also the third-least penalized team.
There is a lot of room for interpretation for whistles that happen between the snaps. However, pre-snap penalties are a reflection of mental and coaching discipline. In 2016 under Fisher, the Rams had the seventh-most pre-snap penalties. That improved to 13th in 2017 and in 2018, they were the 12th-least penalized team pre-snap. For the most part, that’s where they’ve been under McVay.
Over the last three years, the Rams have been among the five least-penalized teams in the NFL when it comes to pre-snap penalties. They already have 13 pre-snap penalties this season and are the seventh-most penalized team in the NFL . Between 2021-2025, the Rams were penalized 10 or more times a total of two times. They’ve had 10 or more penalties in two of the last three games.

title: Rams Week 5 Snap Counts Reveal Major Shift in Wide Receiver Rotation
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams lost to the Buffalo Bills on Monday Night Football in Week 5, 37-34 in overtime. Throughout the season, the Rams have been adjusting their wide receiver rotation, which has seemingly changed on a weekly basis. Against the Philadelphia Eagles, Tutu Atwell got more snaps in the offense and that carried into Monday. Let’s take a deeper look at the Week 5 snap counts.
Last week, Tutu Atwell played just four snaps fewer than Konata Mumpfield . That changed drastically on Monday night as Atwell out-snapped Mumpfield 32 to six on offense. Mumpfield barely saw any time, while Atwell was used in motion and even had one catch for four yards that resulted in a first down.
It will be interesting to see whether this continues or if it was simply matchup-based. Jordan Whittington also outsnapped Mumpfield 11 to six. Mumpfield played almost 70 percent of the offensive snaps in Weeks 2 and 3 and was down to 7.3 percent on Monday night.
What makes the Atwell situation odd is that he seemed to fall out of favor in the offense last season. Atwell’s role was diminished so much that the team didn’t make an effort to re-sign him in free agency. However, they traded for him before the season. It's possible that with Xavier Smith gone, Atwell's role has opened back up, but it's certainly notable.
Over the past two seasons, Jaylen McCollough has been the dime linebacker for the Rams on defense. Last week, he played just three snaps. On Monday against the Bills, that was down to just one. This season, McCollough has arguably been the Rams’ best tackling safety, and his absence was noticeable against the Bills as the Rams struggled to tackle in the secondary.
Most of McCollough’s snaps over the last few weeks have come on special teams.It’s worth wondering if the Rams are sacrificing McCollough's role on defense so he can contribute more on the coverage units. However, McCollough had just a 32.5 special teams grade via PFF against the Bills.
Last week, the Rams had to abandon 12 and 13 personnel because of the injury to Colby Parksinon. With Parkinson back in the lineup on Monday, the Rams were able to return to what they do best .
With only three tight ends active against the Bills, Allen, Colby Parkinson, and Tyler Higbee were all very active. All three played at least 50 percent of the offensive snaps as they rotated in 12 and 13 personnel.
Davis Allen played 41 snaps, his highest total of the season. While Allen played a higher percentage of the offensive snaps in Week 2, Monday marked a season-high in total snaps. Allen finished with two catches for 24 yards.

title: Alaric Jackson's Suspension Puts Rams in Difficult Position on Offensive Line
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams will be without starting left tackle Alaric Jackson for the next two games. Following Monday night’s game with the Buffalo Bills, Jackson was caught on camera throwing a punch at Bradley Chubb . ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported on Tuesday that Jackson has been suspended for two games by the NFL.
Rams left tackle Alaric Jackson is expected to be  suspended two games for punching Bills outside linebacker Bradley Chubb during Monday night’s postgame gathering, per sources. But the NFL has not yet notified the team nor the NFLPA. pic.twitter.com/ZR54be9z1n
There is the possibility that Jackson appeals the suspension and it gets dropped to one game. However, given Jackson's history, that may be unlikely.  Any appeal will be heard by either Derrick Brooks, Jordy Nelson, Ron Rivera, or James Thrash, the hearing officers jointly appointed and compensated by the NFL and NFLPA to decide appeals of on-field player discipline.
Through the first five games, the Rams have remained healthy on the offensive line. Outside of three snaps, the Rams have had the same offensive line all season. Due to a poor decision from Jackson after the game on Monday night in which he let his emotions get the best of him, the Rams will have to make a change at left tackle.
When the incident was brought up on Monday night after the game, a suspension was to be expected. This isn’t Jackson’s first incident with the NFL. Back in 2024, Jackson was suspended for recording a sexual interaction with a woman without consent. This past summer, Jackson was arrested on a felony domestic violence charge, and that is still a pending legal situation.
According to the NFL's release, Jackson will be eligible to return to the Rams’ active roster on Monday, October 26, following the team’s October 18 game against the Arizona Cardinals and October 25 game against the Las Vegas Raiders. If Jackson is set to miss the next two games, that would put him back in the lineup for Week 8 against the Los Angeles Chargers.
With Jackson potentially out for the next two games, the Rams will need to work on how to replace him. The most likely scenario is that the Rams would play David Quessenberry at left tackle for the next two weeks. Quessenberry is the more experienced option and is listed as Jackson’s backup on the depth chart.
However, it also wouldn’t be surprising if the Rams were to activate Keagen Trost off of injured reserve . The Rams drafted Trost in the third round, but he was placed on injured reserve before the season after injuring his hamstring.
Following Week 4, Trost was eligible to come off of injured reserve. McVay was asked last week if the team had discussed elevating Trost or Justin Dedich. “We could open that up, but that's not a conversation that we've had at this point,” said McVay.
Trost may not start, but he would provide good tackle depth behind Quessenberry and give the Rams another option if needed. Trost brings the versatility to play on both the left and right sides of the offensive line. While Trost is more comfortable on the right side, he does have the ability to play left tackle. In a worst-case scenario, the Rams could also move Warren McClendon to left tackle and play Trost on the right side.
As the Rams look ahead to their game against the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, the most likely immediate solution will be Quessenberry at that spot. Even against the Cardinals, the loss of Jackson will be a significant one. Last season without Jackson, the Rams lost to the Atlanta Falcons. When Jackson was suspended in 2024, the Rams lost to the Cardinals, 41-10, while Dennis Gardeck had three sacks.
With the offensive line being one of the few areas where the Rams have had stability, Jackson's absence creates an unnecessary challenge. The Rams will now have to rely on their depth at one of the most important positions on offense because of a situation that could have been avoided.

title: Rams' Special Teams Problems Persist and Sean McVay Is Running Out of Answers
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams used to be renowned for how good they were on special teams. While Jeff Fisher didn’t do a lot well, the Rams’ special teams with John Fassel were always among the best in the NFL.
In Fisher’s last season, the Rams ranked third in special teams DVOA. It was one of the few things that looked good as the Rams finished that season 4-12. Sean McVay kept Fassel when he took over and the Rams ranked second in special teams DVOA in 2017.
When Stedman Bailey scored on the fake punt return vs the Seahawks #RamsHouse pic.twitter.com/fRQrvfkMf5
From there, things began to spiral. In 2018, the Rams were 17th and ranked 30th by 2020 when McVay moved on from Fassel. Despite having the seventh-ranked special teams unit in 2021, the Rams were last in 2023.
Things hit a tipping point last year when the Rams lost multiple games with special teams playing a major role in those losses. After Week 16, McVay made his first in-season coordinator change , firing Chase Blackburn.
Heading into this season, there was some optimism around the Rams’ special teams unit. McVay moved special teams periods toward the start of practice in an attempt to prioritize that phase of the game. He hired a respected special teams coordinatora in Bubba Ventrone. The Rams also signed Joe Cardona and Grant Stuard. They’ve added special teams players such as Maximus Pulley during the season.
“If you were at their camp, you’d heard about all of this, and the optimism that this would all be fixed—with a new commitment to getting it right,” wrote Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer . “Having Ventrone, Cardona and Stuard helped, but more than just that, they were symbolic of a renewed commitment.”
However, here we are after Week 5, and the Rams are in an all-too-familiar situation . The problems started in Week 1. In Australia, the Rams allowed a 45-yard kickoff return to Deebo Samuel to start the second half. Against the Giants in Week 2, Mevis missed a 43-yard field goal and the Rams took a 15-yard penalty that resulted in points.
In Week 3, the Rams had issues on both the punt and punt return units, sparking a change as the team cut Xavier Smith. Against the Eagles, the Rams allowed a 41-yard punt return that turned into a touchdown. On Monday night, Harrison Mevis missed from 50 yards and had a potential game-winning kick blocked in overtime . McVay was asked after the game if he expected changes on special teams.
“Yeah, I'm going to evaluate everything,” said McVay.
It’s been a weekly theme despite it being something that the Rams and McVay have tried to fix. An argument can be made that they should have done more. Following last season, it was always odd that the Rams didn’t bring in replacements or competition for Harrison Mevis, Xavier Smith, or Ethan Evans.
It made sense why McVay was so upset after the game on Monday night. A great performance from Matthew Stafford and the offense and a timely turnover from the defense were put to waste because of special teams.
“We did some really good stuff and in the kicking game, especially with our PAT field goal, not even close to good enough,” McVay said. “It cost us the game tonight.”
This is about as upset as I’ve seen Sean McVay after a game. He blames himself for the conservative third and five call in OT and kicking the long field goal. There will likely be special teams changes this week. pic.twitter.com/Y06H3vLON1
As McVay has done so often since taking over as head coach, it was as if he expected to simply hire an experienced coordinator and let them figure it out. Again, few changes were made to the core personnel outside of Cardona and Stuard – two Ventrone guys.
Following Monday night’s loss, it was clear that changes needed to be made. However, the changes don’t seem simple at this point. It’s hard to pinpoint exactly what fixes the Rams’ current special teams situation. What exactly is the solution?
Since the Rams moved on from Fassel at the end of the 2019 season, they’ve gone through four different special teams coordinators, including interim Ben Kotwica last year. They hired John Bonamego, who lasted one season. Joe DeCamillis was better, but lasted just two seasons. McVay hired a young, up-and-coming coach in Blackburn. Blackburn arguably lasted longer than he should have at 2.5 seasons before he was fired. This offseason, McVay hired a well-respected special teams coordinator in Bubba Ventrone.
In eight years, the Rams have had five different special teams coordinators. While the Rams could fire Ventrone after five weeks, that would seemingly only continue the coaching carousel that they’ve had at that spot.
Back in 2023, the Rams opted not to bring back Matt Gay. The Rams signed Tanner Brown as an undrafted free agent before cutting him in the preseason and eventually adding Brett Maher ahead of Week 1. Maher was inconsistent and the Rams signed Lucas Havrisik. Havrisik didn’t make it to the end of the year and Maher was brought back.
In 2024, the Rams drafted Joshua Karty, who finished 29-for-34 as a rookie before being cut halfway through his second season. Karty was one of the best kickers in the NCAA at Stanford and was a finalist for the Lou Groza award in 2022, given to the best kicker in the country. The Rams then moved on to sign Mevis to finish out the year. They are now onto Blake Grupe after cutting Mevis on Tuesday.
Grupe is the sixth kicker that the Rams have signed since 2023. They’ve averaged almost two kickers per season.
Multiple things can be true here. The Rams needed to make a change at kicker. However, it’s also fair to say that Grupe may not be the answer. The Rams have done this kicking carousel for the last four years. Why is this time any different?
At this point, the Rams have done this same dance over and over. They’ve pulled the plug at kicker only to be back at square one. They’ve added a respected coordinator and are still one of the worst special teams units in the NFL.
In 2023, the Rams had the seventh-worst special teams unit in DVOA history through five games. This year, the Rams top the list. Over the last four seasons, the Rams have had two of the seven worst special teams units. Only the 2023 Rams and 1977 Vikings made it to the playoffs.
If something doesn't change, this year’s Rams might be making some unfortunate history 😬 pic.twitter.com/zwlLkVR8PB
It’s easy to say that the Rams should just fire the special teams coordinator or make a change at kicker. A lot can be said about how much McVay prioritizes special teams. However, the Rams have fired the special teams coordinator and made changes at kicker for the past five years. It continues to be the same story. This offseason, McVay acknowledged that special teams needed to be better and he did prioritize it, yet the results haven’t reflected that.
We’re at a point where you ask, “where do the Rams even go from here?” It almost seems hopeless. While the names and processes have changed, the problems have persisted.
McVay has gotten so much right as the head coach of the Rams. However, special teams have remained his biggest blind spot. Despite all the changes he's made, none have produced sustained results.
The Rams have a roster capable of competing for a Super Bowl, but their special teams are actively holding them back. Until McVay finds a solution that lasts longer than a few weeks, it's hard to see how this story ends any differently.

title: Rams Signing Kicker Blake Grupe Is a Necessary Change That Was Long Overdue
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams have made a change at kicker following their Monday night loss to the Buffalo Bills . On Tuesday morning, the Rams signed kicker Blake Grupe off of the New York Jets’ practice squad to hopefully bring some stability to the kicking operation.
Through the first five weeks of the season, the Rams have had problems on special teams, primarily with the kicking operation. Heading into Monday’s game, Mevis was still just 5-for-7 and had a miss from 48 yards last week against the Eagles. In Monday night’s loss, Mevis missed from 50 yards and also had a potential game-winning kick blocked in overtime.
While Mevis brought some stability to the kicking operation last season, there were always questions about his range. Mevis had been perfect with extra points and 19-for-20 inside of 45 yards. However, beyond 45 yards is where Mevis lacked consistency , and in today’s NFL, teams need a kicker who can hit from range when called upon.
Mevis had some strong moments, including hitting the game-winner last year against the Chicago Bears in difficult conditions in overtime. However, he was too inconsistent to start 2026 and the Rams were forced to make a change.
Grupe will now replace Mevis in Los Angeles. An undrafted free agent in 2023, Grupe spent three seasons with the New Orleans Saints. He had missed eight field goal attempts in 2025 and was eventually cut.
However, Grupe does have proven range. After being cut by the Saints, Grupe made a 60-yard field goal with the Indianapolis Colts. While he was brought back in the offseason, he lost the competition to Spencer Shrader in training camp. According to ColtsWire , Grupe was steady in training camp but struggled in the preseason games. During the preseason, Grupe was 2-for-4 with one miss inside of 40 yards and another miss beyond 50.
BLAKE GRUPE NAILS A CAREER-LONG 60-YARD FIELD GOAL FOR THE LEAD 😱 The Colts take a 1-point lead with 47 seconds left 🍿 pic.twitter.com/Ys9EJcPXar
Grupe has a career field-goal percentage of 81.9 percent. He’s 86-for-105 in his career and 19-for-27 beyond 50 yards with a long of 60.
While the Rams signed Grupe, it shouldn’t be the only move that they make. The Rams should also consider signing another kicker, such as Tanner Brown or Joshua Karty, to their practice squad in case they need to make another change or simply want to hold an active competition.
Adding Grupe is a step in the right direction, but an argument can be made that this should have been done a long time ago. The Rams should have made these special teams changes in the offseason, but instead stuck with the status quo. After sticking with Xavier Smith, he was cut after Week 3. The Rams stuck with Mevis and didn’t bring in any competition, only to cut him after their Week 5 loss.
The Rams have now made changes at both punt returner and kicker in the span of two weeks, but it remains to be seen whether those moves will be enough to fix a special teams unit that has consistently cost them games. Grupe may not be the long-term answer at kicker, but the Rams can't afford to continue learning lessons on special teams the hard way.

title: Rams Position Grades: Matthew Stafford Shines, Special Teams Falter in Loss to Bills
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams lost to the Buffalo Bills in disappointing fashion on Monday Night Football, falling 37-34 in overtime. Let’s get to this week’s player and position grades.
For the fourth time in the last two seasons, the Rams lost a game in which Matthew Stafford threw for at least 370 yards and three touchdowns. Stafford played well enough for the Rams to win , which included leading a game-tying drive at the end of regulation. He completed a career-high 40 passes on Monday night. It’s a shame that the Rams couldn’t reward his performance in what was his best game of the year. PFF Grade: 67.9
The Rams struggled to get much going on the ground. Kyren Williams averaged just 3.1 yards per carry and Blake Corum had five carries for 19 yards. At the same time, both running backs found the end zone and made an impact in the passing game. Corum had a career-long 34-yard reception and Williams set the Rams up to score in the final seconds of the game.
Puka Nacua carried this group with 17 receptions on 24 targets. His 17 receptions marked a career-high and his 24 targets were the most for a wide receiver since Brandon Marshall in 2009. Davante Adams added two touchdowns of his own. The Rams didn’t get much production outside of those two, but Nacua and Adams played well.
Tyler Higbee has looked like his former self this season and remains a reliable option in the passing game. Without Terrance Ferguson, Higbee proved that he can still deliver in big spots, finishing with five receptions for 83 yards. Davis Allen got involved in the passing game as well. Had the Rams made the game-winning field goal, we would likely be talking about Allen’s 21-yard reception in overtime. Colby Parkinson made his impact felt in the run game as a blocker.
The offensive line was fine, but didn’t protect well in some moments. Stafford may have had a few opportunities to go down the field in the first half, but the Bills had a great game plan defending the Rams’ play-action bootlegs. Warren McClendon allowed five pressures at right tackle.
Defensively, the Rams got pressure on Josh Allen, but Josaiah Stewart was the only player to finish with a sack. They weren’t disciplined in their rush lanes and consistently allowed Allen to escape. The defensive line also struggled defending the run and limiting James Cook. As a group, they missed five tackles.
A lot of the Rams’ struggles in the run game came at the second and third levels. Nate Landman had two forced fumbles and created the turnover in overtime. However, Allen consistently made him look silly in the open field. Omar Speights got washed out in the run game too often. The Bills took advantage of the Rams’ lighter defensive fronts.
From a coverage standpoint, the Rams were actually very good. The Bills were not able to attack the Rams down the field very often in the passing game. However, this group, especially the safeties, struggled in space. This was by far Quentin Lake’s worst performance. AAs a group, they missed seven tackles, with Kam Curl being credited with three. A better tackling effort from the secondary and the Rams may have won this game convincingly.
There were plenty of negatives with this group on Monday night, but there were also some positives. Ethan Evans had a nice punt in this game. Following the 70-yard kickoff return, the coverage unit looked good after that. Additionally, Jordan Whittington had a few nice kickoff returns. With that said, all of that is overshadowed because of the missed field goal from 50 yards and the blocked kick that lost the game.
Sean McVay undoubtedly played a big role in this loss . His play call on 3rd-and-5 in overtime and his management of that entire sequence weren’t good enough. He made the right decision to go for two and made some great second-half adjustments. With that said, as much as the kicking unit deserves blame for the block, McVay deserves just as much criticism for how he managed the situation.

title: Hondo's Raiders Musings: Inside Vegas' Prep for Potential Upset
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-2) host the Buffalo Bills (4-1) on Sunday at Allegiant Stadium, and while the Bills are looking to keep their season rolling, the Raiders are looking to get back on track.
Each Thursday, I offer you my musings from around the team and take you inside where you can’t go. Let’s dig in.
In my previous seven years covering the Raiders , there have been only two reactions when the team takes its first bad loss of the year. Make no mistake, every team has them, but up to this point there have only been two separate reactions.
Panic, and the other is essentially 'We stink again.'
But since the collapse of the 2025 season, things have been and are different.
This week it is resolve, embarrassment, and a sense of individual failure. For the first time since this team arrived in the desert, the Raiders have suffered their first bad loss (documented thoroughly in my report card), and the only finger-pointing is a big thumb back at themselves.
This team knows they aren’t a Super Bowl team; they also know what they represented on the field last week in New England is far from who they are.
They are on a mission to prove that Sunday.
On Tuesday, I watched every snap of the 2025 Seahawks and noticed that even then the NFL stacked the box against Klint Kubiak’s penchant for running the ball; when defenses showed cover zero, Kubiak used a lot of slants and rub routes to defuse it.
We didn’t see that from the Silver and Black on Sunday, so I asked Kubiak whether the Raiders need to add it quickly once teams see the Patriots' success this past weekend on film.
"Absolutely yeah, just trying to attack what the defense gives you. And when you're getting man coverage, that's always an option, yes."
Kubiak mentioned, when I asked him about getting backups, Caleb Rogers and Bryce Cabledue, some reps after the poor play of his guards on Sunday. He elaborated more on that today and went beyond the offensive line.
"Just promoting competition. And whether it's a corner this week or guys on the offensive line this week, there's always competition, and I think that gets the players to play their best. But just telling someone that he's going to go this week, I don't think that's fair to the Raiders or to the players. So, really want to promote competition, especially offensive line and at corner this week."
Darien Porter played very well on Sunday, and Hezekiah Masses struggled, but don’t forget Jermod McCoy is on this roster, and Kubiak spoke on the youth at that CB spot, and what he is expecting this week, specifically from McCoy.
"He certainly can. We're counting on him. We drafted him for a reason. More specifically, I see DP [Darien Porter] and Zeke [Masses] fighting for who's going to start the game, and we know that everybody's going to play."
Kubiak was asked what he is looking for from the Boise State Bronco in terms of his health this week.
"I think Ashton [Jeanty] is really starting to feel a lot better physically. So, excited about giving him even more reps in practice, more full speed reps. And with Mike [Washington] and with Dylan [Laube], all those guys have to factor in for us." Kubiak made it clear that the young man is part of the game plan this week. "He's playing."
The Rams' game plan against the Bills last week shocked me. Rams DC Chris Shula is an elite DC, and it is a matter of when, not if, he becomes an NFL head coach. But the reality is that everyone is paid big money in this league, and Josh Allen, a top-three QB in the NFL, torched the Rams last week.
Kubiak spoke of facing the young superstar.
"Yeah, very difficult. He's an elite athlete, elite thrower, great instincts to know when to run, and definitely between [James] Cook [III] and their quarterback those are two guys that can really hurt you with their legs."
Kubiak didn’t reveal any secrets because it isn’t a secret. The Bills are a legitimate Super Bowl-caliber team, and how you beat them is obvious, but doing it is the hard part.
"Yeah, well, you've got to get first downs to stay on the field. So, going three and out and punting the ball back is not the way to go. So, you've got to sustain drives. A big part of sustaining drives is not being one-dimensional. So, that's a part of our team that we got to improve."
Kubiak was asked if all the turnovers the Raiders' defense produced perhaps hid some of their shortcomings. He took some of that assessment unbridled.
"I think that you do what you got to do to win the game, man. Your weaknesses come out, and what the numbers say that they are, and we're just trying to go win the game. So, we're trying to improve all of our weaknesses. That's offensive, defense, special teams, and the other side of the ball, they're going to come after what you're good at."
"They're going harp on, 'Hey, this team, they've taken the ball away,' so they're going protect it better. So, we've got to continue to take the ball away and just continue to improve as a team."
Kubiak knows his offense has to run the football to work. He also knows that with teams stacking the box, he can’t afford an atrocious offensive line performance like last week. He explained how to fix it.
"Yeah, many areas, and it's coaching, it's playing, and at the end of the day, you kind of go back to the basics and make sure you're focused on the fundamentals and not trying to get too cute with your schemes. And just giving guys a good plan, they can go execute fast."
The NFL and the NFLPA have a CBA. That CBA limits practice time, so how does Kubiak achieve the in-season competition he craves while balancing the CBA rules that dictate practice? Here is a hint: carefully.
"Yeah, well, job's on the line, that fosters it. There are only so many reps, but that's the NFL, and that's why you have training camp. That's why you have the off season, and we got plenty of reps under our belt. So, yeah, there's not a ton during the week, but there's enough to get ready to play a football game."
Brock Bowers is a top-15 player in this league at any position. He is a unicorn. But the Raiders can’t just sit back and expect him to do all the work; other receivers must stand up and make an impact, per Kubiak.
“Yeah, we need everybody to move the ball. We need everybody. So, Brock [Bowers] is doing a good job, his teammates are doing a good job, and they deserve more opportunities. So, that's on myself and the coaching staff of getting them in position."
I have had Klint described as a “Film Junkie,” a “Film Nerd,” and a man in a personal love affair with “Watching plays a million times.” So I asked the first-year coach, who prefers to show his players what they did, good or bad, on film over talking, if the poor film from last week helps even more.
“Yeah, that's the best tool. You know, the guys are visual. You can only tell them so much. If you show them, it definitely helps get your point across. That's definitely something that I like to do, a lot of coaches on our staff like to do. But you got to make the correction somehow, someway. So, whatever hits the player's brain the fastest you got to use that technique.”
The Raiders sophomore WR Dont’e Thornton Jr. needs to show up and out soon, or he could spend the rest of the season back on the IR. Kubiak bluntly assessed his long road back.
“Yeah, he's got to prove to us he's ready to go play in the NFL game. That his conditioning is there. He didn't have a lot of training camp, guys. He's coming back from a lot of time off, but he's worked really hard and he's put himself in position last week to prove to us this week and maybe next week that he's ready to go.”
Are there any certain benchmarks? “Yeah, just with any player coming back from an injury that's been out for a long time, number one's conditioning, and number two is being assignment sound, and number three is making plays.”
One of the many reasons this team loves Klint Kubiak is that he isn’t afraid to go after himself when he feels like he failed. He mentioned…

title: How Raiders Going Back to Drawing Board Ahead of Bills' Arrival
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are on yet another streak. After starting the season with three consecutive wins against three bad teams, the Raiders have lost two straight games to two of the league's top teams: the Kansas City Chiefs and the New England Patriots.
Las Vegas has been on the road plenty, as Week 5 was their third road game in the last four weeks. They now have two consecutive home games against two of the league's best, starting with the Buffalo Bills this Sunday.
The past two weeks have made it clear where the Raiders stand among the league's best, just as the season's first three weeks confirmed that they're no longer the worst team in the league after finishing last season with the No. 1 overall pick in the draft. Las Vegas is somewhere in the middle.
The next month of the season will clarify where Las Vegas falls between the league's best and worst. In the meantime, Klint Kubiak's Raiders have handled their two losses much like their wins, which is a sign of progress inside the locker room.
The team has had an even temperament through the season's first five games. They now turn their attention to a tough Bills team. Both Buffalo and Las Vegas are coming off recent losses to the Patriots and wins over the Los Angeles Chargers. Still, both teams are at very different points.
Las Vegas is working through the first half of the season with new parts across the board. The team's potential and limitations have shown themselves over five weeks. The next few weeks will test the team's ability to battle through extended adversity, as they face a challenging schedule.
Few teams, other than the Chargers, have a four-game stretch as tough as the one the Raiders are working their way through. Yet Kubiak's first year was always going to be about him and his coaching staff working through the remnants of what was arguably the worst roster in the league last season.
The complete rebuild the Raiders began by hiring Kubiak is going through the expected learning curve of a first-year coaching staff with a revamped, but not fully rebuilt roster . The Raiders showed their progress in the first three weeks and where they still needed to improve in the last two.
The Raiders got back to work on Wednesday as they look to shake off the past two weeks and steal one of their next two games before heading to the East Coast to face the New York Jets. Despite two losses, Las Vegas is in position for a strong season, assuming they get back on track.
That will be easier said than done, but not impossible. A productive week of work, along with some changes to the game plan in all three phases, would go a long way. Yet a realistic understanding of where the roster currently stands would help, even after a productive offseason.
The Raiders' coaching staff must make a few tweaks, as the Bills do many things on both sides of the ball that Las Vegas struggles with. Offensively, the Raiders need to run the ball better and sustain drives more consistently. Defensively, Las Vegas' pass rush must rediscover itself.
The past two weeks have been bad matchups for the Raiders, exposing roster holes and deficiencies that most already knew existed. There really have not been any surprises over the past two weeks, other than how quickly their loss to the Patriots got out of hand.
The Raiders' return to Allegiant Stadium might be just what they need to get back on track. Yet the game's location doesn't change the uphill battles they will face at home over the next two weeks. On paper, the Raiders face a roster on the opposite end of the spectrum.
Kubiak and his coaching staff will have to find the right buttons to press throughout the rest of the week, as the Raiders cannot afford another performance like the one they had against the Patriots.

title: NFL Trade Deadline: Update From an Executive on Raiders Rumors
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3–2) are barreling toward a matchup Sunday at Allegiant Stadium against one of the two favorites to represent the AFC in the Super Bowl, the Buffalo Bills (4–1).
Later this year, they will also play the three favorites to represent the NFC. To say that their schedule is difficult would be an enormous understatement.
But looming on the horizon for the rebuilding Raiders is the NFL trade deadline on Nov. 10, 2026, at 4 p.m. ET.
Rumors fly around a gigantic fanbase like the Raiders because Silver & Black fans see their fandom more as a way of life than a simple football game. It is personal.
Good, accurate information must reach fans through reputable sources.
Earlier this year, we spoke of the Raiders and Tyler Linderbaum in December of 2025, the Raiders’ interest in Fernando Mendoza early in September 2025, and Brock Bowers as the main target for the Silver and Black in February of 2023.
Earlier this year, erroneous reports claimed the Raiders made head coaching offers. They were rejected by our reporting, including Jesse Minter (now the Ravens' head coach) and Brian Daboll (now the Tennessee Titans' offensive coordinator), neither of whom received an offer from the Silver & Black.
Even more recent rumors claimed the Raiders had “made an offer” for Tampa Bay Buccaneers DT Vita Vea, and had strong interest in WR Marvin Harrison Jr. and were “in it at the end.”
Again, our reporting rejected all of it long before those situations were settled.
As we enter this rebuild, we told you the Raiders saw it as a three-year process. This is a year of implementation; 2027 will be a get-right season, and the expectation is that the Raiders will reach the playoffs in 2028 (if not sooner) and remain there consistently, as the New England Patriots were when Tom Brady led them.
When the Raiders signed Kirk Cousins, we told you he would be the starter, and as long as he played at a high level and the team was truly in contention, he would remain so.
A long-time highly successful GM let us in on Tuesday what the conventional wisdom is around the NFL, and he named names.
“Everybody knew when they saw the contract Tommy (Tom Delaney, Raiders SVP, Director of Football Administration) put together for Cousins, that he was trade bait, once the season went south. Aidan O’Connell staying on the 53-man proved that.”
In a league starved of QBs, he went on, “Kirk is playing great football. That (Male Cow Excrement) in New England wasn’t his fault at all. If the right team needs a QB, once this season goes south, he has great value.”
The executive believes, and I have confirmed with one other team executive, that once the Raiders make the inevitable move to the rookie No. 1 overall QB selected in the NFL Draft, who had executives calling the best QB prospect in the last four years, Fernando Mendoza, Kirk is instantly on the market.
He went on, “The moment they make that move (to Mendoza), as much as they love Kirk, it would be foolish not to trade him, get value in return, and the Falcons paid him for playing for you for free.”
So what does this executive think of Cousins’ value?
“If you are a team that is all in on 2026, like the Rams and you lose Stafford, or whatever QB an all-in contender has, you could maybe even get a fourth (Round pick in the NFL draft) depending on how many other players, but if it is an all-in team, or a contender and maybe only one is looking, a fifth.”
The issue is not just Cousins, but the executive believes that the Raiders are buyers before the deadline for sure, “Everybody knows that,” but added, “If they are out of the hunt (for the NFL Playoffs) I think they are for sure sellers. Why would you not be? You are rebuilding, and you have some assets that won’t be here long-term, or certainly diminished.”
He then added the caveat again, “But they have to be out of it in their mind.”
The Raiders have been buyers all year. The issue is that they are now led by the master of discipline, John Spytek. They aren’t going to make deals that aren’t singularly focused on the plan and the future. No more Raiders futility chasing pipe dreams and overplaying players for a temporary high who, when the price tag comes due, hinder your team.
The Raiders will always be buyers under Spytek. He is aggressive but does not mistake aggression for stupidity. As one NFL coach told me, “I would have to play poker with that (SOB).”
No matter what happens over the coming weeks, the Raiders will always be willing to upgrade and get better. But it must fit the Spytek narrative and doctrine that now lead this organization.
So what would turn the Raiders into sellers, and what could that possibly look like?
Per the executive, “The Raiders aren’t going to sell short their guys if they are in the hunt. No way, (Klint) Kubiak would go ballistic, and so would Spy (Spytek), and Tom Brady is the single-most competitive human being on earth.”
He elaborated, “But the moment they determine 2026 is done from a standpoint of the playoffs, and make the move to Mendoza, I think every veteran is in play that doesn’t fit the narrative.”
He didn’t want to talk about names, so I called another executive and relayed this opinion to him. He agreed and was quick to name names.
The next executive told me, “The Raiders aren’t shopping Maxx (Crosby), and from what I know he isn’t looking to leave, but that trade deadline people are going to call. He burns for a title; he craves it and maybe a contender could make the offer that would make John (Spytek) say yes, and Maxx as well.”
He continued, “Don’t forget (Adam) Butler. He is playing great, is 32, and has the rest of this year and next on his deal at a terrific price. That was a great deal for the Raiders by John.”
Right there are three names. We talked about a few others, and he thought the interest level would have been from nominal to possible, but none were overly substantial.
The Raiders want to keep their promising young players and veterans who fit the long-term narrative. Still, they’ve already decided that the veterans and young players they have aren’t part of the answer, and NFL teams feel strongly that those players are available now.
But around the NFL, they also think veterans who are absolutely part of the dream right now could hit the market the moment the team’s brain trust thinks the dream of the NFL playoffs in 2026 is dead.
Or as one executive said, “If Cousins loses his job because he stinks (not the case presently) moving to the kid (Fernando Mendoza) is a smart move. But if he is playing well, and they replace him, game on. They have moved on to a 2027 mindset, and the Raiders are smart enough to become sellers to the right buyers.”
The Raiders are buyers; they always will be. But with the Bills this Sunday, the Rams next Sunday, the Jets the following week, and the 49ers in the final game before the deadline, the Raiders will quickly assess the reality of the NFL Playoff dream in 2026.
At worst, they would be 3–6, with a good chance at 4–5, and if they play as they did against the Chiefs, they have a legitimate puncher's chance at 5-4.
No matter what, there is plenty of time before the deadline to learn what they are.
The playoffs are looming, but so is a rookie QB who looks the part. Make a playoff push with a veteran in Cousins? Great. Get your rookie in, trade your veteran for quality compensation, and get his play and mentoring for your rookie, with the Falcons paying the bill? Great.
Either way, the Raiders win, or we get a front-row seat to what may be the most exciting NFL trade deadline around the Silver & Black in years.

title: Raiders' Trade Deadline Targets Ranked by Fit, Cost, and Chance
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are reeling after losing their last two games in a row. The Raiders are 3-2 after starting the season with a winning streak and a losing streak. Still, the Raiders are ahead of schedule.
The first three weeks of the season showed the team's potential; the past two weeks have made it clear what position groups still need attention. With the trade deadline right around the corner, we take a look at where the Raiders stand.
Las Vegas entered the season with several position groups still needing additional talent. They also knew that adding significant talent during the season was unlikely. They are essentially in the first year of actually building out their roster, after last season helped determine who to move on from.
With the trade deadline just a few weeks away and the team on a two-game losing streak, Las Vegas is at the point in its rebuild where developing the players on their new-look roster and protecting the remaining financial and draft capital matter most.
Still, several players across the league are on the trade block that may fit some of the Raiders' needs. These players include CB Zyon McCollum and DL Daron Payne, among others. Las Vegas will likely also look to add players along the offensive line, cornerback,  safety, and wide receiver.
According to Spotrac, the Raiders currently have between $7 million and $11 million in available cap space following the restructuring of several of the sizeable contracts they doled out during the offseason. They could likely find other ways to make some cap space to free up more money.
Still, between the lack of cap space and the significant roster and contractual commitments they made this summer, only so much is possible in terms of a trade. Las Vegas' front office may rightfully consider the moves it has already made to be enough.
Still, Las Vegas has funds available and can free up more through other measures, should they need to make financial room for a trade of some sort. The Raiders' front office would also likely weigh the immediate benefits of a trade against the potential long-term roster and financial costs.
Two of the biggest trades that happened at the deadline were at the two positions Las Vegas needs the most help at. Those trades confirmed that either the Raiders are not heavily involved in the trade market or were unwilling to outbid the teams that successfully put together trade packages.
Wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. was traded to the Houston Texans for a 2027 second- round pick and a 2027 sixth-round pick. The Dallas Cowboys traded for cornerback Joey Porter Jr., sending the Pittsburgh Steelers a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick in return.
Harrison and Porter have had their issues, but both would be among the most talented at their respective positions had the Raiders added them. The fact that Las Vegas did not trade, or even reportedly attempt to trade, despite their desperate need at both positions speaks volumes.
Nobody can blame the Raiders' front office for deciding not to trade a second-round draft pick in either of the next two drafts for either player. Las Vegas' front office reserves the right to make no more moves after the offseason they had.
There is still plenty of time to make a trade of some sort, even if it is not for players in return. However, for the Raiders to make a substantial trade to add talent to their roster would be at least somewhat gambling future resources to add talent after a summer filled with doing so.
The Raiders are in their first season under a new coaching staff that is working with a largely revamped roster. Las Vegas made a lot of new additions this offseason, but it takes time for those pieces to gel. Rebuilds take time in general, and this is essentially the first year of Las Vegas.
Las Vegas could use a trade to build their current roster with an incoming player now or with additional future draft picks to add to the roster later. However, there is a difference between being aggressive and reckless. The Raiders should avoid an unnecessary trade.
Las Vegas' star defensive end, Maxx Crosby, who would coincidentally be the Raiders' most significant trade piece, couldn't have said it better after the team's disappointing Week 5 loss to the New England Patriots.
“It is process-oriented. You could feel like you’re the best team in the world in one week, and the next week, it could be real tough. But that’s not this locker room. That is not the guys that we’ve got. It’s just about getting better, and we’re all going to look in the mirror. It is going to take every single one of us, and we’ve just got to improve," Crosby said.

title: Raiders Game Review: 3 Takeaways From Week 5 Blowout Loss
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders lost in horrific fashion as they were demolished by the New England Patriots, 45-17, in what can only be considered a humbling experience for head coach Klint Kubiak and his team.
The Raiders did have some good moments, including the debut of their highly anticipated rookie quarterback and another great performance from tight end Brock Bowers. I decided to give this game a second look (yes, I am a brave soul) and wanted to share three observations from this game that fans should want to read about.
The Raiders' No. 1 overall pick from the 2026 NFL Draft played his first regular-season snaps on Sunday against the Patriots as the score was already well out of hand for any comeback attempt. Mendoza finished his lone drive completing six passes (technically seven passes after half of Malik Benson's foot stepped out of bounds) on eight attempts for 48 yards on nine dropbacks.
Mendoza was impressive . I loved the three-level accuracy he displayed while making sure he worked left to right and vice versa in his progressions, making mostly good reads and being evasive on a quick pressure from the Patriots, which allowed him to navigate the pocket and find Dylan Laube for a quick completion and yards after the catch. Mendoza had a touchdown to Tre Tucker on the second & 10 following Benson's incompletion but opted for his first read.
Does this performance say that Kirk Cousins should be benched soon? No; however, I do think that if Cousins has rough performances against the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams in the next two weeks, the calls for No. 15 will be not only significant but loud across the board.
The last three games have shown me exactly why Brock Bowers is the best tight end in football and one of the best overall skill position players in the game. You might ask yourself how Bowers can come down with some of the incredible passes thrown his way, and it's pretty simple, if you ask me.
Bowers is gifted with excellent hand-eye coordination to track the ball into his mitts, while using awesome play strength at the catch point to corral and maintain the ball through the catch. His concentration to haul in contested catches is second to none.
Bowers also pairs this with the speed of a wide receiver and the quickness to create both vertical separation and generate yards after the catch, and to win at the top of routes and break them off with snappy movements for his size. Until someone can slow him down, Bowers is the No. 1 tight end and wide receiver on the roster and arguably their best player not named Maxx Crosby.
It was a rough day for the Raiders' two rookies at cornerback and safety. Hezekiah Masses only played 20 snaps as defensive coordinator Rob Leonard worked veteran Darien Porter into the lineup.
Masses didn't have an outright terrible game; I thought he did a good job with some of his press technique to stay step for step with no false steps, though physicality can get to him still— he doesn’t have the big frame to handle that religiously. However, on a Romeo Doubs reception he allowed, Masses was a step slower both to react to the break and to drive to the catch point, allowing a chunk play underneath.
On the touchdown to Kyle Williams, No. 18 froze Masses with a false step, who simply lacked the recovery speed to get back to the hip pocket to make a play on the ball. Two rough reps out of 20, but all were notable and important.
As for Treydan Stukes, he may have had the worst game of his young career. On the wide-open touchdown from Demario Douglas, there was a miscommunication about who would pick up the post on the drive concept (outside dig, inside post), which was Stukes responsibility. Stukes was also a tick late in matching Efton Chism III in man coverage on a dig pattern, while the fourth-down conversion to Hunter Henry was allowed by widening too much on the motion against the angle route.
Overall, better days are ahead for Stukes and Masses. I wouldn't be too concerned about their latest performances; the Patriots had a good game plan and executed well against this young defense.

title: 3 Things Raiders Need to Keep in Mind After Week 5 Loss
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are now in the midst of a two-game losing streak after falling to the New England Patriots in a blowout loss in Week 5.
It goes without saying that the Raiders' performance left much to be desired and served as a wake-up call to the organization. After starting the season 3-0, Las Vegas suddenly finds itself at 3-2, with the schedule not lightening up. With that in mind, here are three bold takes after watching what transpired this past Sunday.
Cousins has exceeded the expectations of some in the media who thought he shouldn't have opened up the season as the starter. Through five games, the 38-year-old quarterback has compiled 1,269 passing yards, 12 touchdowns, and four interceptions while completing 65.1 percent of his passes.
That being said, the Raiders have lost two consecutive games and are staring at a potential four-game losing streak, with the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams on tap. The more losses that pile up for Las Vegas, the more calls there will be for Fernando Mendoza to be allowed to start . Not to mention, the San Francisco 49ers, Seattle Seahawks, and Denver Broncos are also on the horizon for the Raiders. Cousins has been a great solidifier, but Mendoza could be a potential elevator.
It's obvious that Jeanty's injuries are hampering his ability to be fully effective, and even head coach Klint Kubiak admitted that during his postgame press conference on Sunday. The 22-year-old running back suffered a sprained ankle during training camp and a foot injury in Week 3 against the Kansas City Chiefs.
This season, Jeanty is averaging 3.3 yards per carry and has zero rushing touchdowns. He's been incredibly effective as a pass catcher out of the backfield, with 22 receptions for 215 yards and two touchdowns. However, these injuries will linger as long as Jeanty continues to play. Considering that the next two games are against Super Bowl-caliber opponents, sitting the star running back and having him return in Week 8 against the New York Jets should be taken into account.
Crosby was traded this offseason before the Baltimore Ravens nixed the deal. There were already rumors before that deal materialized that the two-time All-Pro pass rusher was a trade candidate. That fallen-through deal only amplified the noise, but it simmered down as the season opener neared. That speculation was put on hold after the 3-0 start.
Now that Las Vegas has lost two consecutive games and an avalanche of losses potentially in the near future, Crosby's name will re-emerge in trade rumors. If the Raiders are trending downward as the trade deadline nears, trading their best asset will definitely be in play.

title: The Biggest Decision Klint Kubiak, Raiders Got Wrong vs. Patriots
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' Week 5 loss to the New England Patriots featured a long list of mistakes by Klint Kubiak's Raiders.
This article is not to say that any one decision made by Kubiak, his staff, or players led to the loss. It takes a significant number of bad coaching decisions, poorly executed plays by the players, and solid play from the opposing team for a team to be down by 30 points in the NFL.
Pointing fingers gets us nowhere, but it is fair to acknowledge the blatant negatives of the Raiders' all-around disappointing performance against the Patriots. Las Vegas entered Week 5 without two receivers from an already questionable group. Yet, the Patriots were significantly shorthanded, too.
There was nothing more roster-wise that Kubiak and his staff could have done to put themselves in a better position to win Sunday's game, logistically. Considering how quickly things went south for the Raiders, it is fair to assume there was not much more they could have done play-calling-wise, either.
I understand that resting your starting running back while 3-1, with a shot at going 4-1 against a solid Patriots team, may not make sense to some. It could be argued that sitting Ashton Jeanty entering Week 5 goes against all logic, which is fair. However, the Raiders' 3-0 start went against all logic, too.
It is also fair to note that Jeanty is too critical to an already limited passing attack for the Raiders. Sitting Jeanty while already missing Jack Bech and Jalen Nailor would have hurt Las Vegas' passing game even more.
The biggest mistake the Raiders' coaching staff made was not resting Jeanty and putting Roman Hemby on the field. Hemby is not the answer to the Raiders' struggles on the ground, but he could have helped in the short and long term on Sunday against the Patriots.
Las Vegas is in the middle of a four-game stretch that included games against the Kansas City Chiefs and the Patriots. The Raiders will now face the red-hot Buffalo Bills and the Los Angeles Rams. They cannot rest Jeanty during those two games. Sunday against the Patriots was the time to do so.
New England entered the game with more injuries and critical players out than the Raiders, and it was not close. The Patriots entered the game without four of their cornerbacks and multiple wide receivers. They then lost their starting tackle and starting running back before halftime.
Few teams the Raiders will face moving forward will be as injured as the Patriots were. That was the time to rest Jeanty. Doing so would have given him a light workload during the week leading up to the Patriots game, a game off his clearly sore ankles, and extra time off before two tough games.
After facing the Bills and Rams at home in consecutive weeks, the Raiders are on the road for two consecutive weeks. Again, I understand the reasons for not sitting Jeanty, but a significantly shorthanded Patriots team was the week to rest Jeanty.
Also, Hemby has a similar style of play to Jeanty. He isn't Jeanty, but the Raiders did not need him to be. As is, Hemby would have been serviceable enough to get them through what became nearly a 30-point loss anyway. Instead, the Raiders took a huge loss, and Jeanty added wear and tear to his body.
The Raiders don't have any other upcoming games where sitting Jeanty for an entire game makes sense. Their Bye Week is not until Week 13. The closest they can get is to activate Hemby moving forward and begin using Jeanty, Mike Washington, Dylan Laube, and Hemby on more of a rotation.
Jeanty being the team's workhorse is good in theory, but he is hurt. Theory goes out the window here. Las Vegas' coaching staff must start thinking outside the box, as they are another injury or two away from their depth chart getting to a very uncomfortable spot at multiple positions.
Soon, it will be time to begin rotating playing time throughout the secondary levels of the depth chart, in the name of development, and to keep their best players healthy as long as possible. This will require more attention to the latter part of this season and future seasons.
In other words, giving players further down the depth chart experience and letting their best players rest could soon matter more than wins and losses. Hemby was not going to help the Raiders beat the Patriots, but he could have given Jeanty a valuable Sunday off his ailing legs.

title: Hondo’s Raiders Mailbag: Fans Make Their Demands Clear
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-2) have turned the page from their brutal loss this past weekend to the New England Patriots (3-2) and are already fully focused on the Buffalo Bills (4-1), who are coming to town for a tilt this weekend at Allegiant Stadium.
If the Raiders play like they did last weekend (we already detailed that in our report card ), they will get blown out.
But, led by a coach who shone brightly in the Patriots' loss , his worst moment as the Raiders coach last week, Klint Kubiak, if they play as they did versus the Kansas City Chiefs, they could steal a win.
I asked the Raider Nation, as I do each week, to let me know via my X account: besides the obvious answer of a win, what are they looking for?
Once again, one of the elite and smartest fan bases, who see their fandom as their way of life , and not just a game, responded in a big way.
The Raiders have no chance of winning over the next two weeks without some semblance of a running game.  I couldn’t agree more.
The issue isn't whether Ashton Jeanty or Mike Washington Jr. is playing; the issue is that the offensive line, as a unit, looked terrible on Sunday.
Tyler Linderbaum and Delmar “DJ” Glaze, the Mule, didn’t look bad, but guards Spencer Burford and Jackson Powers Johnson did, along with LT Kolton Miller.
I asked Kubiak about the poor guard play mentioned above and whether it opened an opportunity for Bryce Cabeldue and Caleb Rogers to get some reps this week.  Not one to lie or deceive, the Raiders' head coach was blunt as always.
"Yeah, we always want competition. We're looking at how to get better at all positions. So, yes."
The Raiders' mindset is to win this weekend, and QB Kirk Cousins said it best on what that takes in this league.
“I think anytime you're one-dimensional, it probably does make it a little bit easier on a defense. I think also playing from a lead, they can probably afford to be flexible with what they're doing because they've created a bit of a cushion. But you certainly want that run-pass threat at all times if you can have it.”
Competitiveness.. like the KC game
This is one of the many reasons why Matt Millen sold me on this fan base, and why I genuinely love you all.  You get it.  You are not unrealistic or foolish.  You don’t ask for much, and in a rebuilding year, facing a team with legit Super Bowl aspirations, you are fair.
Two weeks ago, the Patriots went to Buffalo, then played the Raiders and beat the incoming Bills. Theoretically, that makes the Bills a worse team.  I emphasize theoretically because, despite the loss at home, I think the Bills are better.
Asking your team to be competitive, considering what they did in that same building versus the Chiefs, who I think are better than the Bills and the Patriots, is not asking too much.
“We have a whole lot to prove to ourselves and our fans this week. Really looking forward to playing in front of our fans this week. And our men, our leadership, our coaches, we're up to the challenge, and we have to bounce back.”
A response. Not a reaction. Go Raiders ☠️
I love this for a million reasons, not least of all because my father used to instill this in his sons regularly.  Most don’t know the difference, so let me quickly explain it to them.
A reaction is an automatic, instant reflex fueled entirely by emotion, often creating mistakes that make us, in our best Homer Simpson voice, slap our forehead and say, “Why did I do that?”
A response is a conscious, deliberate choice made after taking a moment to think. It uses your brain to assess and make the right decision.  It is calculated.  Essentially, a reaction is controlled by the situation, but a response keeps you in control.
The Raiders, for the entirety of the time I have covered them, and long before I got here, have been reactionary as a franchise.
With Tom Brady, John Spytek, and Klint Kubiak, that is no longer the plan of attack.  I don’t think the Raiders will win this Sunday.  I do expect them to look better than last week, and the biggest reason is that they aren’t panicking; they are reactionary.  They are calculated.
