title: Hondo’s Raiders Report Card: Why This Week Was So Ugly
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-2) host the team that many feel will be heading to the Super Bowl to represent the AFC on Sunday when the Buffalo Bills (4-1) and their throngs of “Mafia” come to town.
It will be the toughest test of the season so far for the overachieving, rebuilding Raiders.
Led by first-year head coach Klint Kubiak, who shone for other reasons in New England, the Raiders won't just accept a loss and lay down.
This Raiders team will come in swinging and try to shock the NFL world once again.
But before we turn our attention to the Bills on Sunday, today, after having already reviewed the winners and losers, we offer our weekly report card recap.
Not a good grade by any standard, but the issues are deeper than that. Kirk Cousins wasn’t the issue at all; he was under pressure the moment he got off the plane, and rumors are rampant that when he dropped off his duffel bag at team headquarters when they returned Sunday night, four Patriots fell out and hit him.
A QB can’t do his job with zero protection.
The same is true for Ashton Jeanty. No Raiders running back could run the football with an offensive line that played so poorly. Jeanty had dropped passes for the second week in a row, but his pass blocking was exceptional, and his lack of yards carrying the ball was an offensive line issue, and not on him.
I asked Kubiak about Jeanty’s drops, and subsequently, the terrific pass blocking.
"Yes, he's always been an excellent pass protector. We count on him on third down, obviously running routes and protecting. And yeah, those are things that are continuing to show up that we have to get fixed as a coaching staff."
Certainly, LT Kolton Miller had to face situations with multiple defenders, and you can’t expect him to block two or three people, but he also got beat one-on-one on multiple occasions, and the guard play was, to be frank, horrendous.
The reality is that the Raiders' offensive struggles against the Patriots came down to blocking breakdowns and an inability to run the ball.
Rick Dennison is the best OL coach in the NFL, but on Sunday, his OL was not good at all, and I am being nice.
​The Patriots dominated the line of scrimmage; they owned it wherever it was on the field, holding the Silver and Black to an abysmal 38 rushing yards with a 2.1 yards-per-carry average. How bad is that? You should be able to simply fall forward for that.
With the score quickly out of hand, the Raiders had to abandon the run, allowing the Mike Vrabel Patriots' pass rush to attack and swarm Kirk Cousins like a tiger hunting a gazelle, pressuring him on nearly 48% of his passes, sacking him three times, and forcing a crucial turnover.
Yes, the Raiders don’t have a WR1. But would that have mattered in hindsight?
After watching the film, the Raiders didn’t lose because of a lack at WR1.
That didn’t help, but it wasn’t the reason.
When an NFL team is forced to go one-dimensional, you won't be successful. Kubiak admitted it.
"I give a lot of credit to New England. They did an excellent job. I just didn't have a good plan for our guys. We didn't execute well. We got behind early, and we weren't able to get the run game going. There's just a lot of reasons that that game didn't work out, and it starts with me."
Everything on offense starts with the offensive line. Tyler Linderbaum had a good day, and Delmar “DJ” Glaze, the Mule, did too, but that is only 40% of your offensive line. The OL grade would be a D- at best, if not an F, but I had to grade the entire offense, and I gave them a D+ because of Cousins' leadership and Brock Bowers' heroic play.
Kirk Cousins echoed his coaches’ sentiments. “I think anytime you're one-dimensional, it probably does make it a little bit easier on a defense. I think also playing from a lead, they can probably afford to be flexible with what they're doing because they've created a bit of a cushion. But you certainly want that run-pass threat at all times if you can have it.”
The Raiders' defense let the 2026 Patriots play like the Tom Brady-led 2007 Patriots, and despite coming off last year's Super Bowl, they are nothing like that 2007 version.
They gave up 45 points and were run over, around, and through all day.
Some individuals played well, but as a unit, they were bad.
During the 45–17 blowout loss, the Silver and Black defense was frankly embarrassed, mainly by explosive plays and Drake Maye's aerial dominance, which topped his stat line with five total touchdowns.
Maye’s effectiveness showed up in crisp passes and relatively little pressure. When Maxx Crosby wasn’t double-teamed or even triple-teamed, the Patriots simply held him, daring the officials to call a holding penalty on every play.
The Raiders have to be more engaged and move Crosby around pre-snap to force offenses to search for him and find him on every play. I asked Kubiak exactly about that after being told after the game that the Patriots accounted for Crosby on every play.
"Yeah, I think those are definitely things as a coaching staff that we're talking about. We got to get him in positions to be successful to get near the quarterback."
The Raiders can’t develop an NFL playoff-caliber defense without other players being more consequential at DE.
John Spytek and Klint Kubiak have invested a lot of money in Malcolm Koonce and Kwity Paye, both great young men who were non-existent on Sunday.
They weren’t the only ones, but playing across from Crosby opens up amazing opportunities that, to their credit, they have done all year, until Sunday.
This aforementioned pass-rush void left the Raiders' secondary repeatedly exposed over the top, surrendering major chunk plays to receivers. At the same time, New England also racked up 165 rushing yards as they totaled 536 yards.
The Raiders' young defense was exploited, but Darien Porter actually played well. Perfect? No, but he far outplayed Hezekiah Masses and it stood out on tape. I asked Kubiak about the young Porter, who has one of the highest football IQs you have ever seen and is only in his sophomore campaign.
"Yeah, I would say that he's a guy that was starting, lost his job for a week, and is so mentally tough that he came back in and played really good football yesterday, and played very competitive. And that's not a surprise. That's the kind of guy that he is, and he's just going to continue to get better, and him and Zeke [Masses] will compete for that job."
The Raiders' defense had a bad day. Credit the Patriots, but also credit the Raiders. Along with Porter and Crosby, who both performed better than their teammates, Adam Butler was outstanding, and Nakobe Dean was, well, Nakobe Dean.
This is a resilient group of men who will rebound, but on this day, they failed.
It is no secret that I am all in on special teams coordinator Joe DeCamillis. He is the best the Raiders have had in a long time. The two monstrous mistakes on his side of the ball were both by veterans. That isn’t on the coach; it's on the veterans, and both hurt.
Those two critical errors were brutal. But one was worse than the other.
The one that hurt, but was more explainable in the weather, was a missed 49-yard field goal by kicker Matt Gay before halftime, which denied them a chance to cut into New England's lead.
The inexcusable, brutal mistake came when cornerback Darrell Luter Jr. failed to down a punt from AJ Cole near the goal line, giving the defense prime field position.
Cole, as always, was exceptional; Alex Ward was terrific, and overall the teams were fine. But that missed FG that I believe the forthright Gay would tell you he has to make, and an egregious error by Luter, hurt. Badly.
It doesn’t change that Luter was a good addition to this team, and Gay has done a very good job as the kicker. But Luter can’t make that mistake again and expect to keep a roster spot.
With a first-year head coach, defensive coordinator (Robbie Leonard), and offensive coordinator (Andrew Janocko), you expect mistakes, and I prepared…

title: What Raiders' Week 5 Loss Changed About Its Trade Deadline Plans
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are coming off their worst performance of the year after a Week 5 blowout loss to the New England Patriots. Las Vegas entered the game 3-1 and looked like one of the league's best teams. However, the Patriots quickly confirmed that Las Vegas has a long way to go.
The Raiders' front office was diligent this offseason, making a slew of changes that quickly helped Las Vegas rise above the league's worst teams. However, Klint Kubiak and the Raiders' coaching staff were always honest about where the team stood.
The Raiders' past two games reminded everyone of their roster deficiencies, even after a quality offseason. Las Vegas has improved, but it is still a young team in the early stages of a rebuild and is currently on a two-game losing streak.
After starting the season 3-0 with wins over teams they would have lost to a season ago, the Raiders' offseason progress was undeniable. Yet Sunday's double-digit road loss to the defending AFC Champions was undeniable. Kubiak explained where Las Vegas currently sits.
“Well, in the NFL, there's always people working on your weaknesses at all times. So, the Patriots did a great job of exposing ours, and all I'm asking them to do is their jobs, and it's our jobs as coaches to get them prepared and put them in position to play successfully. So, they're young guys, they'll keep playing, and we count on them to play at a high level," Kubiak said the day after the game.
The season's first three weeks and Las Vegas' past two weeks have been polar opposites. However, so have the teams the Raiders have faced this season. The Raiders faced some of the worst teams to start the season, then some of the league's best.
Kubiak's staff did a solid job of keeping the team grounded when undefeated. Now, he and his coaching staff will have to keep getting the most out of the roster they have.
“I just think that if guys know what to expect from you that you're the same guy, whether you win or you lose, at least that's what I try to be; I'm not saying that I'm successful at that, but that's what I want from others to be consistent,” Kubiak said.
“Some of that you can count on, hold someone to a standard, and if it's not there, tell you the truth. If it is there, tell you, 'Good job'. But however you handle something, win or loss, the goal is to win the game. And we did not win yesterday, and we have a long season ahead of us, and we have big goals."
The sheer number of moves the Raiders made this offseason left little room for more quality moves. The money spent and the talent that was brought in were more than enough for the Raiders to work with this season. They were more than aware of the roster's pitfalls.
Still, Las Vegas' front office did all they realistically could to address as many of those pitfalls as possible. The Raiders are in the beginning stages of rebuilding what has been one of the league's worst overall rosters over the past three seasons. It will take more than one offseason.
Las Vegas' front office must stay the course regardless of what happens during the regular season. The Raiders' roster is all but set. If they add another player, it likely will not be via trade.
Doing so would give up draft capital during a season when the Raiders were not expected to contend for the playoffs. If the Raiders were going to make a trade, Marvin Harrison would have been a logical target. Now that he is gone, few sure-bet players worth giving up resources for.
The 3-2 Raiders are what they are, and the chances of Las Vegas' front office making a sizeable trade, or any trade at all, before the deadline appear slim to none. The Raiders' front office did more this offseason than any other. Kubiak and his staff have to work with the roster they have.

title: Why This Disappointing Dolphins Season Actually Isn't That Disappointing in the Big Picture
full_text:
It's been a rough start for the Miami Dolphins in this 2026 season, the 0-5 record bad enough in itself but made worse by the fact the team hasn't had a lead for even one second in 300 minutes of game action.
It's absolutely been rough to watch, but there are two questions that need to be asked, or rather two points that need to be made.
The first one is pretty simple: Is the Dolphins' bad start really start surprising?
The second is more important: Has it changed the overall outlook for the franchise at all?
The Dolphins' struggles basically boil down to not having enough talent on their roster and also having an awful lot of inexperience with some players who do have enough talent.
And a roster full of young players usually means the kind of mistakes that veteran teams don't make, whether it be untimely penalties or missed assignments.
It's not a big secret that the roster would be deficient this season became GM Jon-Eric Sullivan himself discussed the lack of depth more than once in the buildup to the regular season.
Most of it, of course, was a conscious decision by the organization to reset the salary cap heading into 2027 and that meant getting rid of most of the front-line players who could have helped the Dolphins win some games this year.
The Dolphins' roster moves this year all have been about trying to unearth some hidden gems in the form of young players looking to break through or failed former high draft picks looking to revive their career.
With all of the player acquisitions other than QB Malik Willis, though, the common them has been operating on the cheap.
And, as the old saying goes, you get what you pay for.
What the Dolphins are experiencing right now is a lot of growing pains and paying the price for blowing up the roster, and head coach Jeff Hafley said more than once this season was about more than wins and losses — maybe in large part because he, Sullivan and the entire organization knew full well there likely would be way more losses than wins.
The 2026 season, as we wrote in the offseason, was about the progress and development of the young players who hopefully will form the core of a contender sooner rather than later — a group that included Miami's entire rookie draft class as well as recent high picks like Chop Robinson, Kenneth Grant and Jonah Savaiinaea.
It also was about building a foundation, identity — or culture, if you prefer that term. It's about the new Dolphins way, not to be confused with the Green Bay way because Hafley and Sullivan want to put their own stamp on the Dolphins.
And it also was about evaluating Willis to see whether he could become the long-term answer at quarterback.
Looking at those three objectives, there have been enough good performances from young players through the first five games to take some encouragement, the list including Jacob Rodriguez, Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Michael Taaffe, Trey Moore in training camp, with Robinson showing some improvement.
In terms of building an identity or foundation, that's going to be a work in progress and it obviously will be easier once there's some success in the form of a win or two, though there have been positive signs already based on how the Dolphins have competed.
With Willis, the early returns haven't been very impressive, but there never was a guarantee he was going to be the guy and there's also a lot of time left in this 2026 season for him to provide those signs — because the Dolphins aren't about to pull the plug on his audition anytime soon. Let's also understand that Willis' performance should improve the more time he spends with his teammates on offense, though he does need to stand out on his own merits.
The bottom line is we stand right now about where we were at the start of the regular season, except with five losses, some good performances from some rookies, not nearly as good a start from Willis as hoped, but in the big picture pretty much in the same place.
So, yeah, the 0-5 start does kind of stink a little bit. But this season always was going to be a starting point as the early part of a rebuilding project.
And all things considered, things aren't so terrible because they're not entirely unexpected. And that, like or not, is a better place to be than constantly underachieving.

title: Dolphins Week 6 Power Rankings Roundup: Race for No. 1 Pick Starting to Form
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins remained winless with their loss against the Cincinnati Bengals, a game that wasn't as close as the 31-24 final score might have suggested, and they now stand as one of three teams with an 0-5 record.
If we're not already there, it won't be long before we start focusing on the 2027 NFL draft and more specifically exactly how high the Dolphins' first-round pick will end up being.
Based on the latest round of national media power rankings, they'll have stiff competition for the No. 1 overall pick from the Tennessee Titans.
The Dolphins came in at 31st in the Week 6 power rankings among our 10 national outlets — Yahoo Sports, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, The Athletic, NFL.com, USA Today, Pro Football Talk, FOX Sports, The Sporting News, CBS Sports — with an average ranking of 31.2 compared to 31.5 for the AFC South team.
For a second consecutive week, the Dolphins did get a ranking as high as 29th, that coming from Nick Shook of NFL.com.
Before we get to our weekly rundown of the Dolphins placement in the rankings with the accompanying commentary, we'll again examine the other winless teams and that race for the No. 1 overall pick.
The Dolphins and Titans were joined at 0-5 this past weekend by the Los Angeles Chargers after their loss against the Denver Broncos.
While the Dolphins have a bye this weekend, the Chargers will face the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium and the Titans will face the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium.
Of the three teams at 0-5, the Chargers obviously are the big surprise considering they went into the season after back-to-back 11-win seasons, while Tennessee won three games each of the previous two seasons.
The Chargers look highly dysfunctional on offense in their first year with Mike McDaniel as their coordinator and now they're dealing with a rash of injuries that had them starting four rookies plus former Dolphins guard Cole Strange against Denver.
Working against the Chargers also is a brutal schedule. After their game at Kansas City, the Chargers will return from their bye to face the Rams, Texans (who probably are on their way to a rebound) and Baltimore, with games against the 49ers, Chiefs and Broncos over the last month.
Tennessee's bigger problem is the team just doesn't look much better than either of the previous two seasons, even if the Titans' schedule is a lot more manageable than that of either the Chargers or Dolphins. After Indy, Tennessee has a home game against Cleveland, followed by a road game against Cincinnati.
The Sporting News (Vinnie Iyer)
Analysis: The Dolphins cannot blame their continued skid on the absence of running back De'Von Achane. Another backfield star has been born, helped by Malik Willis, as Ollie Gordon II has turned 27 carries for 188 yards and 2 TDs the past two games. Gordon will help them finish an upset soon after one-possession losses to the Vikings and Bengals.
Analysis: They stay in their spot as they lost to the Bengals. The question is will they win a game.
Analysis: They're terrible and will remain that way for the duration of this season. But give them credit for fighting for first-year coach Jeff Hafley, which (unexpectedly) gets them out of the power rankings basement.
FOX Sports (Ralph Vacchiano)
Analysis: The Dolphins head into their bye week 0-5, which is exactly what everyone expected. Head coach Jeff Hafley’s defense has been OK, but they’re one of the worst offenses in the league and there isn’t a quarterback anywhere playing as poorly as Malik Willis. Bright sides? There are a few. RB Ollie Gordon has 188 yards and two TDs in two starts since they lost De’Von Achane. And on Sunday, they scored a season-high 24 points and out-gained the explosive Bengals 331 yards to 307. Want another one? When they come out of the bye, they get the Jets twice in a month span, which might be their only two chances for wins this season.
Analysis: First, the good: RB Ollie Gordon II has legitimate juice. The young playmakers out wide (plus TE Greg Dulcich) are fun to watch. LB Jacob Rodriguez is a stud who should be a front-runner for Defensive Rookie of the Year. Now, the bad: QB Malik Willis learned a hard lesson about not playing outside of his limits. Miami’s defensive weaknesses were still evident when Joe Burrow hit big plays and led steady scoring marches. The Dolphins are still winless. But for another week, they competed and didn’t make a ton of mistakes that would suggest a team headed into the abyss. That first win will come eventually.
The Athletic (Chad Graff and Josh Kendall)
Analysis: Hey, at least they fight! That’s more than can be said about the only team behind them in the rankings. The Dolphins don’t have much talent, but one week after keeping it close against the undefeated Vikings, they at least hung around with Cincinnati.
Analysis (on the biggest issue on defense, rushing the passer): It took the Dolphins until the first snap of their fourth game of the season to record their first sack; they have the NFL's second-worst sack rate. Their issues pressuring opposing quarterbacks has compounded into easy completions -- Miami ranks last in both opposing QBR and completion percentage. Going into the season, the Dolphins were thin at pass rusher behind Chop Robinson, but the 2024 first-round pick also started slow. With one of the NFL's youngest secondaries, Miami will continue to struggle against the pass until it can impact opposing QBs more consistently. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques
Pro Football Talk (Mike Florio)
Analysis: 32. Maybe Jon-Eric Sullivan and Jeff Hafley should have waited a year.
Sports Illustrated (Conor Orr)
Analysis: This week’s installment of Jacob Rodriguez corner: He’s leading the league in tackles but he just wants a W. How do you not love this guy?
Yahoo Sports (Frank Schwab)
Analysis: The good news for the Dolphins is they won't lose in Week 6. They have a bye. Good for the Dolphins to lose by only seven points against the Bengals on Sunday, but the true story of the game was a 28-10 deficit after three quarters. The Dolphins have trailed by at least 14 points in four of five games. There are two main goals after the bye: getting one win to avoid the 0-17 questions, and finding out if Malik Willis can be the quarterback of the future. A decision in the 2027 NFL Draft looms. Willis was 1-for-7 passing for 22 yards with a minute to go in the first half Sunday. He threw two interceptions and lost a fumble. It wasn't good enough, and garbage-time stats don't fix that. Of 32 qualified quarterbacks he's 30th in adjusted EPA (expected points added) per play and 29th in success rate. It is hard to judge Willis fairly because there's not much talent around him, but he has to prove he can elevate his teammates.

title: What to Know About New Dolphins WR Jared Wayne and the Latest Wave of Tryout Players
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are in their bye week, but the quest to upgrade their roster never takes a break.
Miami made a swap of wide receivers on their 53-man roster Tuesday when they waived Ryan Miller and claimed Jared Wayne off waivers from the Houston Texans. They also made some moves on the practice squad, signing defensive lineman Jordan Jefferson and releasing former Dallas Cowboys first-round pick Mazi Smith.
Additionally, the team continued its series of tryouts with 10 more players, including Jefferson.
It's been a long time coming for Wayne after he went undrafted in 2023. He made his NFL debut in 2024 but had appeared in only four games before playing in all five games for Houston this season, producing 65 yards on four receptions.
Wayne was waived by the Texans after they acquired Marvin Harrison Jr. from the Arizona Cardinals in a trade Sunday.
At this point, any additions are welcome. The Dolphins currently average 153.6 passing yards per game, the lowest in the NFL. Part of this issue can come from the inconsistency at the wide receiver position. Aside from Malik Washington, who has been reliable enough, the door is wide open for Wayne to become another option for Malik Willis to throw to.
Caleb Douglas showed exciting upside when he's healthy, but he missed the past three games because of an ankle injury. Chris Bell, meanwhile, was almost a non-factor in Miami's loss to Cincinnati , which could partially be his own doing thanks to some struggles creating separation.
Coming out of Pittsburgh, there was upside ahead of the 2023 Draft for Wayne, according to his draft profile. The frame is there at 6-3, 210 pounds. More than anything, though, Wayne is a strong receiver who can battle through contested catches. In addition, something that Miami might want to consider is his ability to serve as an efficient run blocker, which is a welcome attribute in an offense that can live and die on the run.
With that said, the route-running, speed, and acceleration have left a lot to be desired in his skill set, according to his draft profile and his inability to create separation could be reminiscent of Bell's struggles.
The Dolphins have held tryouts for a mix of veterans seeking another chance to get on the field and college graduates looking for an opportunity after being waived during final roster cuts August 30. Still, any chance at improvement is welcome when you're 0-5.
As mentioned at the top, Jefferson joins the Dolphins' practice squad following stops at four different teams: Jacksonville (2024 fourth-round pick), San Francisco, Cincinnati, and the Los Angeles Chargers. He's been waived by every single team he's played for, having only 12 tackles and a sack in his NFL career so far.
One name that stands out is running back Jerome Ford, who is currently in his fifth year in the NFL. He was prominent in 2023 and 2024 with Cleveland, taking over for an injured Nick Chubb before falling to the third-string role in 2025, partly due to a shoulder injury.
Defensive back Cobee Bryant could have potential based on his college resume alone. With Kansas, he showcased impressive longevity, earning three First-Team All-Big 12 Awards. He signed with Atlanta in 2025 after going undrafted, but hasn't had the opportunity to blossom in the league, recording 10 tackles and a pass deflection for the Falcons in 2025.
Tryouts are absolutely no guarantee that a player will be signed. They can simply be a shot for an unproven player to showcase their talent to an NFL coaching staff, and quarterback Jacob Clark did just that. He spent most of his college career at Missouri State, leading the Bears to their first bowl game in their first year in FBS as members of Conference USA in 2025.
Similarly, center Jaren Kump won't be vying for snaps at the position with the Dolphins anytime soon, but he did showcase flexibility at Utah by being a multi-year starter at all five positions in the trenches. He was part of a phenomenal O-line for the Utes, which also featured Cleveland's 2026 first-round pick, Spencer Fano.
Miami Hurricanes fans might recall linebacker Jahfari Harvey, who was a member of the Canes from 2019 to 2023 before transferring to SMU in 2024. He went undrafted and signed with Las Vegas in 2025 before being waived and re-signed to either the practice squad or the active roster three times in that year alone. He showcased solid pursuit and doubled as a pass rusher in college, but he hasn't had the opportunity to make the most of his versatility in the NFL just yet.
Unlike some players on this list, cornerback Dwight McGlothern didn't have trouble finding the field, appearing in 15 games for Minnesota since signing in 2024. However, he only managed a single pass deflection in 2024, and there are no listed stats for 2025. He was remarked as a ball-hawk coming out of college at Arkansas, specializing in zone coverage but being weak against the run.
Linebacker Jeremiah Moon signed with Baltimore as an undrafted free agent in 2022 before being waived, then signing with both Pittsburgh and Carolina not once, but twice from 2024 to 2026. All in all, he's appeared in 25 games and has recorded 31 tackles and two forced fumbles. Strength is his specialty in the NFL, as it was in college at Florida, but if he were to find a home with Miami, it might be for punt coverage, as it was something he was known to do with the Gators.
Likewise, tight end Messiah Swinson's list of NFL teams since 2024 is a bit convoluted, but the bottom line is that he hasn't had an opportunity to record playing time with Green Bay, Carolina, San Francisco, Arizona, or Cleveland. He was a solid target in the red zone at Arizona State, but of all the players on this list, he might have the least chance of landing a spot on Miami, almost solely due to a lack of film and a lack of need at the position.
Offensive tackle Da'Metrius Weatherspoon was a recent release from New England's practice squad. This followed a stellar season for Syracuse in 2025, mainly served as a right tackle but did start one game at left guard. He only allowed four sacks and committed three penalties in 817 snaps, and was the highest-rated player on the Orange's offense, with a 76.5 rating, according to Pro Football Focus.

title: Dolphins Week 5 Report Card: Running Game Delivers, but Mistakes Keep Miami Winless
full_text:
There’s the cliché that numbers never lie, but don’t put too much stock in the final score of this one.
The Miami Dolphins may have lost against the Cincinnati Bengals 31-24, but an impending mistake always felt around the corner.
Cincinnati led 28-10 entering the fourth quarter before Miami’s late touchdowns made things look more competitive.
As the score shows, the Dolphins found ways to produce while rushing for 217 yards and outgaining Cincinnati 331-307 and finishing with more first downs, but three turnovers and another special teams breakdown helped turn any advantages into a loss at Hard Rock Stadium.
Here’s how each position group graded out as Miami fell to 0-5.
After giving Malik Willis some time to adjust to leading a new, inexperienced team, the past couple of weeks have made it clear that pointing to the problems around him can’t explain away his own glaring flaws.
Willis completed 15 of 27 passes for 137 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions, finishing with a 51.0 passer rating. He also fumbled twice, losing one with the Dolphins trailing by 10 late in the fourth quarter.
His first interception came on a tipped pass, when Boye Mafe batted a pass intended for Kevin Coleman Jr., and Jordan Battle came down with the deflection, but the second was a much more avoidable mistake, with Willis throwing back across his body while scrambling and finding Battle again.
And that’s where the feeling of an impending mistake was proven to be correct. Miami had just recovered a Cincinnati fumble near its own goal line, but three offensive plays later, the Bengals had the ball back and were on their way to a 21-7 lead.
The third-quarter goal-line possession was another costly example. After Gordon was stopped for a loss from the 1, Willis took an 8-yard sack on second-and-goal from the 3, a mistake he took responsibility for after the game. Miami eventually settled for a field goal.
He did throw a touchdown, however, rolling to his right and finding Kevin Coleman Jr. in the back of the end zone for a 3-yard score in the fourth quarter, the rookie’s first NFL touchdown.
His legs are still a weapon, as he rushed for 74 yards and a touchdown, including a 39-yard scamper on third-and-13 that helped launch Miami’s first fourth-quarter touchdown drive.
Losing De’Von Achane would have sounded like one of Miami’s biggest potential crises, but Ollie Gordon II looks right at home in an offense that wants to load up on blockers and run through people.
A week after rushing for 100 yards against Minnesota, Gordon followed it up with 88 yards and a touchdown on 18 carries. The Oklahoma State product ranks sixth in rushing yards across Weeks 4 and 5, with 188, through Sunday night.
His 22-yard run on third-and-10 helped keep Miami’s opening possession alive, and he eventually finished that drive with a 1-yard touchdown. He also put together runs of 7, 10 and 13 yards during the third-quarter drive that reached Cincinnati’s 1-yard line.
After Miami got just 2.8 yards per attempt out of the sixth-round pick during his rookie campaign in 2025, Gordon II has thrived off being able to find a rhythm without the one-dimensional predictability that came with being a 6-foot-2, 225-pound back used only in short-yardage situations.
Jaylen Wright continued to struggle, managing 11 yards on six carries. Three of those attempts came while Gordon II briefly was sidelined with an injury early in the fourth quarter.
Malik Washington continues to be Miami’s most reliable receiving option, catching six of eight targets for 43 yards. He also continued to mix in snaps out of the backfield, adding an 18-yard run.
But he averaged just over 7 yards per reception Sunday, and his skill set is better suited to being a reliable, complementary slot option than carrying a team’s entire aerial attack.
Coleman offered more this week, catching three passes for 30 yards, including a 3-yard touchdown and a 23-yard reception that set up Willis’ late rushing score. That said, with Coleman offering a similar but less developed skill set to Washington’s, Miami is yearning for a true No. 1 outside receiver who can put pressure on defenses at every level.
Jalen Tolbert added a 22-yard catch. Chris Bell didn’t record a reception, but his 26-yard reverse helped get Miami into scoring position in the third quarter. His fourth-quarter false start also helped create the third-and-13 that Willis had to escape.
Greg Dulcich caught four of five targets for 37 yards and added the two-point conversion after Coleman’s touchdown.
His 13-yard reception converted fourth-and-1 near the end of the first half, although Miami ran out of time before turning that possession into points. He also moved the chains on third-and-5 during the final touchdown drive.
Will Kacmarek caught just one pass for 5 yards, but on Bell’s 26-yard run, he led the way up the right side of the field before laying a solid block on Bengals cornerback DJ Turner II to help Bell pick up a first down.
Miami averaged 6.4 yards on 34 rushing attempts, with Gordon, Willis, Washington and Bell all producing runs of at least 18 yards.
Willis’ scrambling helped that average, but Gordon’s 88 yards also showed consistency in the ground game.
Unlike last week, no gain was wiped out by a holding penalty.
The protection still had costly breakdowns, however, as Cincinnati finished with three sacks for 23 yards, including Jonathan Allen’s late strip-sack.
That said, Willis’ 8-yard loss near the goal line shows how a quarterback’s decision to keep a play alive can make the protection look worse.
The unit had to adjust after right guard Jonah Savaiinaea left with an ankle injury in the second quarter, with Jarrett Kingston replacing him.
A week after finally collecting their first four sacks of the season, the Dolphins finished with none while also allowing 117 rushing yards
Chop Robinson hit Joe Burrow twice, but Cincinnati’s star quarterback still threw four touchdown passes without an interception.
The Bengals’ rushing total was more a product of volume than efficiency, as Cincinnati ran the ball 31 times for an average of just 3.8 yards per carry. But the bigger problem was how often the Bengals kept possessions alive while converting nine of 13 third downs.
Robinson seemed to come through on a desperately needed fourth-quarter sack with Miami trailing 28-18, only to erase it himself with an offside penalty. Cincinnati received a first down and kept draining the clock. Zach Sieler later turned third-and-7 into third-and-2 with an encroachment penalty, although the defense eventually forced a punt.
Josh Uche did help preserve Miami’s second-quarter takeaway, recovering the ball after Robinson fumbled during his return.
Rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez finished with a team-high 11 tackles, but Mike Gesicki beat him on a double move, selling an inside break just long enough to freeze Rodriguez before catching a red-zone touchdown.
With 11:51 left in the second quarter, he gave up another touchdown after allowing Samaje Perine to cut inside of him on an angle route.
Burrow’s third touchdown pass went to Tanner Hudson with Willie Gay Jr. in coverage.
Cincinnati converted seven of eight third downs in the first half, and its first three touchdowns went to two tight ends and a running back.
The secondary made some of Miami’s most important defensive plays.
Chris Johnson forced Chase Brown’s second-quarter fumble near the goal line, and rookie Michael Taaffe also forced a fumble earlier in that possession, but Miami’s recovery was reversed after the referees determined that Gay Jr. was out of bounds after picking up the ball.
Taaffe left with a chest injury before returning, while JuJu Brents dealt with injuries and eventually was ruled out with a stinger.
Jason Marshall Jr. surrendered the game’s biggest passing play, Chase’s 45-yard touchdown late in the third quarter. The second-year cornerback was close enough to contest the catch, but jumped a step early,…

title: Good NFL News for Johnson As He Continues to Deliver for the Dolphins
full_text:
Things have been moving in the right direction for Miami Dolphins rookie Chris Johnson since a rough start to the season.
His performance keeps getting better every week to the point he's as effective as any rookie on the roster — yes, even on a par with the much more heralded Jacob Rodriguez.
And there's been good news on the field as well for Johnson, who successfully appealed his NFL fine resulting from a tackle against Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty.
In addition to getting back the $17,911 he had been fined for a hip-drop tackle — and remember that there was no flag on the play — Johnson also saw disappear one of his three strikes for that particular violation.
As part of a new rule in 2026, repeat offenders in one of three categories now can be suspended for a game with three violations, and hip-drop tackles is one of them — the other two are blindside blocks and hits on a defenseless player.
So now Johnson has his fine money back and he's again got a clean slate with the league.
On the field, Johnson has come a long way since that opener against the Raiders when he was victimized for a couple of touchdown passes.
His performance in Week 5 against the Cincinnati Bengals might have been his best yet, and it went beyond the forced fumble he produced with a perfectly executed "Peanut punch" in the second half.
While we understand that Pro Football Focus' grades shouldn't be viewed as the ultimate gauge, their game-by-game grades for Johnson have indicated the steady and consistent progress everybody who has watched Dolphins games can plainly see.
PFF gave Johnson an 86.9 overall grade for Week 5, his third consecutive game with at least a 69 mark after he was under 50 for the first two games against the Raiders and San Francisco 49ers.
"I thought Chris had a solid game," Hafley said of Johnson's work against Cincinnati. "There's a couple plays where, just like any of us, I'm sure that he wants back, but I see the confidence overall just growing with him. I mean, you can see it when he's playing out there. Early in the season, when he had some moments where guys caught balls on him, I kind of didn't feel like the response was where we needed it to be. I don't feel that anymore. I thought this was a big test for him with the wide receivers they had as a rookie and overall, I'd say he answered it pretty well and regardless of the outcome of certain plays, I love the confidence and the energy that he's playing with."
What always needs to be mentioned when discussing Johnson  is the fact he continues to split time between the slot and outside, a difficult assignment for any cornerback, let alone a rookie.
Whether inside or outside, what's been consistent about Johnson has been his tackling ability, which would have to be considered high end for a cornerback.
Because he hasn't gotten an interception just yet and because of the bend-but-don't-break style of defense the Dolphins have employed, where they're willing to give up underneath completions to protect against the deep ball, Johnson has flown under the radar a lot more than Rodriguez, who keeps racking up the tackles, but the Dolphins have reason to be as excited right now about Johnson's future potential as that of Rodriguez, with the two making up a good start for a foundation on defense.

title: Breaking Down the Latest Dolphins Practice Squad Moves
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' latest practice squad moves was most noteworthy for the player they let go than the one they brought back.
The team announced Tuesday morning they had signed quarterback Brady Cook to the practice and released running back Jarquez Hunter to make room.
The move with Cook should have been expected (and was predicted here) because the Dolphins need three quarterbacks, even if one of them is on the practice squad.
Cook was on the 53-man roster for the first four games before he was waived Saturday to make room for defensive tackle Kenneth Grant being activated off injured reserve.
The Dolphins did not a minor gamble in another team claiming Cook off waivers, though it seemed pretty safe that it wouldn't happen.
While it's always a possibility that he will be brought back to the practice squad, this move seems to end the Jarquez Hunter experiment that began when he was acquired in a summer trade from the Los Angeles Rams in exchange for veteran wide receiver.
A fourth-round pick out of Auburn in 2025, Hunter represented the kind of player the Dolphins have been looking to investigate and evaluate as they look for hidden gems to carry along beyond this season.
But Hunter never made enough of an impression to earn playing time in Miami.
While he didn't have a chance for the 53-man roster because he was acquired the day before the preseason finale, Hunter saw training camp running back Carlos Washington Jr. overtake him on the depth chart, with Washington getting the call the last two games with injuries at running back.
And then it really was over for Hunter when the Dolphins claimed rookie running back Kaytron Allen off waivers from the New Orleans Saints late last week.
While the move didn't pan out, acquiring Hunter still was a good move because it was a no-risk deal with the potential for good value, and that's because Atwell wasn't going to make the 53-man roster coming out of training camp. He was going to be released, and the trade actually took the Dolphins off the hook for the small guaranteed salary they had committed to Atwell.
Hunter panning out would have been a great bonus. That it didn't happen was no big deal, but it again proved the idea that we've repeated many times about tempering expectations whenever the Dolphins bring in a player who basically was discarded by another organization.

title: What the Week 5 Film Told Us About the Miami Dolphins
full_text:
In the Miami Dolphins' 31-24 loss against the Cincinnati Bengals, a poor mixture of talent and scheme was the difference, but the youth continued to shine. Let's take a look at some of the film from the Week 5 game, along with some key takeaways.
Joe Burrow picked apart the Dolphins’ defense underneath in Week 5. Pending Monday Night Football, he was sixth in EPA per dropback on dropbacks of less than 2.5 seconds and eighth in the same stat on throws of fewer than 10 air yards.
pic.twitter.com/KXcIrAzve5
Burrow was decisive against a defense that dedicated their second- and third-level defenders to stopping over-the-top throws to Ja’Marr Chase or Tee Higgins. On this play, Miami’s quarters look ends up playing similar to a prevent coverage, with the linebackers dropping too deep, leaving Chase Brown open for a ten-yard gain.
It’s a perfect storm of miscues for Miami right now. Their umbrella coverages put too much stress on the linebackers, who haven’t been up to snuff in coverage. Meanwhile, with Chop Robinson receiving chip help and double teams throughout this game, the Dolphins don’t have someone up front who can force the issue. It’s a marriage of below-average personnel with a scheme that’s sticking with the philosophy of limiting possessions, even when the quarterback is more than willing to take the checkdown.
Much like the defensive struggles, Miami’s passing offense garners blame for just about everyone involved. Bobby Slowik couldn’t consistently scheme targets open, the receivers struggled to create separation, and Malik Willis made several back-breaking errors.
Slowik’s designs clearly draw inspiration from his former boss, Mike McDaniel. The issue is, some of these concepts already had outworn their welcome, and without Tyreek Hill or Jaylen Waddle, they’re simply not an efficient way to use your eligible receivers.
pic.twitter.com/1NRVDNxXdi
On too many occasions, there are only two or three receivers out on routes, and in this case, it’s paired with a long-developing play-fake. On second-and-10, Cincinnati’s backers are able to drop into the intermediate window, and Chris Bell can’t sufficiently break the press.
Regardless of the long-term outlook for Bell or Kevin Coleman Jr., Miami does not have the quality of pass-catchers right now to make these looks a staple. To make things easier on Willis, it may be in their best interest to opt for quantity and attack more of the field with their route designs.
pic.twitter.com/sL0MxXtmgO
This doesn’t absolve Willis, who made multiple abysmal decisions in this game. His process has been slow, he hasn’t been willing to move off of his downfield reads, and his awareness of his immediate surroundings has made already poor situations worse.
One of the few positives from this game was that the rookie class continues to show out. This was easily the best game of Chris Johnson’s young career. On top of a forced fumble, I was particularly impressed by a pass-rush rep where he fought through the blocks of three different players to pressure Joe Burrow.
pic.twitter.com/s2uzbkfF7q
Kadyn Proctor and Will Kacmarek also have continued to showcase their physicality. On a toss play to Malik Washington, Proctor was able to cut off Dexter Lawrence while Kacmarek made a crucial crack block on Boye Mafe.
pic.twitter.com/3arYuNtlT4
This class already has shown considerable promise, and if they keep it up, they’ll set the foundation for this Dolphins team by the time they’re ready to compete.

title: Why Dolphins Coach Is Right in Squashing Idea of Benching Willis
full_text:
The question truly was ridiculous, except it needed to be asked because it's fans are talking about it and would want to ask the question themselves, and journalists are conduits between fans and coaches.
So it was that the first question in Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley's regular day-after-the-game media session Monday was this: "Are you giving any thought to starting Kyle McCord against the Jets after the bye?"
That would be quarterback Kyle McCord and the suggestion was whether Malik Willis' performance and stats through five games and maybe even in the Week 5 loss against the Cincinnati Bengals was enough to considering making a change.
But Hafley quickly, and absolutely correctly, shot down that notion.
And the thinking in saying so?
"We've played five games, and Malik is our quarterback."
During the remainder of his 20-minute session, Hafley was asked other questions about Willis and he made it clear that he expects better from his starting quarterback while also indicating that several factors are involved in the success — or lack thereof — of the passing game, such as pass protection and receivers running the correct routes and getting open.
All of it is off right now, up to and including Willis.
Before the Week 5 Monday night game, Willis was last among 29 qualifying quarterbacks in passer rating and completion percentage with only two touchdown passes against four interceptions.
There is nobody who should be happy with Willis' work so far this season or think it's anywhere near good enough for him to even begin being considered as a long-term answer.
And it's five games with a young and sub-par supporting cast, one that's been without it's best player (De'Von Achane) for almost three games and without its most dynamic wide receiver at the moment (Caleb Douglas) for three-plus games.
Remember when some folks were calling the Dolphins wide receiver corps about as bad a group as there's been in the NFL in a long time? Well, that group always was about long-term potential and that potential has not been reached yet.
And let's also not pretend that Willis has benefited from great pass protection, either, because pressure is getting there in a hurry on a pretty regular basis.
This isn't to excuse everything that Willis has struggled with, but it absolutely does explain some of the poor numbers.
"I think you guys are going to get tired of my answers however the questions are phrased, it's everything," Hafley said. "It's a detail of the route running. It starts with the protection. It's going through the progression. It's everybody being on the same page, and everybody being more efficient in their 1/11."
But, of course, the quarterback is the one who's going to be in the spotlight and Willis also is the one outside free agent the Dolphins signed all year for something beyond the minimum or almost-minimum salary.
Hafley and GM Jon-Eric Sullivan talked about Willis in terms of handing him the keys to the offense and building around him, and so far that construction project is not looking very good.
But would it make any sense whatsoever to give up after five games?
Or even go with this idea of having Willis sit for a bit and give Kyle McCord a shot to see what he can do?
Sure, the idea of McCord might be intriguing for those who liked him at Syracuse, but do we need to remind everyone that after the Philadelphia Eagles selected him in the sixth round of the 2025 draft, they waived him and then let him leave off their practice squad for Green Bay this year, only to have the Packers trade him to the Dolphins for a 2028 sixth-round pick?
Again, let's repeat that: 2028 sixth-round pick. Using the gauge of dropping a pick for every year down the road, that's the equivalent of a 2026 eighth-round pick.
Yes, the Packers don't believe in keeping three QBs on their roster, but if they valued McCord, would they have basically just given him away like that, much the same way the Dolphins gave away Quinn Ewers?
Maybe McCord will become a good NFL quarterback at some point, but the reality is it's probably a long shot.
And maybe the same holds true for Willis.
Except that Willis actually has appeared in an NFL regular season game and he actually looked very good doing it during his time with the Packers, where Hafley and Sullivan also got to watch him first-hand on a daily basis.
What's happened so far in the 2026 season probably isn't what they had in mind or hoped, but suggesting for even a millisecond they would give up on Willis this quickly bordered on ridiculous.
The Dolphins have 12 games remaining in the 2026 regular season and that's plenty of time for things to change, to get better with Willis, the passing game and the entire offense.
None of it is good enough right now. But the Dolphins don't have to make any decisions right now as it applies to 2027 and they owe it to Willis and more importantly to themselves to give him a chance to show what he can do.

title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 5 Snap Counts Stories: Injuries Cause Shuffling
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 31-24 loss against the Cincinnati Bengals on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, which was highlighted by four players missing the game with injuries, including wide receiver Caleb Douglas out for a third consecutive game with an ankle injury.
The only Dolphins player who was active but did not play was backup quarterback Kyle McCord.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to six rookies Will Kacmarek at tight end, Chris Bell at wide receiver, guard Kadyn Proctor, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- The Dolphins opened with two tight ends and two wide receivers, which was why rookie fullback DJ Herman didn't get a start.
-- After the Dolphins had only 39 offensive snaps against Minnesota, that number jumped to a lot more respectable 66 against the Bengals.
-- After playing fewer snaps than Kacmarek against Minnesota, Greg Dulcich got a very heavy work load in Week 5 with 49 offensive snaps. That was his second-highest total of the season behind the 51 he played against the Kansas City Chiefs in the Week 3 home opener.
-- Besides QB Malik Wilis and the offensive linemen, the player with the most offensive snaps was wide receiver Malik Washington with 53, yet another indication of his value.
-- At running back, practice squad elevation Carlos Washington Jr. got as many offensive snaps at Jaylen Wright, who continues to struggle to find his footing in his third season with the Dolphins. Ollie Gordon II got 43 snaps firmly established as the No. 1 back in the absence of De'Von Achane.
-- Jonah Savaiinaea ended up playing 18 snaps before leaving the game with an ankle injury and being replaced by Jarrett Kingston for the final 48 snaps at right guard.
-- Rookie tight end Seydou Traore got his first offensive snap against the Bengals after being used exclusively on special teams in the first four games — but it was only one.
-- With Jordyn Brooks, JuJu Brents and Michael Taaffe all temporarily leaving the game with injuries, Jacob Rodriguez and Dante Trader Jr. became the only players who played every snap on defense.
-- 2025 first-round pick Kenneth Grant made his return to action but played a very modest 16 defensive snaps, which probably made sense in helping him work his way back into the action. That number better increase once the Dolphins return from their bye, though.
-- The Dolphins opened the game in the nickel and played a good portion of the game with that five-DB alignment, with Chris Johnson Jr. playing 64 of the 65 snaps and Jason Marshall also played 57 snaps.
-- Josh Uche, who's become the most effective edge defender on the team, got the snap count to reflect that, with 45 snaps compared to 36 for Chop Robinson. Practice squad elevation Rodney McGraw played 14 snaps, not far behind Malik Herring.
-- With Brooks leaving the game temporarily, Willie Gay Jr. got extra work at linebacker and finished with 37 snaps, his highest total since the opener against the Las Vegas Raiders when the Dolphins used a lot more three-linebacker looks.
-- With Brents missing some snaps when he was banged up, newcomer Jaylin Simpson got five snaps on defense and had a nice third-down pass breakup against Ja'Marr Chase.
-- Because of the injuries, only four non-specialists saw action only on special teams, down from eight against Minnesota. This time it was Andre Jones Jr., Julius Wood, Marcellus Dial Jr. and Andrew Meyer.
-- Speaking of special teams, Traore again led the way with 21 snaps, followed by 17 for Jones and 15 for McGraw.

title: Four Losers And Four Winners From the Week 5 Dolphins Loss
full_text:
Don't let the 31-24 final score deceive you; this was not a close game between the Miami Dolphins and Cincinnati Bengals. In an important game for Cincy regarding the standings in the AFC North, they took care of business and handed the Fins their fifth straight loss.
At the minimum, if you're looking for player and team progression in the same vain as the Minnesota game, you won't find it here. The offense was stonewalled for three quarters, only finding rhythm when it was too late, and the defense gave up over 300 total yards and four touchdowns.
The Dolphins head into the bye week battered and bruised, figuratively and literally, and worst of all, still searching for answers. Only three teams remain winless in the NFL: Miami, Tennessee, and the Los Angeles Chargers. Based on their performances against the Bengals, it's difficult to predict when they'll finally shower Jeff Hafley with Gatorade.
Yes, Willis doesn't have a star-studded list of weapons to throw to. But Willis flat-out held the offense back, was unable to deal with Cincinnati's commanding front seven, and was more of a liability in the passing game than ever before.
Regardless of how you felt about the comments that Bengals DB Jordan Battle made about Willis's ball-tapping and how it's a tell that he's going to throw the ball, is it purely a coincidence that the DB who caught both interceptions that Willis threw was Battle?
Willis also lost a fumble pretty much by himself near his own goal line and was sacked three times. One of those sacks came on second-and-goal in the third quarter — a case of holding onto the ball for too long, trying to make an impossible play happen instead of throwing the ball away — a consistent mistake he's made this season.
To his credit, he looked decent as a scrambler with 74 yards and a touchdown, but this was by far his worst game of the season purely from a mistake standpoint. His game looks extremely limited, and because the weapons at his disposal are also limited, you get an offensive performance like the Dolphins got against the Bengals — simply not good enough.
Johnson and Miami's secondary had a tough task against Cincinnati since two of their wide receivers, who were questionable — Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins — ended up playing. But Johnson held his own with six total tackles, a low number because he locked down most receivers he was matched up against.
Like the other rookies on defense, Johnson also achieved his first major highlight of the season, a Peanut punch on Chase Brown in the red zone, forcing a fumble that was picked up by Chop Robinson — ignore that Robinson also had the ball punched out, only for JuJu Brents to corral it in the end.
There were only a handful of receptions that Johnson gave up, but nothing major. He may have had a slow start to the season in terms of effectiveness, but he's heating up for the Dolphins at a solid pace.
After being stuffed by the Minnesota defense, Wright needed a bounce-back game to genuinely help out this offense whenever he was on the field, but once again, he was made a non-factor — six carries for 11 yards.
The offensive line has been able (for the most part) to create gaps for Miami's running backs, but Wright's running can be predictable, purely horizontal, and he's been unable to either evade or shake off tacklers in the same way that Ollie Gordon has been able to do.
Both wide receivers Chris Bell and Malik Washington  were both used in the running game for one play each and recorded more rushing yards than Wright (26 & 18). Miami's duo in the backfield was once De'Von Achane and Gordon, and now it's forced to be Gordon and Willis because Wright isn't doing enough to justify remaining the backup running back.
It might not look like much, but Coleman had a breakout game for the Dolphins that was well-needed — three receptions for 30 yards off seven targets, including his first touchdown in the NFL that came in the fourth quarter, beginning a way-too-late rally for Miami that obviously fell short.
Miami's fifth-round pick showcased the ability to create separation even with limited space, headlined by the aforementioned touchdown. He also showcased his athleticism when he dove for a catch at the six-yard line with a minute to go, leading to Willis sneaking into the end zone right after.
Caleb Douglas is still injured and, spoiler alert, Chris Bell had a disappointing game. So, seeing Coleman have the performance he did is reassuring, and maybe Miami's offense could turn to him more often as the season progresses.
The aforementioned "rush" for Bell was an end-around play that he made the most of, assisted by solid blocking from both Kadyn Proctor and Will Kacmarek. As a receiver, Bell was targeted twice but did not record a single reception.
It feels like a combination of the Dolphins not utilizing him as much as they could, along with Bell being unable to create distance between himself and the defensive backs he's matched up against. It's a problem that reared its ugly head against Minnesota and continued into this game.
All in all, it's clear the Dolphins are looking elsewhere in terms of who they want Willis to throw to, and when Douglas is once again available, it wouldn't be shocking to see Bell's already small snap count be erased.
Things got scary for Brooks when he suffered a foot injury in the first half. He would return later on in the game and still come away with eight tackles, tied for the second-most in this game.
Aside from showing the toughness and grit that's to be expected from a veteran like Brooks, he made good on his responsibility to limit tight ends following what TJ Hockenson was able to do for the Vikings. Erick All Jr. was held to 25 yards on three targets. Mike Gesiscki scored a touchdown on Cincinnati's opening drive, but didn't record a single reception the rest of the way.
We have our first coach on one of these lists, and it's been a long time coming for special teams coordinator Chris Tabor. Between the punting, kicking, returning, and especially fielding, this has been a horrific start to the season for the Dolphins, and the blame needs to fall on someone.
Miami, which hasn't had a lead all season, was denied one out of the gate when the Dolphins gave up an 81-yard return on the opening kickoff. Not long after, one of their kickoffs missed the landing zone, which would have placed the ball on the 40-yard line if not for a Cincinnati personal foul that set them back 15 yards.
Riley Patterson cashed in on a 29-yard field goal, but missed an extra point following the final touchdown with a minute to go. It ultimately didn't mean anything because the Dolphins didn't recover the ensuing onside kick, but what if they had? Since he missed the PAT, seven points would have forced overtime instead of winning the game outright.
Bradley Pinion, at the least, had a decent game with a pair of 57- and 59-yard punts, but this was another overall messy performance by the special teams. Miami's offense and defense have enough on their plates to worry about without the special teams putting them in awful situations.
Miami's safety net in the offense, Gordon had another quality game with 88 yards on 18 carries and a touchdown in the first half. Thankfully, his visit to the blue medical tent was brief, and he immediately returned to the game.
The only "negative" you could say about Gordon was that his emotions spilled out on the sidelines, which was caught on video from multiple angles. It occurred following Miami's field goal in the third quarter, despite the offense having a first-and-goal on the 1-yard line.
But honestly, Miami's offense has played and looked so stale up to this point that the outburst from Gordon was genuinely a welcome sign. It shows he cares and wants to see the offense improve more than any other player or even coach for the Dolphins.

title: 5 Roster Concerns Vikings Must Address Before Bye Week Is Over
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings are fortunate to be 5-0 entering their bye week. An anemic offense has been helped out immensely by a stout defense and excellent special teams play, but that formula will not last all season long.
There are some issues that the Vikings need to address during their bye week to stay competitive for the rest of the season. Some of those changes can be made internally, while others may need to come from free agency or a trade.
Let's take a look at some areas Minnesota needs to evaluate while they have no game in Week 6. Unsurprisingly, most of these areas are on the offensive side of the ball.
Aaron Jones Sr. has done an admirable job carrying the running back position while Jordan Mason was on injured reserve healing from thumb surgery. Jones played through a knee injury during that time and got little to no help from rookie Demond Claiborne and veteran DeeJay Dallas.
Mason can return in Week 7 and take some of the pressure off Jones, but that is still a lot of wear and tear on the veteran's back. Unless head coach Kevin O'Connell thinks he can get some help out of Claiborne or Dallas, the Vikings may need to look for an established rusher to add to the mix for the remainder of the season.
Health has been an issue for the Vikings this season. Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison both missed time due to injuries, but it is the ineffectiveness of Jauan Jennings that is truly hurting Minnesota.
While Jefferson and Addison are great players, having a third wide receiver option would be a great benefit for quarterback Kyler Murray, but Jennings hasn't been that guy, and neither have Tai Felton or Myles Price.
Unless someone can step into that role, Minnesota will have to continue relying on tight ends or putting a lot of focus on their top two receivers, which isn't ideal for the offense.
T.J. Hockenson left the game against the Saints with a possible concussion and is currently in protocol. With blocking tight end Josh Oliver on IR with a torn bicep, Gavin Bartholomew and Ben Yurosek are left to pick up the slack.
Bartholomew and Yurosek looked good against New Orleans, so there might be enough trust in them not to look outside Minnesota for help, but nonetheless, it is a situation that general manager Nolan Teasley will need to keep an eye on.
Starting left tackle Christian Darrisaw missed last week's game due to a concussion, and starting left guard Donovan Jackson suffered a torn meniscus and will miss the remainder of the season. Those injuries raise concern for the left side of the offensive line.
Ryan Van Demark filled in at left tackle and Joe Huber covered left guard on Sunday. They held their own, but can they be trusted if they need to fill in for an extended time? That's the biggest question facing the offensive line.
The Vikings' defense has been amazing this year, but the team has an issue at safety. Veteran Harrison Smith is playing a much smaller number of snaps than in the past, which puts pressure on his teammates to play at a high level.
Josh Metellus has a Pro Football Focus grade of 40.2 this season. He is ranked No. 91 out of 96 qualifying safeties, which is definitely not good for a player who has been on the field for all 295 defensive snaps that Minnesota has played this year.
Minnesota has options at the position, but some are untested. Jacob Thomas and Jakobe Thomas are unproven, but could use an opportunity to see if they can help out the defensive backs until Metellus can get back on track.

title: 3 Vikings Changes I'd Make Over the Bye If I Were Kevin O'Connell
full_text:
The Vikings are undefeated at the bye, and it now provides the perfect break to implement a few changes going forward. While 5-0 is an impressive feat, things haven't always been sunshine and rainbows, and head coach Kevin O'Connell needs to take this extra time to fix a few troublesome spots.
After a perfect start, here's how I would handle the bye week if I were O'Connell, starting with a problem on offense.
With just two catches on the year, it's no secret things haven't been going according to plan with the addition of Jennings. Brought in to round out what was supposed to be one of the best receiving trios  in the league, Jennings is now at the forefront of NFL trade rumors after a less-than-ideal start with Minnesota.
While I do think the Vikings eventually move on from their prized free agent, I also don't think they should be in any rush to do it. The deadline is still weeks away, and if O'Connell and company can salvage this thing at all, it's going to happen over the bye. There are nearly a dozen other Vikings with more receiving yards than Jennings this season, so if they Vikings do truly value his skillset, there's no reason he can't get a few designed plays each game.
If Jennings comes out in Week 7 against the Indianapolis Colts without any obvious role in the offense, though, he's probably on his way out. It just doesn't make sense for either side to stay if neither is benefiting from the relationship.
After T.J. Hockenson exited just two plays into last week's win over the Saints, Bartholomew stepped up, and the drop-off was virtually non-existent . Maybe it's time the Vikings start to give their potential future starter some more looks.
Outside of his Week 4 13-catch eruption, Hockenson has just 10 catches for 83 yards in his other starts. That's certainly not unproductive, but after seeing Bartholomew notch five catches and what could have been another long touchdown if he were an inch or two taller, it's easy to see his role expanding in the future. With Hockenson turning 30 on an expiring deal, there's no guarantee he'll return to Minnesota in 2027. If the Vikings think that Bartholomew could be his successor, the litmus test couldn't have gone better, and it might be time to start splitting time.
Hockenson is currently in the protocol, but regardless of whether he clears in time for Week 7, O'Connell should try and work toward a 50/50 split between his two pass-catching tight ends.
The duo of Harrison Smith and Joshua Metellus have been the weak link on the otherwise dominant Vikings defense, and at 5-0, it's probably time the Vikings get serious about the position. Of the 96 safeties graded by Pro Football Focus , Smith and Metellus rank 95th and 91st respectively . They both still provide value, with Smith's brains and Metellus' downhill attacking, but adding a ball-hawking safety via trade may be the final piece to this defensive puzzle.
There are plenty of bad teams who may be sellers at the deadline, including the Los Angeles Chargers or Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and adding Derwin James Jr. or Antoine Winfield Jr. would be huge upgrades. Still, if O'Connell and general manager Nolan Teasley agree that the price isn't right for a trade, they'll have to start to get more production out of that group somehow. Potentially, one or both of the Thomas rookies could be ready for an increased snap count?
Either way, the already elite defense could become generational with some upgraded safety play, and the coaching staff needs to identify a different path forward.

title: Ranking 3 Vikings Most Likely to be Traded Before the Deadline
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings are 5-0 entering their Week 6 bye. Despite being undefeated, there is a lot of improvement that can be made on the roster to not only improve their situation this season but also prepare for the future.
There is no urgency for the Vikings to make a move before the November 10 trade deadline, but if a deal can be made that makes sense for both teams, it would be silly for Minnesota to dismiss the possibility of a change.
The defense is playing amazingly, and special teams have been great, but there could be some changes on offense for the Purple and Gold. Head coach Kevin O'Connell needs to find an offensive spark to complement the other phases of the game.
Last season, Jauan Jennings was a major offensive weapon for the San Francisco 49ers. In 15 games, he caught 55 passes for 643 yards and nine touchdowns. That production gave the Vikings hope that he could be a significant contributor for Minnesota this season.
Instead, Jennings has been a non-factor in 2026. In four games, he has caught two passes for nine yards on five targets while playing 201 offensive snaps. That production does not match his $8 million contract that Minnesota paid for his services this season.
The Vikings could attempt to get some kind of asset for him before the trade deadline instead of continuing to put him on the field. ESPN and NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport stated on "The Pat McAfee Show" that he " wouldn't be surprised " to see interest in him on the trade market.
Trading him would save Minnesota about $2.6 million against the salary cap.
Let's be honest, the Vikings probably don't want to trade away Jordan Addison. Minnesota announced that they will use the fifth-year option on his rookie contract, which will cost the team approximately $18 million.
If Addison plays on that fifth-year option in Minnesota, the team will need to sign him to a long-term extension to keep him around. Recent extensions for other WR2s around the league have been expensive, and the Vikings might not be willing to fork over around $20 million per year to retain his services.
Minnesota could get a decent draft pick or a quality player for Addison if they trade him. The team would likely rather not ship him out, but there are teams out there who might be willing to make the Vikings an offer they can't refuse.
This preseason, it was unclear how Ivan Pace Jr. would fit into the Vikings' defense . Eric Wilson and Blake Cashman are cemented as the starters, and rookie Jake Golday is working to find his role in Brian Flores' defense.
Pace could be a contributor on another team in need of a defender in the middle. This season, he has played 47 defensive snaps for Minnesota and 113 snaps on special teams, putting him on the field for 160 total snaps in five games played.
The bad part is that Pace has only accumulated 12 combined tackles, with two quarterback pressures and one QB knockdown in those reps. If Minnesota can get a mid-round pick for him, they could give his snaps to Golday and not lose production.

title: What the Vikings' Week 5 Win Changed About Their Trade Deadline Plans
full_text:
The Vikings are coming off their most complete game of the season and are now a perfect 5-0 as they head into their Week 6 bye . With the trade deadline less than a month away, the time off will provide the perfect opportunity to examine the needs of the roster.
And as one of the few remaining undefeated teams left, Minnesota will surely be buyers, right?
Despite the unblemished record, there are still plenty of skeptics downplaying the Vikings' perfect start. As of Tuesday afternoon, Minnesota was only tied for the ninth-best Super Bowl odds (+2000)—along with the Bears, Broncos and Patriots. And yet, it's hard to find a team playing better football than the Vikings right now.
Of course, the offense was quite literally the worst in the league early on, and the combined record of the opponents the Vikings have defeated is a lowly 8-17, so there's some fair criticism.
Still, barring another 2016 collapse, the Vikings are well on their way towards a playoff berth and could look to boost the roster via trade over the next few weeks.
After the bye, Minnesota will essentially be at full strength with the likely returns of Jordan Mason, Christian Darrisaw and T.J. Hockenson. Donovan Jackson is the only offensive starter already gone for the year, but finding a starting-caliber guard is typically easier said than done. Reserve lineman Joe Huber has filled in admirably and, given time, could be a solid replacement.
Beyond that, the Vikings don't seem keen on adding another running back unless it's to give him a week-long stay on the practice squad, and Gavin Bartholomew stepped up at tight end in the absence of Josh Oliver. The only logical move appearing to be gaining steam is dealing wide receiver Jauan Jennings, who has just two catches on the year. NFL insider Ian Rapoport reported on Tuesday that he wouldn't be surprised if the buzz increases moving forward.
From @PatMcAfeeShow : In the wake of the Marvin Harrison Jr trade, another WR whose trade market is expected to heat up is #Vikings WR Jauan Jennings. Would a #49ers reunion make sense? pic.twitter.com/DR6mY1OvYb
What was supposed to be the big-ticket free-agent signing (you remember all the Golden State Warriors/Big 3 comparisons), Jennings has instead been a complete afterthought in the Vikings' offense. There are 11 other Vikings with more receiving yards than Jennings after Week 5, and right now he's getting paid a lot of money to just get in some cardio on Sundays.
While moving Jennings for a pick clearly doesn't help the 2026 Vikings, maybe it'll give them the capital to go out and get someone who does.
On defense, the Vikings have been the best unit in the league through five weeks and have very few weaknesses to exploit. One looming issue, however, may be their concerning depth. Minnesota has stayed healthy so far, but if injuries rear their ugly heads, there are a lot of question marks behind the starters.
Eight of the defensive starters have played 80% of the snaps so far (h/t ESPN 's Kevin Seifert), including several untested rookies who haven't needed to step up yet. Caleb Banks, Domonique Orange, Jake Golday and others have played just sparingly, and Minnesota may not be ready to give them the nod just yet.
It's certainly something to watch, and if a key starter goes down, the Vikings may look to add a veteran, especially if they continue their march toward a potential playoff run.
Despite their record suggesting the Vikings should be buyers at the deadline, they will likely sit tight. Injuries haven't ravaged them like certain teams, and general manager Nolan Teasley has seemed very intent on holding onto his 2027 draft picks.
Apologies to the fans hoping for a splash trade, but unless a big injury hits, Jennings might be the only player on the move.
