title: Saints Must Accomplish 3 Things to End Minnesota's Perfect Start
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (1-3) enter Sunday's Week 5 matchup against the unbeaten Minnesota Vikings (4-0) looking to bounce back from a humbling 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night.
However, getting back on track won't be easy against a Minnesota team that has relied on one of the NFL's most dominant defenses to overcome its offensive struggles.
Sunday's matchup will also be a special occasion for the franchise as legendary quarterback Drew Brees will be inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor, adding even more significance to a game in which New Orleans desperately needs a victory.
For the Saints, the challenge will be giving their former quarterback and the home crowd something to celebrate while avoiding a third consecutive loss at the Caesars Superdome.
Doing so will require significant improvements on both sides of the ball, particularly against a Vikings defense that has consistently overwhelmed opposing offenses.
Here are three keys to victory for the Saints as they look to hand Minnesota its first loss of the season.
The Saints’ matchup against the Vikings will hinge on whether New Orleans can handle Minnesota’s league-leading blitz and pressure package. Minnesota enters Week 5 with arguably the NFL's best defense through four games, allowing a league-low 12.8 points per game while racking up 16 sacks, four interceptions and a plus-five turnover differential, the second-best mark in the league.
That is a major concern for a Saints offense that has struggled with consistency, protection, and turnovers. New Orleans has surrendered 12 sacks through four games, turned the ball over too often and enters Sunday with a minus-five turnover differential. Against a defense that thrives on disguising coverages, generating pressure from different alignments and forcing difficult decisions, the Saints cannot afford to fall behind early or repeatedly find themselves in obvious passing situations.
The biggest individual matchup is quarterback Tyler Shough against Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores ’ blitz-heavy system. Shough has already been sacked a dozen times this, with nine coming against the blitz, and New Orleans will need clear answers built into the game plan to avoid exposing him to the same issues again.
There are reasons for optimism. When Shough has gotten the ball out against blitzing defenses, he has been productive, posting a 105.1 passer rating while completing 71.9% of his passes and throwing for 442 yards, four touchdowns and one interception. But Minnesota has been uniquely effective at creating negative plays, and the Vikings’ No. 2 pressure rate will make life difficult if the Saints cannot keep the pocket clean.
Containing opposing top receivers has plagued the Saints through four games, making Sunday’s matchup against Vikings superstar Justin Jefferson a severe challenge.
Despite Minnesota ranking last in passing and 31st in total offense, Jefferson’s elite route-running, explosiveness, and contested-catch ability threaten New Orleans’ vulnerable secondary.
These defensive struggles were evident in Week 3 when Raiders tight end Brock Bowers posted 10 catches, 119 yards, and a touchdown from Kirk Cousins in Las Vegas' 31-28 win.
They continued Monday against Atlanta, as Drake London caught five passes for 96 yards, including a 37-yarder over Kool-Aid McKinstry , despite the Falcons leaning on the run.
New Orleans' secondary has struggled with missed tackles, blown coverages, penalties, and big plays.
Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. averaged 11.2 yards per attempt, going 15-for-20 for 223 yards and a touchdown.
Cornerbacks Quincy Riley (58 yards, TD allowed; 28.0 PFF grade) and McKinstry (60 yards allowed, two penalties; 29.5 PFF grade) were especially exploited.
These defensive flaws create major concerns facing Jefferson.
Unlike Bowers' versatile tight end mismatches or London's size, Jefferson combines route precision, speed, and versatility across alignments.
Leaving McKinstry or Riley isolated on Jefferson could prove disastrous for defensive coordinator Brandon Staley .
New Orleans must disguise coverages and offer safety help to force Kyler Murray elsewhere.
However, over-committing to Jefferson risks leaving tight end T.J. Hockenson (13 catches, 119 yards last week vs. Miami ) open underneath against an injured Saints linebacker corps.
Ultimately, New Orleans must force Minnesota into long, sustained drives without letting Jefferson dominate.
The four-game difference between these teams centers on protecting the football and capitalizing on errors.
Minnesota's plus-five turnover differential ranks tied for second-best in the NFL, whereas New Orleans ranks among the worst at minus-five. This 10-turnover gap clarifies how undefeated Minnesota overcomes an unproductive offense, while New Orleans loses despite averaging 367 yards and 26.3 points.
The Saints cannot afford to let turnovers, defensive breakdowns, and self-inflicted mistakes ruin offensive output against Minnesota's elite defense. Additionally, the Vikings lead the league in punt return average and rank second in kickoff return average, threatening a Saints squad already struggling with field position.
To succeed, New Orleans must secure the ball, limit penalties, convert in the red zone, force long drives, and avoid slow starts that play into Flores's pressure scheme. Even with Drew Brees honored at halftime and a supportive home crowd, emotional momentum will not offset repeated mistakes.

The New Orleans Saints will have their hands full Sunday when they welcome one of the NFL's remaining undefeated teams to the Caesars Superdome.
Coming off a 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night, New Orleans (1-3) will look to avoid its fourth consecutive defeat against a Minnesota Vikings team that has emerged as one of the NFL's early surprises.
Minnesota enters Week 5 with a 4-0 record following a 15-10 victory over the Miami Dolphins. While the Vikings haven't necessarily overwhelmed opponents offensively, their defense has been among the league's best, and they've consistently found ways to win close games.
Under head coach Kevin O'Connell , Minnesota has relied on a combination of aggressive defense, timely offensive production and an ability to capitalize on opponents' mistakes.
Here are three things Saints fans should know about the Vikings heading into Sunday's matchup.
Sunday’s matchup between the Saints and Vikings will hinge on whether New Orleans can handle Minnesota’s league-leading blitz and pressure package. Minnesota enters Week 5 with arguably the NFL's best defense through four games, allowing a league-low 12.8 points per game while racking up 16 sacks, four interceptions and a plus-five turnover differential, the second-best mark in the league.
That is a major concern for a Saints offense that has struggled with consistency, protection and turnovers. New Orleans has surrendered 12 sacks through four games, turned the ball over too often and enters Sunday with a minus-five turnover differential. New Orleans (1-3) will need to rely on a game plan that can sustain those positive trends under pressure. Without much help from the rushing attack, the Saints must produce through the air to pull out their first home win, and Minnesota is built to complicate exactly that.
A key question for Sunday's game is whether Minnesota All-Pro receiver Justin Jefferson will play.
Jefferson, who has 13 catches for 179 yards and two touchdowns in three games, is recovering from a Week 3 ankle injury. After missing last week's game against Miami, he returned to practice on a limited basis and has been listed as questionable for Sunday’s game.
With a bye following Sunday's game, Minnesota is evaluating whether to rest Jefferson to allow additional recovery time before Oct. 25, according to head coach Kevin O'Connell.
The Vikings face other offensive injury concerns: receiver Jordan Addison (hamstring) and tackle Brian O'Neill are also questionable, while tackle Christian Darrisaw will miss the game.
Jefferson's absence would aid a struggling Saints secondary, though Minnesota still retains offensive threats like tight end T.J. Hockenson .
Despite being undefeated, the Vikings have averaged just 21.5 points (18th in the NFL) and 263 yards per game.
Quarterback Kyler Murray has 433 passing yards, one touchdown and two interceptions. Running back Aaron Jones leads Minnesota with 297 rushing yards, while tight end T.J. Hockenson leads the team with 22 catches for 195 yards and one score.
In their 15-10 win over Miami, the Vikings did not score a single touchdown, highlighting their reliance on defense.
If New Orleans can contain Jones, limit Murray and force long third downs, it will have a chance to keep the game competitive. However, the Saints must still score against a formidable Minnesota defense to avoid another loss.

title: Giants’ Early Success Hinges on Winning the Line of Scrimmage
full_text:
Nobody said establishing a new identity overnight would be easy.
Head coach John Harbaugh wanted to transform the New York Giants into a team that would dominate the trenches on both sides of the ball, with an eye on returning the team to playoff contention in his first year on the job. So far, the road has included a few detours, but it’s still being paved in the right direction.
The Giants sit atop the NFC East at 3-1-1 and hold a two-game lead in the loss column over the rest of the division heading into Sunday’s game against the New Orleans Saints at MetLife Stadium. So, yes, they’ve gotten through nearly the first third of the season in good shape. However, they’re unlikely to maintain that course if they don’t win the line of scrimmage on both sides of the ball.
On offense, the running game has gained some traction in alternating games, putting up at least 100 yards in Weeks 1 (win), 3 (win) and 5 (tie). But they ran for just 52 and 87 yards in Weeks 2 (loss) and 4 (win).
“We definitely need more explosives in the run game. That’s definitely something that we’ll be chasing and looking for,” Harbaugh said this week.
“Every play has got its own story that is told. We look back at it and study it. I think everybody in the offense will tell you this play, that play, whatever. There’s always something we can do better. A lot of times it’s the difference in the play. It’s really our execution mostly, usually. Sometimes you’re overwhelmed with numbers or something like that. But there’s definitely been plays where we can get more yards on.”
The Giants lost control of the narrative in last week’s 27-27 tie at Washington, falling behind by 14 points midway through the fourth quarter.
Forced to go to the air, quarterback Jameis Winston went 33-of-54 for 326 yards and three TDs. It was four pass attempts short of his career high. It was the 29th time he’s thrown at least 40 passes in a game, the sixth of those without an interception and his most attempts without being picked off.
The defense is a bigger cause for concern. Opponents have run for 69, 163, 81, 123 and 202 yards through the first five weeks.
“Yeah, I think we’ve had too many chunk plays, overall. We’ve played kind of feast-or-famine run defense,” Harbaugh said.
How well will the Giants’ front fare against New Orleans, given that the Saints, who are weak in the trenches, can be expected to try to turn the day into a passing affair?

title: Dru Phillips Praises Giants Aggressive Defense: ‘Definitely a Fun Thing’
full_text:
New York Giants cornerback Dru Phillips might have a little “Cobra Kai” in him.
When it comes to pressuring the quarterback, New York’s third-year defensive back makes every effort to “strike first, strike hard, and show no mercy.”
In perhaps his best outing of the season to date, Phillips collected five total tackles, four quarterback hits, two sacks, and two tackles for loss in the Giants’ 27-27 tie with the Washington Commanders.
It’s no surprise that Phillips appears to be enjoying coordinator Dennard Wilson’s aggressive pass-defense style.
“It’s definitely a fun thing, yeah,” Phillips told reporters earlier this week. “It was cool to get out there and blitz a little bit.”
After blitzing at a conservative rate (22 percent of their defensive snaps) for much of the season’s early stages, the Giants have clearly increased the defensive pressure in recent weeks.
Since team captain Brian Burns suffered a season-ending injury in Week 3, the team has blitzed on 56 percent of its defensive snaps against the Arizona Cardinals in Week 4 and 62 percent against the Commanders in Week 5.
In fact, Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels looked as wide-eyed as a pre-Miyagi Do Daniel LaRusso on more than one occasion — thanks largely to Phillips’ heat-seeking style of play.
For as long as Wilson continues his aggressive approach, Phillips will be ready to turn up the pressure.
“Dennard (Wilson) has a way of cooking things up, but I definitely wouldn’t say it is a consistent thing,” Phillips said.
“It’s a week-by-week thing. It goes off of what we’re seeing and the flow of the game. So, you go out there, and if they send me, I’m going to try my best to go get it.”
At his best, Phillips is an elite run defender due to his physical, downhill style. When deployed as a pass rusher, his speed and short-area power let him quickly close on opposing quarterbacks — as shown against Daniels and the Commanders.
Phillips not only earned high praise for his Week 5 effort, but he also performed at a historically high level for the franchise. The 24-year-old became the fifth Giants defensive back since 1982 to record at least two sacks in a game.
He was also the fourth cornerback since 2006 to record four-plus quarterback hits in a single game.
With New York’s Week 6 matchup against the New Orleans Saints fast approaching, Phillips is likely to be an integral component of the club’s defensive game plan once again. Though he may be having a great deal of fun in Wilson’s aggressive system, he also remains aware of his responsibilities to his teammates.
In that regard, Phillips is rapidly becoming the embodiment of a complete football player — one whose value lies not only in his versatile skill set, but also in his commitment to doing what’s best for the team.
“I feel like anybody that blitzes, you have to look out for the people behind you,” Phillips said.
“As a DB as well, when you cover it, you depend on guys to get home. So, when I am blitzing, it’s like, ‘yeah, I got to rush my tail off so I can help these guys in the back.’
“You’ve got to be aware of that. Not trying to ease your way in there … you’ve got guys fighting for their lives behind you.”

title: Giants Open as 1.5-Point Home Underdogs Against Struggling Saints
full_text:
The New York Giants held onto first place in the NFC East despite a 27-27 overtime tie with the Washington Commanders in Week 5.
Now, they return to East Rutherford to face the New Orleans Saints, an opponent that looks like a favorable matchup for extending their lead.
Oddsmakers aren’t sold. FanDuel Sportsbook opened Big Blue as a 1.5-point home underdog in its lines for the NFL’s Week 6 slate.
While the opening spread is an improvement, the Giants are being doubted for the second consecutive week after they were 3.5-point underdogs against Washington. FanDuel also set the total at 45.5 points, up two points from last week.
This isn’t the first time the Giants have been handed an odd opening line, but this week’s number may be the most confusing of the season.
After three gritty performances by John Harbaugh’s group, including two defensive shutdowns that closed out a pair of thrilling victories, the Giants have earned more respect against inferior opponents like the Saints, who arrive in East Rutherford at 1-4.
However, like the Commanders, who went up 27-13 in the third quarter but failed to set up a game-winning field goal in the waning seconds of overtime, the Saints are desperate for a win.
New Orleans opened the season looking like one of the biggest surprises, losing 31-30 on the final play of overtime to the Detroit Lions before stunning the Baltimore Ravens on the road for its only win of 2026.
Since then, the Saints have dropped three consecutive games to fall into last place in the NFC South, a division that has been less than impressive overall. Even so, they sit only two games behind the first-place Carolina Panthers.
The rough stretch, which included their defense allowing a combined 80 points in two weeks, has drawn sharp public criticism from Saints owner Gayle Benson, who challenged her franchise to provide the results its loyal fans deserve.
With the weak state of their division and the outcry from their owner and fanbase, the Saints should arrive motivated to challenge a Giants team that has started slowly in its last few contests.
The Saints offense is not one to overlook, ranking 16th in the NFL in points per game (23.6) and 20th in yards per game (322.0). Its strength is the passing game, led by second-year quarterback Tyler Shough, who is off to a solid start with the seventh-most passing yards and third-most touchdown passes in the league.
Shough and the offense are asked to score often because of the defense, which has allowed the second-most points per game, including at least 23 in each of the last three games.
The ground game is where the Giants could have an edge. The Saints defense has given up an average of 148.8 rushing yards per game and 10 rushing touchdowns, the most in the league through five games.
If the Giants clean up the run game and ball security and get back to playing bully ball in the trenches, they should be able to handle a Saints team still searching for the early-season form that grabbed everyone’s attention. The oddsmakers may be underselling them at home.

title: Giants Jon Runyan, Jr. Credits Coaching Staff for Success Through Adversity
full_text:
In the immortal words of legendary singer-songwriter James Taylor, the New York Giants have clearly seen their share of “fire” and “rain” through the first five games of the 2026 NFL season.
From losing incumbent starting quarterback Jaxson Dart to a season-ending knee injury in Week 2, to defensive team captain Brian Burns suffering both a torn ACL and torn meniscus in Week 3, New York has been forced to push through adversity.
Still, the Giants have endured. Under new head coach John Harbaugh, the team has found renewed vigor. Playing solid, fundamental football, Big Blue sits alone atop the NFC East at 3-1-1.
Though several factors have contributed to New York’s unexpected return to relevance, veteran offensive lineman Jon Runyan Jr. knows the foundation for that success was laid months ago.
“I think it says a lot about our coaching staff and what they’ve tried to build throughout the whole offseason program and into training camp,” Runyan said. “It says a lot about them, the foundation that they’ve built, and a lot of us as players. Because of that, we’re sitting 3-1-1 right now.”
Originally drafted by the Green Bay Packers in the sixth round (No. 192 overall) of the 2020 NFL Draft, Runyan has been with the Giants since signing a free-agent deal with the club in 2024. The 6-foot-4, 307-pound left guard has started all 34 games he has appeared in for the team.
This season, he has played 347 offensive snaps and earned a pass-blocking grade of 78.5, which ranks sixth among 75 qualified offensive guards, per PFF.
While Runyan’s on-field skills have helped the Giants’ offensive line perform at a high level, his veteran leadership remains integral to the unit rising above its middle-of-the-pack preseason rankings. The line has not only provided improved protection for quarterback Jameis Winston, but it has also strengthened its run blocking.
Despite injuries to key starters such as right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (calf) and left tackle Andrew Thomas (groin), the Giants’ O-line continues to press forward. Even as they have weathered the storm through the first five weeks of the season, Runyan has enough experience to know situations can always worsen.
In that regard, Runyan is confident that Big Blue has the structure in place to persevere — even if the club has yet to reach its on-field peak.
“I still feel like we have a long way to go on this team,” Runyan said. “Luckily, we are 3-1-1 at the moment. And as I said, we still have a long way to go. This whole division stacks up how it does, as long as we take care of what we got. Coach Harbaugh has been saying go 1-0 every week, and that’s been our mindset, and it’s been working so far this year.”
With their Week 6 matchup against the New Orleans Saints at MetLife Stadium approaching, the Giants will continue to require a total team effort to return to the win column.
As players begin to hit their stride, Runyan believes the strong solidarity throughout the organization will be the primary reason the Giants accomplish their mission — should they choose to accept it.
“In my opinion, it’s about really good communication back and forth between players and coaches,” Runyan added.
“That is going to help us when we get further down the road in the season. And especially going to be helpful when we face a little bit more adversity, knowing that we have that solid foundation with everybody around us.”

title: Giants Look to Stay Atop the Division Against Desperate Saints
full_text:
The New York Giants will keep building positive momentum as they grind toward their bye week, two weeks away.
The first five weeks have been quite the adventure. They upset the Cowboys, lost to the Rams, squeaked out wins against the Titans and Cardinals, and tied with the Commanders, with most of those games played without quarterback Jaxson Dart and outside linebacker Brian Burns.
And yet they have prevailed, sitting alone at the top of the division and looking to stay there when they host the New Orleans Saints this weekend.
“Yeah, I think it says a lot about not only our coaching staff, what they’ve tried to build throughout the whole offseason program and into training camp. It says a lot about them, the foundation that they’ve built, and a lot of us as players, we’re sitting 3-1-1 right now,” said left guard Jon Runyan.
It’s also not lost on Runyan or his teammates that they could have easily been 1-4, especially given how some of their recent games have played out. As such, Runyan said the players and coaches are not about to rest on their laurels.
“We still have a long way to go. This whole division stacks up how it does, as long as we take care of what we got, like we got the Saints coming in this week. (Head) Coach (John) Harbaugh has been saying go 1-0 every week, and that’s been our mindset, and it’s been working so far this year.”
Here’s a look at some of this week’s storylines ahead of their game with the Saints.
The only thing worse than facing a really good team is facing a desperate team, and that’s exactly what the Giants get this weekend when the Saints march into MetLife Stadium.
The Saints (1-4) have lost their last three games by two or more scores. They have been a little bit better on the road, losing to the Lions by one point in Week 1 and upsetting the Ravens by seven in Week 2.
But in an NFC South division that seems wide open every year, the Saints will be desperate this weekend, knowing that if they lose, their chance to win the division will likely be over. And that’s what makes them so dangerous.
Head coach John Harbaugh said right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (calf) and safety Tyler Nubin (neck) are out, while cornerback Colton Hood (concussion) will likely be day-to-day. If Hood is in the concussion protocol, he may be out a little longer, so that bears watching.
And speaking of injuries, the Giants obviously hope to have safety Jason Pinnock (concussion) back, while the expectation is that left tackle Andrew Thomas (groin) will have his practice reps managed.
A funny thing happened to the offense last week. The Giants, who have been trying to stick with their power running game, ultimately went to the passing game 54 times in their tied game against Washington. Granted, a big part of that was that the Giants were trailing, but when they trusted Winston with the ball, he made things happen and brought the Giants back from a 14-point deficit.
The game, by the way, marked the second straight time Winston threw three touchdown passes. That’s good news for a Giants offense that is about to face a Saints pass defense that has allowed an average of 3.6 touchdowns per game so far.
“We’ve been talking about some of the tempo stuff. We’ve been working on that. It’s been part of our system from day one, really. We built it in from the beginning. And it was good to get to it,” Harbaugh said of the offense last week.
“We got to it maybe because we had to. Maybe game flow forced us to do it, but it was a good thing in that sense. So yeah, it opened up the offense. It was good to see, and it probably needs to be part of what we’re doing going forward.”

title: Born of Necessity, Giants’ Pass-Heavy Approach Could Stick
full_text:
There is an adage that “necessity is the mother of invention,” and for the New York Giants , that might very well be the case as Big Blue continues to redefine its identity on offense after losing starting quarterback Jaxson Dart seven snaps into Week 2 of the 2026 season.
Dart's injury forced the Giants to drop many RPO calls from their playbook because they don’t fit Jameis Winston’s more traditional pocket-passing style.
And thanks to this past week’s crazy showing against Washington, the Giants coaching staff may have had another epiphany regarding the league’s 21st-ranked offense (308.2 yards/game) and how to improve it.
In a nutshell: sit back and ride the Jameis Winston experience.
In two of the Giants’ five games this season, New York has leaned more heavily on the pass when in catch-up mode.
That showed up in Week 2 against the Rams, when the Giants threw the ball 32 times while running just 21.
It was also seen this past week again when the Giants, who never had a lead in what ended up a 27-27 tie, threw the ball 54 times while running 28 on a rainy, sloppy day that was crying out for the run game to take center stage.
The passing game, as it turned out, helped to open up the Giants offense and erase a 14-point deficit that ultimately sent the game into overtime.
“It was good, no question,” head coach John Harbaugh said. “We’ve been talking about some of the tempo stuff. We’ve been working on that. It’s been part of our system from day one, really. It’s something we built in from the beginning. And it was good to get to it.
“We got to it maybe because we had to. Maybe game flow forced us to do it, but it was a good thing in that sense. So yeah, it opened up the offense. It was good to see, and it probably needs to be part of what we’re doing going forward.”
Given the Giants’ run game struggles — New York is ranked 16th in total rushing yards (545) and 24th in average yards per rush (3.7) — the philosophy shift makes sense, though it should be noted that the Giants probably won’t be looking to throw the ball 40+ times per game unless they are in catch-up mode.
Still, there's precedent for leaning a bit more into Winston than pulling the plug and handing the keys to the offense to J.J. McCarthy at this point. Winston, who is 1-0-1 as a starter this season, has completed 61.1% of his pass attempts in his last three games.
He has also thrown three touchdown passes in each of his last two starts, which is good news for a Giants offense going against a New Orleans Saints pass defense that has allowed 18 touchdowns ( 3.6 per game ) so far.
Turnovers are always a risk. Per PFF, Winston has six turnover-worthy plays , ranking 11th among quarterbacks with at least 140 dropbacks this season. But having him sling the ball a little bit more might even help the Giants’ sluggish running game.
According to Next Gen Stats , Giants running back Najee Harris has seen a loaded box (8+ defenders) on 25.93% of his rushing attempts, and Cam Skattebo on 22.22%.
Having Winston sling the ball around the field more to receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely, two pass targets with whom Winston seems to have built a solid rapport, could help loosen things up for the running game, which is in search of more explosive runs.

title: Giants Hold Their Position in Week 6 MMQB Power Rankings
full_text:
For most New York Giants players and fans, it was tough to say how they should have felt after the franchise’s 27-27 overtime tie with the Washington Commanders in Week 5.
Head coach John Harbaugh summed it up best, saying he was “happy it wasn’t a loss and sad it wasn’t a win.” It was a performance that showed two very different sides of his locker room on either side of halftime.
Even SI’s Conor Orr seemed stuck in the middle about how to analyze Big Blue’s surprising final result, which is why he held firm on their spot in his weekly MMQB NFL power rankings , leaving the Giants at No. 21 ahead of Week 6.
“I think my favorite part of the disastrous end-of-game Commanders-Giants footage is when Deonte Banks flies across the line of scrimmage after the clock strikes zero. Followed closely by the fact that the most game situation-aware player on the field during that moment was rookie Arvell Reese,” Orr said.
Sunday’s draw might go down as one of the craziest finishes of the season, but for Harbaugh’s Giants, it was a Week 5 testament to the never-say-die culture the Super Bowl-winning coach has instilled in every player and coach under his wing.
Aside from another week of less-than-favorable weather, the Giants fell behind the Commanders early as their offense struggled to move the ball. Even when they did, the kicking game didn't help, as Dominic Zvada missed three field goals.
The Commanders came out swinging in the second half. They scored back-to-back touchdowns off the speedy legs of quarterback Jayden Daniels to extend their lead to 27-13 entering the final frame of regulation.
Given the organization’s recent history, that used to be the kind of situation that would make the Giants keel over and accept defeat.
Instead, they made the right adjustments, including letting Jameis Winston go a little off-script and testing the Commanders’ secondary with his arm and a duo of active pass-catchers in Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely.
The result was Winston regaining his confidence as he completed 74.6% of his passes in the second half, including three touchdown connections to Nabers and Likely that leveled the score and gave the Giants a chance to win in overtime.
New York never found the one scoring play it needed to escape Washington with the coveted win, but the tie helped it hold its first-place lead in the division.
More importantly, Winston found a way to silence the outside critics who were about two more ugly quarters away from shouting from the rooftops for the recently acquired backup J.J. McCarthy to supplant him as the starter.
The only question that lingers is whether he and the Giants offense can learn from the few mistakes that nearly cost them the game against the Commanders and get back into the win column next Sunday, when they host the New Orleans Saints at MetLife Stadium.
Any result on the NFL gridiron can offer some takeaways for a growing team, and this past week’s game showed that the Giants have the heart and talent to compete with whoever is in front of them and overcome adversity.
Even against tougher opponents in the second half of the year, that fight should remind everyone that an early lead on the scoreboard won’t be enough to feel comfortable that they’ve buried this Giants team.

title: NFL Insider Explains Why Giants Really Traded for J.J. McCarthy
full_text:
New York Giants quarterback Jameis Winston, one of the league’s best veteran backups , is playing well enough to keep the Giants at 2-0-1 since taking over as the starter for the injured Jaxson Dart.
But some skeptics still believe it’s only a matter of time before Winston is benched in favor of J.J. McCarthy, whom the Giants acquired in a trade with the Minnesota Vikings a couple of weeks ago.
Speculation has intensified after Giants head coach John Harbaugh not only acknowledged that a package of plays was ready for McCarthy just one week into the quarterback’s tenure with the team, but also said McCarthy saw the field for a handful of snaps Sunday.
Does that mean Winston is officially on notice that he will be pulled from the lineup the moment he has a bad game?
“I don’t see a scenario anytime soon in which J.J. is playing,” NFL insider Jordan Schultz told the Locked On Giants podcast .
“I think as long as Jameis continues to play well, it’ll be a minute before J.J.’s on the field.”
Winston, a team captain and member of the eight-player leadership council, is highly respected in the locker room. He has also drawn praise from Harbaugh and offensive coordinator Matt Nagy, both of whom, at least for now, are willing to take the good with the bad.
So why trade for McCarthy, the No. 10 overall pick in the 2024 draft? What’s the plan for him going forward? And is there a world in which McCarthy might actually challenge Dart for the starting job?
“Dart’s the guy, and they want him to be the guy for the next decade,” Schultz said. “There was a misconception, I think, nationally about the McCarthy trade. They did not trade for J.J. McCarthy to supplant Jameis Winston. They traded for him because the price had dropped significantly.
“Jim and John Harbaugh had multiple conversations about the type of person and player he can be. As he explained to me, John Harbaugh loved [McCarthy’s] hockey background, his toughness, and much of the winning he did at Michigan. But he’s not going to be the starter.”
Jim Harbaugh, John’s brother, coached McCarthy at Michigan.
McCarthy, according to Schultz, is additional insurance in case the injury bug hits the Giants’ quarterback room again. However, the league insider acknowledged that if the wheels fall off on the Giants offense with Winston under center, things could change.
For now, the Giants are simply evaluating what they have in McCarthy, who has a positive relationship with Nagy.
“They do wanna see whether or not someone drafted that high and that young is capable of being a backup or even a starter at some point,” Schultz said, adding that there could be more sightings of McCarthy on the field “in certain situations.”
But not as a starter, at least not for the immediate future.
“That would really surprise me,” Schultz said. “If Jameis were to play really badly in a couple of weeks in a row and they lost two in a row, I think it’s a different conversation. I don’t really expect that to happen.
“Not only did they sign Jameis, but they extended him, and they gave him real money in a two-year extension. And that was, I think, a manifestation of how they feel about him, knowing that if he did need to start and play, he could win them football games.”
“There is a lot more unknown about McCarthy than Jameis,” he continued. “I think McCarthy will play at some point, but I’m thinking more of a supplemental role.”

title: Giants Rookie Report after Week 5 Tie Vs. Commanders
full_text:
The New York Giants had to place a lot of trust in their rookies from the jump, and after five games, they should be pretty satisfied with the results.
There have been rough patches, and there will be more before the season's end, but the newcomers have made a noticeable difference overall.
Justin Melo of NFL Draft On SI agrees, as he ranked Big Blue's 2026 draft class No. 2 in the league (the Cleveland Browns got the top spot). The Giants’ group is teeming with upside, with a few players already contributing meaningful snaps to winning football. Others require more development, however.
Here’s a close-up look at the Giants Class of 2026, including key undrafted rookie free agents, following their 27-27 tie with the Washington Commanders in Week 5 . (Note: Offensive lineman J.C. Davis and defensive lineman Bobby Jamison-Travis were inactive in Week 5, as has been the case for both all season.)
Reese, the 21-year-old linebacker, did not dominate the Washington Commanders on the stat sheet as he did the Arizona Cardinals in Week 4.
Per PFF, he missed a tackle and allowed three receptions for 36 yards in coverage. Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels also beat him with his speed.
That said, Reese still made his presence felt at various points of the game. The No. 5 overall pick posted his first career sack and also recorded nine total tackles.
Also, the stat sheet doesn't necessarily capture the hidden contributions that the rookie first-rounder has made by setting his teammates up for success on a given play.
Despite whatever hiccups he had against Daniels, Reese continues to show stellar athleticism, a high motor, and unyielding power that will keep drawing attention from opponents.
Analysts appear split on tackle-turned-guard Francis "Sisi" Mauigoa’s development so far, but he did not allow a single sack against Washington. He also displayed his eye-catching strength multiple times, bowling over guys while protecting Jameis Winston.
There are still some flaws, though. Mauigoa is learning the intricacies of the interior, which shows in his spotty run-blocking. The offensive line as a unit needs to improve there, and with time, the 6-foot-6, 335-pounder should get more comfortable.
It is, however, fair to say he’s trending in the right direction.
Expectations are reasonably high for a top-40 draft selection, and cornerback Colton Hood could still meet them. Still, the solid play of starters Greg Newsome II and Deonte Banks has given Hood time to acclimate to the speed of the game, where he has done so by contributing on special teams.
In Week 5 against Washington, Hood led the Giants with three special teams tackles before a head injury forced him out of the game. He was particularly sharp on kickoff coverage, taking smart angles to force the returner into the coverage.
Defensively, Hood was pressed into action when Banks missed two games with a calf injury. Per PFF, he’s allowed six catches for only 49 yards , and yes, he’s been a magnet for opposing quarterbacks.
But Hood has shown the intensity and skill set that will ultimately pay off for him in this aggressive defensive system.
Although he has only 17 targets, Fields, the big-bodied pass-catcher, is showing impressive skills and instincts.
He totaled two receptions for 20 yards this past Sunday, but might have racked up bigger numbers if he had been thrown to more often. Right now, the coaches seem to be asking him to put his strong downfield blocking skills on more of a display.
But as a pass target, Fields gained notable separation at times, making him a valuable deep threat in the long term. The 6-foot-4 wideout has also yet to drop a pass this season, displaying the kind of sure hands the Giants have lacked in the past.
It might just be a matter of time before Fields gets more involved in the deep passing game, especially if the Giants move away from a struggling, run-heavy offense and let quarterback Jameis Winston do what he does best: sling the ball downfield.
Kelly, the sixth-rounder out of BYU, has not logged a snap at linebacker but has, as expected, stepped into a big role on special teams.  This past week, he nearly blocked a punt late in the first half. He also has one special teams tackle on the year.
New York has made significant progress in the third phase of the game, and this Day 3 pick is one reason why.
It was unrealistic to expect rookie kicker Dominic Zvada never to miss a field goal attempt. So after converting the first nine attempts of his NFL career, his bad day at the office came against Washington in clearly unfavorable weather conditions.
Rain is often unkind to this position, and this outing was no exception. Nevertheless, three misfires warrant fair criticism if you believe a kicker should be able to function regardless of the weather.
Zvada was unsuccessful on attempts from 50, 57, and 46 yards. He did connect from 51 and 56 yards, though, so perhaps there is little reason to worry moving forward. The 22-year-old has earned the benefit of the doubt.

title: Why Omar Cooper Jr.'s Return Is Even More Crucial for the Jets' 2026 Outlook
full_text:
Although the Jets’ offense is significantly better than last year, the unit hasn’t been great. Through five games, Gang Green is tied for 27th in points (18.6) and 23rd in passing yards per game (190).
Geno Smith and Garrett Wilson have done everything they can to keep the offense afloat; however, injuries to New York’s key offensive players have held them back. Fortunately, head coach Aaron Glenn gave fans some good news on Wednesday, announcing that rookie receiver Omar Cooper Jr. will return to practice this week.
The former Indiana Hoosier sustained an ankle injury in New York’s Week 1 win over the Titans and was placed on injured reserve.
The news couldn’t come at a better time, as Gang Green is currently without Breece Hall and Adonai Mitchell, both week-to-week, while Kenyon Sadiq remains in the concussion protocol after suffering a head injury in the Jets' Week 5 victory over the Browns.
With Cooper nearing a return in the lineup, New York hopes he can help improve the unit's play immediately and emerge as the second option behind Wilson.
The Smith-Wilson connection has been strong. Over the first five weeks, Wilson is tied for seventh in receptions with 31 and ranks 11th in receiving yards with 374.
Besides Wilson, the Jets haven’t gotten consistent production from their other pass catchers. Sadiq ranks second on the team in catches (14) and third in yards (146). However, most of the rookie tight end’s production came in Week 3 against the Lions, where he posted seven receptions for 105 yards.
Isaiah Williams ranks behind Sadiq with 11 receptions for 151 yards, although 58 of those yards came on a touchdown in Week 3’s loss to the Bears.
We’ve only seen Cooper play five snaps, but in that small sample, he proved that he can be an impact player.
In the Jets' first offensive drive of the season, Cooper caught a short pass on third-and-nine and turned it into a 30-yard gain. His 26 yards after the catch put New York inside the 10-yard line and helped set up a touchdown two plays later.
Cooper’s playmaking ability was a major reason why New York traded back into the first round to select him.
In his final collegiate season, Cooper recorded 494 yards after the catch, which ranked 16th among qualifying receivers, per Pro Football Focus. He also averaged 7.2 yards after the catch per reception, highlighting his ability to generate extra yards.
The Jets’ offense has desperately missed this playmaking ability. New York has struggled to find consistent production from the rest of its receiving corps and continues to rely on Wilson to move the ball downfield.
Mitchell ranks second on the team in receiving first downs, but his absence over the last three games has further limited Smith’s options. Cooper’s return could help fill that void. He’s already shown that he can make plays with the ball in his hands and give Smith another reliable target.
With another playmaker in the receiver corps, defenses would have to account for Cooper, which could create more opportunities for Wilson.
Getting Cooper back could be crucial for the Jets heading into this week’s matchup against the Patriots. With New England’s defense ranking 11th in passing yards allowed (212.2), the rookie’s skill set could give Gang Green an extra boost against their rival.

title: How Jets Can Continue Unlocking Darrell Jackson Jr.'s Full Potential in Week 6 (And Beyond)
full_text:
Behind a dominant defensive performance up front and a career day from running back Braelon Allen, the Jets prevailed in a hard-fought 17-12 win over the Browns last Sunday in the sloppy conditions at MetLife Stadium.
As the Jets prepare for their first AFC East matchup of the season when they face the Patriots on Sunday, all eyes will be on Gang Green to see how they fare with a record of 25-65 against division opponents since 2011.
If anything was clear from the Week 5 win over the Browns, it was that they found a defensive blueprint that can succeed long term after head coach Aaron Glenn called blitz plays on more than 50% of the snaps.
While rookie David Bailey was the force behind that success with three of the team's eight sacks in the game, fellow rookie Darrell Jackson Jr. was a stud in his own right with his first career NFL sack and two huge pass deflections in the fourth quarter. As David Onyemata remains on injured reserve after undergoing core muscle surgery, the opportunity remains in front of Jackson to make a strong impression and become a steal as a fourth-round draft pick.
Jackson had more of a rotational role on the depth chart to begin the season, but he had the type of performance that everyone was waiting for against Cleveland. Jackson had four tackles, one sack, two pressures and two pass deflections in 29 defensive snaps in his best NFL showing to date and showed what he is truly capable of in an increased role .
Through the first four games, Jackson only had seven tackles and zero pressures in 85 defensive snaps and was primarily expected to be a rotational run-plugger in the middle of Glenn's defensive schemes. He was far from quiet against the Browns and proved that it could be difficult to take snaps away from him if he can build off the all-around performance from last Sunday.
According to Pro Football Focus , Jackson has the 77th-ranked overall grade (56.2) and 93rd-ranked pass-rush grade (57.7) out of 133 qualified interior defenders. Jackson still needs to continue to develop as a pass rusher, but his 50th-ranked run-defense grade (59.5) speaks to the potential he brings when defending the ground game.
The 6-foot-5, 315-pounder out of Florida State was solid during his collegiate career with 77 total tackles (seven for loss), 7.5 sacks and 35 hurries. That said, it was his dirty work that perhaps led to him getting overlooked when the draft rolled around and why he was flying under the radar coming into the season .
In addition to tying for the 16th-most run stops (23) among interior defenders in college football last season, per PFF , Jackson's size and run-stuffing ability make him a key early-down contributor who can give T'Vondre Sweat or Harrison Phillips a breather. He needs to continue growing as a pass rusher if he wants to improve his snap count going forward, but the ceiling is certainly high after a breakout Week 5 performance.
For starters, the Patriots are dealing with multiple offensive line injuries, notably starting left tackle Will Campbell (right knee sprain). While quarterback Drake Maye is coming off a five-TD performance against the Raiders and is capable of using his legs when he needs to, continuing to move Jackson along the front could create some mismatches against a banged-up New England unit and keep Maye out of his rhythm amid a turnover-prone start to the season.
With a 7'2" wingspan and 11-inch hands, Jackson has the ability to utilize his massive frame to disrupt passing lanes and make life difficult on opposing QBs by recording deflections and batting passes down at the line of scrimmage. If he can take advantage of the increased opportunities that he could be in line for while Onyemata is out of action, Jackson could turn into a matchup nightmare.
Going forward, the Jets need to capitalize on Jackson's unconventional "Big End" 4-technique and 5-technique positions to use his rare length to his advantage, in addition to aligning him over the A and B gaps to test New England's front. If they can do that and reap the rewards, Jackson could have a bright future in Gang Green for years to come.

title: Jets' Special Teams Unit Takes a Turn Thanks to Rams
full_text:
Remember when the New York Jets tried out nine different kickers in order to find the right man to trust throughout the 2026 season? So many fans and analysts were concerned that the team's special teams unit would take a massive drop because of it.
Not only has that concerned not been the case, but the rest of the league seemingly wants New York's kickers again. Seriously.
The Los Angeles Rams, the team many predicted to win the Super Bowl after acquiring Myles Garrett in the offseason, have signed Blake Grupe off the Jets' practice squad this week after a struggling start to the season from Ex-Jet Harrison Mevis.
You read that right. Los Angeles is going back to the Jets to solve its kicking problems.
The jokes write themselves.
Before he was cut on Tuesday, Mevis was easily the weakest link to the Rams roster. He went 5-9 on field goals including missing a potential game-winner on Monday night. Grupe, meanwhile, hasn't even attempted a kick for the Jets so far this season.
He was beat out in another competition with Jason Sanders to begin the year. Sanders has gone 8-9 on field goals including a solid 3-4 from beyond 50 yards out.
New York was right to keep Sanders on the roster, but the team losing Grupe highlights another part to their team. New York's special teams unit isn't as elite as they were last season, but they remain an integral part to their future success.
"I think it's been awesome," special teams coordinator Chris Banjo said. "We're talking about grit and resiliency. I think he's been able to show that so far early in the season."
It should not be overlooked that the Rams chose to sign Grupe over the likes of other veteran kickers on the open market like Justin Tucker. Los Angeles clearly thinks highly of Banjo's ability to get the best out of their kickers, and are hoping to get some of that production going forward.
"Appreciate (Mevis's) contributions," Rams head coach Sean McVay said in a video conference with reporters. "I thought he was a rock for us last year when we obviously struggled in that area. But ultimately we need better production, and that's what we're hoping to get out of from Blake."
New York and Los Angeles have the same record. Sounds crazy doesn't it? But in the case of the Jets' their special teams unit looks to be an improved group even with new faces at kicker.
And other teams around the league know it.

title: Breaking Down Jets' Potential TE Plans vs. Patriots If Kenyon Sadiq Can't Clear Concussion Protocol
full_text:
Just when it seemed like the New York Jets were getting healthy. Just when it appeared that the team could start to utilize their two top tight ends. A game like Sunday happens and pushes all the expectations out the door.
Late in the contest, rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq suffered a concussion on a play where he fumbled the ball after a hard hit near the goalline. New York was able to salvage the game by winning 17-12, but the injury from Sadiq could keep him out of Sunday's contest against the New England Patriots.
Much like the last several weeks, though, New York should be just fine with their tight end room. They have the horses now to handle an injury to a starter, because they have another one ready to go.
Sadiq being a first-round pick shows enough about the kind of investment the team has made at the tight end position. The fact that he was the second consecutive tight end taken in the last two drafts only enhances that.
Mason Taylor's 2026 season has been a quiet one so far . Through two and a half games played this season, the LSU product has just five receptions for 22 yards this season. This is after the second-year tight end was second in the team in both receptions and yards.
Without Sadiq, the Jets will need more from Taylor, even if the team believes the best is still yet to come from him.
“We put a lot of work in the offseason, he was always willing to get out there, it was super hot, but he didn’t mind it,” quarterback Geno Smith said. “South Florida kid, seemed to be that way. But he’s a guy who I think is going to be a great player in this league for a long time.”
Jeremy Ruckert and Jelani Woods are two other tight ends that are expected to be used in droves. They may not have the athleticism compared to when Sadiq is out on the field, Taylor's consistency is something that should help the offense in droves, especially against a New England Patriots defense with plenty of physicality across the board.
New York has also been consistent in using all their tight ends across the board this season.
“They’re a well-rounded group, very talented group,” Smith said. “They work extremely hard—kind of the glue guys. They bring everything together on the offense. And so it’s great to see all five of them out there on the field at once and we’ll try and get the ball to each one of them when we can.”
Not having both Sadiq and Taylor on Sunday together can be frustrating for the organization. Until then, however, the team can still rely on the room to be just as good as they have in recent weeks.

title: Jets Rookie Report Card: Grading 2026 Draft Picks After First Month of the Season
full_text:
It was not pretty, but the Jets found a way to take down the Browns in a 17-12 season-saving win in the sloppy conditions at MetLife Stadium. Regardless, New York is now 2-3 and in a much better position than it would have been at 1-4 heading into a Week 6 AFC East tilt against the Patriots on Sunday.
Fresh off the hard-fought win in the rain , the Jets put a three-game losing streak behind them and have their eyes set on continuing to make improvements and learn from their previous mistakes going forward. While the discipline and inability to close out each half remain a concern, there is a lot more to feel optimistic about coming off a win this week.
Before the season even got started, there was a lot of hype surrounding the Jets' 2026 draft class. Although injuries or inconsistent play in the early going have provided some mixed results for some, the rookies' talent has been on display, setting the stage for a promising future in Gotham .
With that in mind, let's hand out grades for each of the Jets' eight 2026 draft picks now that it's been over a month since their season opener.
Even though David Bailey led all NFL rookies in pressures during the first month of the season, a lot of fans were concerned about his early returns on the field . That said, he single-handedly took over the Week 5 win over the Browns with three of the team's eight sacks, in addition to seven tackles (five solo), three tackles for loss and four quarterback hits.
Bailey recorded his third sack of the game early in the fourth quarter (h/t NFL) after the defense forced Cleveland's offense into a third-and-30.
THIRD sack of the day for David Bailey @CLEvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/QTqQqo79NN
The defensive line was easily the best unit on the field for the Jets , which was a huge turnaround from the disappointing play that same group displayed in the games coming in. According to Pro Football Focus , Bailey has the 43rd-ranked overall grade (68.6) and the 10th-most pressures (20) out of 106 qualified edge defenders.
It was a fairly slow start out of the gate for Bailey, but if the Week 5 performance proved anything, it is that he was more than worthy of being selected No. 2 overall and certainly appears to have all the tools to become a star in the league.
Kenyon Sadiq scored his first NFL TD in Week 1 courtesy of the ground game, but his true breakout performance came in Week 3 when he went off for seven catches, 105 yards and his first TD catch. Aside from that, Sadiq has rarely been targeted and has been completely limited in the pass game when the ball has come his way.
Sadiq only had two catches for three yards in the loss to Cleveland and also committed a fumble, so there is definitely some room for improvement . This was also the first game back for Mason Taylor, and it was clear he was going to be a focal point of the tight end group, with 41 snaps to Sadiq's 13.
Granted, the concussion was a setback and limited Sadiq's playing time, but the Jets appear to prefer leaning in Taylor's direction a little more at this stage of the season. Sadiq's raw athletic traits are unmatched and his route separation is elite, but it remains to be seen how much of a factor he will be in this offense when Taylor is on the field.
Omar Cooper Jr.'s NFL career immediately got off to a hot start when he turned a short pass into a 30-yard gain (h/t Glenn Naughton) to set up a TD a few plays later in New York's season-opening win over the Titans. However, that remains his only target and catch of his rookie season after suffering a high ankle sprain during the first quarter of that Week 1 game.
First career catch for @nyjets rookie WR Omar Cooper. Looks like a first round pick if you ask me. pic.twitter.com/NmQRKYSGCK
Cooper has since spent the last four weeks on injured reserve, though the possibility is there for him to play in Sunday's game against the Patriots, depending on the progress he has made in his recovery. The Jets finally figured things out with WR1 Garrett Wilson by looking his way more often and reaping those rewards with seven catches for 104 yards and a TD, but the depth at WR has been an issue, and getting Cooper back sooner rather than later would be a huge benefit.
The grade is not so much a knock on D'Angelo Ponds, but rather due to the lack of playing time he has received as more of a developmental player who is primarily serving a backup role in the secondary. That said, he played a career-high 18 snaps in relief of Jarvis Brownlee Jr. in Week 4 and showcased his run-defense skills when the opportunity presented itself.
It appeared that Ponds was suddenly staring at a bigger role after Brownlee went into concussion protocol following the Week 4 loss to the Bears, but the latter ultimately became a full participant in practice and even recorded his first career sack in Sunday's game, all while Ponds played just two defensive snaps and primarily appeared on special teams.
Darrell Jackson Jr. was expected to be a rotational run-plugger in the middle of head coach Aaron Glenn's defensive schemes. While he only had seven tackles and zero pressures in 85 defensive snaps across the first four games, the fourth-round selection finally broke out and made his impact felt against the Browns.
Jackson had four tackles, one sack, two pressures and two pass deflections in 29 defensive snaps, putting together his best overall game so far in Gang Green. David Onyemata's place on injured reserve has paved the way for Jackson to step up, and the Week 5 performance was the first true sign of what Jackson is capable of.
Veteran Geno Smith has done his part to take care of the ball and manage each game relatively well by completing 72.7% of his passes for 1,084 yards and six TDs. Although he was anything but flashy in the win over the Browns, this is still firmly Smith's job as long as he continues to protect the ball, which could only benefit Cade Klubnik more as the fourth-round pick gets some additional time to learn from Smith and develop under his leadership.
Anez Cooper, the sixth-round pick out of Miami, suffered a right shoulder injury during the preseason finale against the Giants and has been on injured reserve since.
While he is now eligible to return to the roster , it remains to be seen if Cooper will make his season debut or at least be available to play. The offensive line was better against the Browns, but with Dylan Parham dealing with a knee injury and the play up front looking suspect so far, it definitely would not hurt to have an extra body in Cooper to turn to if the opportunity presents itself.
The seventh-round pick suffered a significant bone bruise during training camp before being placed on short-term IR, forcing him to miss at least the first four games of the season. Much like Cooper, it remains to be seen whether VJPayne will be activated back to the 53-man roster soon.
However, this staff is particularly high on Payne's physical traits and special teams potential , which could prove valuable when he does get fully healthy and potential roster holes open up.

title: Jets Ending One Pitiful Trend Is Absolutely Crucial vs. Patriots in Week 6
full_text:
It's Patriots Week, a time when Jets fans gear up for a matchup against Gang Green's biggest rival.
But since 2000, the Jets-Pats rivalry has been as one-sided as it comes. Sure, the Jets have gotten their fair share of licks—a stunning upset in the 2010 divisional round of the playoffs being the top moment—but by and large, this rivalry has gone the Patriots' way for decades.
At 2-3 in Week 6, the Jets have a chance to write a new chapter in this storied rivalry. But as coaches and players have said, they aren't making the game any more meaningful than it already is.
"Every game is important to us; it doesn't matter who you play," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said. "We have a 1-0 mindset every time we go out there. I know it's the Patriots, I know it's a division game, but we want to win this game just like we wanted to win the Cleveland game, and we're going to go out there and prepare to win it."
The Jets may have a central-focused mindset heading into Sunday's contest, but it doesn't take away from one grueling stat they haven't been able to overcome in recent years.
And if the team is going to take the next step in their rebuild, it's a stat that must change on Sunday.
The numbers tell the story. New York is a gruesome 25-65 against AFC East opponents since 2011, including 4-26 against New England during that stretch.
It hasn't gotten much better since Tom Brady left New England either. The Jets are just 2-10 against their rivals since one of the greatest quarterbacks of all time moved on. It highlights the organization's deeper struggles across the division and against their arch nemisis.
Even if Glenn and the Jets aren't focused about what happened last year or over the last 16 years.
The Jets haven't finished over .500 in their division since 2010, the last time they made the playoffs. Many fans are expecting similar struggles when the team travels to Foxborough on Sunday, but there is reason for optimism.
Despite the Patriots coming off a Super Bowl appearance last season and rattling off back-to-back wins against the Bills and Raiders, they are still a team that can be beat. Their defense is a top-five unit, but is league average against the run, and their offense, while potent, can absolutely turn the ball over when you least expect. Drake Maye is currently tied for the league lead in interceptions thrown so far this season (seven).
The Jets still have a long way to go before they can confidently compete for a Super Bowl. The first step to reaching that goal, though, is to win games in the division.
And Glenn's current mindset has Jets players believing their divisional drought may soon come to an end.
Amid the celebration of a Week 5 win over the Browns , one key point rang true throughout Glenn's postgame response to players: Going 1-0 each week, and each day, is how a team like the Jets improves.
And some of the team's biggest stars, including Garrett Wilson, have bought in to that mindset.
According to DraftKings Sportsbook , New England is currently favored by 7.5 points in Sunday's contest . Most people in their right minds would expect the Jets to be unable to compete with the AFC Champions on the road. But what if New York can? What if, instead of a beatdown in Massachusetts, the Jets actually play well enough to win?
Well, that should show that the team is truly heading in the right direction. It would show that the organization, despite falling to 2-4, is capable of playing up to their level of competition.
They may not win on Sunday, but if the Jets put up a quality performance, it could set the franchise up for future success down the road. Heck, a win might catapult the group forward beyond anything fans could have expected this season.
That's what is at stake on Sunday. New York has a chance to show its AFC East problems are over. Correcting a 25-65 mark since 2011 isn't easy, and it doesn't happen in just one game. But Glenn's message of being "1-0 each week" is something the roster and fanbase should get behind.
It might just get the Jets to where they want to go.

title: 5 Jets With Skyrocketing Stocks to Begin Week 6 (David Bailey's Outlook Soars)
full_text:
When you win, it's easy to move forward in the week with rose-colored glasses. For the Jets, their Week 5 win over the Browns not only improved their record to 2-3 , but it also saw plenty of strong performances from key players, stoking optimism for the rest of the season.
From stars like wideout Garrett Wilson to key members of the rookie class, the Jets should be thrilled with what they saw from their core after Sunday's 17-12 win. In fact, five members of Gang Green in particular saw their stock soar after Sunday's victory.
Let's get to the five biggest ones here.
David Bailey has been solid to start his rookie campaign with New York. He hasn't been the transcendent player some Jets fans may have hoped he would be when he was taken with the second overall pick.
Boy, did he look like that on Sunday, though. The Texas Tech product recorded three sacks (h/t NFL), four quarterback hits, and nine pressures. He remains New York's best pass rusher but became one of six rookies since 2000 to record at least five sacks in their first five NFL games.
THIRD sack of the day for David Bailey @CLEvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/QTqQqo79NN
The best part about Bailey has been his improved run defense. His effort and physicality are there. He's looking the part of an everydown edge rusher.
He's on the cusp of a special rookie season if this continues.
A player who has taken a very positive jump in his second season is former Jets third-round cornerback AZ Thomas. The Florida State product was the seventh-highest-rated player by the Jets on Sunday, according to Pro Football Focus , and has the 11th-highest coverage grade of all corners through five games.
He also hasn't been beaten deep. Thomas has yet to give up a completion beyond 20 yards. The way the Jets have developed him has been a sight to see. He's fourth in the league in pass breakups, and has been close to intercepting multiple passes over the last few weeks.
It seems like the Jets got a really good player here that is only getting better.
It's not hyperbole to say this was the best game Jamien Sherwood has had in two years. The veteran linebacker has struggled mightily in the early season , but was the highest-graded Jets player by PFF against the Browns (83.5). Sherwood recorded four tackles, a quarterback hit, and a pass defended.
If Sherwood can play as he did on Sunday, the rest of the year could change drastically for the Jets' defense. Right now, the linebacker position remains a big question for the organization. Things could change if the team gets his Week 5 form moving forward.
This was the breakout game Jets fans have been waiting for since Braelon Allen was drafted in the fourth round three years ago. 24 carries, 116 yards, and the game-winning touchdown run set the stage for New York's offense to be the catalyst for the unit on Sunday.
For the first time in three years, Allen has rewarded Gang Green for their faith . With Breece Hall due back soon, it's nice for the Jets to recognize and accept that they have a perfectly competent backup behind him.
There is no Jets player who's had more of a consistent start to the season than Dane Belton. The veteran safety has been a revelation for the team through five games, sitting at the seventh-best PFF grade (81.4) among 96 eligible safeties this season. He wasn't targeted in Sunday's win, and he even recorded a sack on a blitz.
Belton, like New York's other safeties, is a Swiss Army knife. The more he plays, the better he is.
And right now he's on an All-Pro trajectory.

title: Faria's Focus: 8 Jets Thoughts After Win vs. Browns (Garrett Wilson, Ongoing Concerns, Optimistic Outlook & More)
full_text:
One day, Jets fans will be able to watch their team at home when the weather is not horrid.
Sunday was not one of those days .
New York used the elements to their advantage, though, in outlasting the AFC North-leading Browns in a 17-12 rock fight . The win bumped the Jets' record to 2-3, with an upcoming Week 6 contest against the Patriots to get ready for.
The end of a three-game losing streak will have plenty of takeaways, so let's go through eight of my top thoughts following New York's latest win over the weekend
Some Jets fans believed that the team was already doomed this season. Others felt there was nothing head coach Aaron Glenn could do to earn another year after a dismal 1-3 start. Most fans would argue a five-point win over the Browns in an ugly contest shouldn't be celebrated.
The jury is still out on Glenn and New York's future, of course. No one knows how the rest of the season should go.
But for a team that won just four of their first 21 games under this current regime, celebrating wins should never be frowned upon. The Jets, for the most part on Sunday, played well. In many ways, the game shouldn't have been as close as it was. New York's defense dominated, and their offense did move the ball down the field consistently. Turnovers and penalties were their big issue.
But there's a fine balance between wanting to see the team be successful and actively rooting for their demise. In the case of the Jets, it's clear that people should celebrate a good win against a team that was in first place in their division at the time rather than get angry over a lost draft pick—especially this early in the year.
TL;DR—it's okay to celebrate a win like this, and don't let anyone tell you it isn't.
That was it. That was the blueprint that showed just how good the Jets' defense could be for the remainder of the season. Glenn called blitz plays on over 50 percent of the snaps faced. In turn, the defense recorded eight sacks and harassed Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson for most of the afternoon.
David Bailey was the big winner, posting a team-high three sacks in a breakout performance from the second overall pick. In many ways, the young star was the best player on the field for the Jets throughout Sunday's contest.
"Just relentless," Glenn said. "The other things that really showed up in the game was (David's) ability to play the run, and I think that's one thing that he's not getting enough credit for, but man, he did a hell of a job when it came to run defense too, so he just had an all-around game as far as affecting the quarterback and playing the run."
It wasn't just Bailey, though. Fourth-round rookie Darrell Jackson Jr. notched his first career sack (h/t Glenn Naughton) and two pass deflections at the line of scrimmage. Throw in quality play from Kingsley Enagbare and Will McDonald IV, and the Jets' defensive line played the best it has all year.
Rookie DT Darrell Jackson having himself a hell of a day.  Two batted passes at the LOS and gets in on a big sack here with Enagbare. pic.twitter.com/W5xxCgLUQT
It also helps that Jamien Sherwood had his best game and was the team's leader in PFF rankings at 83.5 Throw in another elite performance from AZ Thomas, Minkah Fitzpatrick, and Dane Belton and New York's secondary also stood out.
All elite defenses need good pass rushes, though. And the team's performance on Sunday provided the blueprint for how good they could be moving forward.
When it comes to the Jets' offensive game plan, I'll let Glenn's response from Monday tell it all:
"Any time we can get Garrett involved, good things happen," New York's head coach said.
Seven catches, 104 yards and a sick touchdown to get the scoring started. Yep, Wilson remains one of the best receivers in football. As long as he keeps getting the overwhelming share of the targets, New York should stay successful on offense.
What does Glenn do well as head coach? What position group has improved under him?
These are questions that have been asked in recent weeks during New York's three-game losing streak. Yet in Sunday's win over the Browns, it was clear that Glenn's importance to the team was clear .
Defensively, the Jets remain vastly improved from last season. Maybe they aren't good enough to dominate elite offenses like the Bears' or Lions', but even the most ardent critic of Glenn can't deny the improvement in their defense.
The coach's top skill is more than just calling plays, though. In years past, the Jets had a history of keeping their heads down during tough moments. When something bad happened, it would cascade into a mountain of bad things.
So far this season, though, the opposite has happened.
Bad things have happened, and the team has responded. The clearest example came in the closing minutes of the game. Gang Green, down 12-10, watched their quarterback fumble at midfield. In years past, the Jets wouldn't have been able to recover from that. Instead, their special teams made a play, the offense responded, and the team won the game.
That is coaching. It's an example of the team not giving up when things seemed low. And it's a good reminder that while Glenn still has a lot to prove, there are some obvious things to build on.
The Jets should be pleased with this win. They did some things they have struggled to do and found a way at the end to win.
That said, many of the same problems the team has dealt with continues to be an issue.
New York committed 10 penalties on the day for over 100 yards. The Jets' lack of discipline remains a major issue going forward. Their passing offense also seems out of whack at times due to a number of pressures given up. Whether it's starters getting beat along the offensive line or Geno Smith holding onto the ball too long, the Jets need to do a better job of getting the ball out quickly in the passing game.
When healthy, Breece Hall is one of the best running backs in the game. New York's biggest problem has been not finding someone to complement the star runner when he comes off the field. For years, it seemed like the duo of Braelon Allen and Isaiah Davis just simply weren't enough.
Allen ran for a career-high 116 yards on 24 carries and the game-winning score from 22 yards out to pace New York's rushing attack. Along the way, he broke several tackles to set the tone for the Jets' offense, earning some praise from his head coach.
It is incredibly important for Allen to continue playing up to this level. It adds a new power dynamic the Jets haven't had - even when Hall is in the game.
Before the season began, it seemed like the Jets had a major question mark at kicker. After five games, that question is no more. Jason Sanders has been excellent since winning the job during camp in a shaky position battle.
Sanders nailed a 54-yard kick in the rain and is 8-for-9 on kicks so far this season. He has missed an extra point, but the former Dolphin appears healthy and is playing very good football.
Even more important, the Jets' punt return unit recovering the muffed punt from the Browns late in the fourth quarter won them the game. New York's special teams unit remains just that: special.
I have been high on Darren Mougey as general manager of the Jets. He seems to understand positional value well and has been very good in the first couple of drafts. The 2025 class has every-down starters in Armand Membou, Mason Taylor and AZ Thomas.
The 2026 class may be even better with Bailey, Sadiq, and Jackson all with breakout games over the first five weeks. New York will need to see more from first-round pick Omar Cooper Jr. when he returns from injured reserve, and more reps for D'Angelo Ponds will be huge for the secondary, but the Jets have six clear starters from the last two draft classes.
It could get up to eight if the aforementioned players are able to produce moving forward.
Getting eight starters in two draft classes is a huge success for any modern GM . For Mougey, his work should be celebrated so far, even with a…

title: Aaron Glenn Is Already a Better Jets Head Coach Than Robert Saleh for One Key Reason
full_text:
In case it wasn't already clear, Jets head coach Aaron Glenn is significantly different from his predecessor .
When Robert Saleh was hired by the Jets in 2021, for the better part of three seasons, he spoke about how the job he took was likened to that of an expansion roster. Glenn, meanwhile, never stooped low to criticize his counterpart —instead taking many of the current struggles on the chin through his first 22 games.
That isn't what has separated Glenn from Saleh, though. The biggest difference between the two coaches has come down to the response from the roster.
And it's something that has shown up in each of New York's first five games to begin the 2026 NFL season.
Accountability comes in all shapes and sizes when teams lose. When teams win, though, the true mark of a quality head coach is how they handle the days after.
In the case of Glenn, Sunday's 17-12 win over the Browns put him in the right mindset. Although he was pleased that the Jets got the win, there was a sense of frustration that they didn't play their best.
"Happy that we got us a win, but as you look at that tape, there are a number of things that we have to improve on, which we will actually address this week," Glenn said.
Compare that to Saleh's answer on Sunday. His Titans roster dropped another game, this time falling to 0-5. Instead of circling the wagons, the coach has made it clear: he won't panic. And that is all there is to it.
“ I’ve always felt like that’s a sign of panic where you’ve lost all answers . And right now, I don’t think we’re in a space where we don’t have answers,” Saleh said, per Teresa M. Walker of the Associated Press . “We just got to continue working and try to help our guys get better.”
As a head coach, there's a difference in how Glenn deals with his struggles compared to Saleh. There's also a difference in how the Jets have played under him in Year 2 compared to Glenn's predecessor.
It's true that over five games, the Jets' record under Saleh in his second season was better. The 2022 Jets were 3-2 compared to the current 2-3 mark this season. But the quality of play is different. The 2022 Jets didn't play well in two of their victories—they marched to wins based on last-moment plays.
The 2026 Jets are playing a lot better than the previous group. They have been more competitive in losses and look to be an improving team in wins . The roster is also more focused on its goals than ever before, as made abundantly clear by star receiver Garrett Wilson.
"We have to get over that hump. Go 1-0 this week. Go 1-0 each rep, and that was the mindset that we all talked about before we took the field," Wilson said. "Winning your one-on-one and playing your part in the play and not worrying about the score. That was (Glenn's) message, and all of a sudden, we came in here, and we won. It was spot on."
It's true that Glenn is working with a better roster than Saleh out in Tennessee, but many believed the former Jets coach was done in by organization-wide struggles. In many ways, excuses were made for him throughout his tenure.
With Glenn, there are no excuses. There's just the expectation to win. While there is disappointment that the wins haven't stacked up yet, there's optimism that they will soon .
Therein lies the difference between the past and present Jets head coaches.
