title: Cam Ward Beats David Carr, Tim Couch and Other Busts for Worst Record in First 22 Starts in NFL History
full_text:
After Sunday's 26-3 loss to the Houston Texans , QB Cam Ward has the fewest wins across 22 starts of any NFL quarterback to begin their career.
In Ward's rookie campaign, he led the Titans to a 3-14 record. The last time Ward guided Tennessee to a win was in December against the Kansas City Chiefs without QB Patrick Mahomes, since the Titans have lost seven straight with Ward at the helm, including a 0-5 start, to begin the 2026 season.
In Sunday's blowout loss to Houston, Titans fans poured boos over the field and held up signs showing their frustrations .
Although football is the ultimate team sport, in recent years, a quarterback's win-loss record has become just as much a position stat as ERA is to pitchers in baseball. Whether or not the blame should fall on the shoulders of the 24-year-old quarterback, the numbers contextualize how medicore Ward's career has been.
Let's take a look at the short list of losing NFL quarterbacks who have started their careers with more wins than Ward.
Former University of Kentucky great, QB Tim Couch, like Ward, was drafted number one in the 1999 NFL Draft to the newly expanded Cleveland Browns.
In 1996, the Browns moved to Baltimore, becoming the Baltimore Ravens. After three years of no football in northern Ohio, the Cleveland Browns were reinstated as an expansion franchise.
Couch made his first career start in Week 2 against the newly rebranded Tennessee Titans; the Browns lost 9-26. Cleveland would only win two games in Couch's rough rookie season, one less than Ward's rookie campaign.
In his sophomore season, Couch led the Browns to a 2-1 start before going on a four-game losing streak. A broken thumb sidelined Couch for missing the remainder of the season.
In 2001, Couch made his 22nd start and lost, going 4-18 in that stretch, earning one more than Ward to begin his career.
Unfortunately, Coach would retire at the age of 26 due to major injuries. He finished his career with the Browns, going 22-37 as a starter, throwing 67 interceptions to 64 touchdowns.
Today, Couch is remembered as the beginning of the Browns' carousel of quarterbacks .
Drafted sixth overall by the Cincinnati Bengals, QB David Klingler was a standout at the University of Houston. The Bengals selected Klingler to be the successor to franchise legend QB Boomer Esaison.
After a rocky start of 4-7, Cincinnati benched Esaison in favor of Klingler. The rookie struggled, losing his first three starts before finally earning his first and only win as a rookie.
The Bengals traded Esaison to the New York Jets, and Klingler was named the full-time starter, but he continued to underperform. In his first 22 starts, he only earned four wins, which is one more win than Ward.
Klingler was benched for good in 1994 after going 0-7 to start the season. Over the next three seasons, Klingler only appeared in five games as a backup.
He finished his career with a 4-20 record, throwing 22 interceptions and 16 touchdowns.
The Houston Texans selected QB David Carr first overall in the 2002 NFL Draft. The Texans were given the first pick because they were an expansion team, bringing football back to Houston since the Oilers left in 1996 for Tennessee.
Similar to Ward, Carr was named the day-one starter as the number one pick. In his NFL debut, Carr steered the newly formed Texans to a 19-10 victory over in-state opponent the Dallas Cowboys.
Carr ended his rookie season with a 4-12 record, earning one more win than Ward despite finishing the season without a touchdown over the final six games. In 2003, Carr made his 22nd start in his sophomore season and lost, finishing with a 6-16 record in that span.
Carr continued to quarterback the Texans for the next several seasons with little success. He made his final start in 2007 as a member of the Carolina Panthers before spending four years as a backup.
In 2012, Carr retired a Super Bowl champion as a backup for Eli Manning. Carr finished his career with a 23-56 record as a starter, throwing 71 interceptions to 65 touchdowns as a pro.
Carr holds an NFL record for the most sacks taken in a single season with 76 , which came in his rookie season.
Coming out of Washington State, QB Ryan Leaf was considered worthy of the first overall pick in the 1998 NFL Draft over Hall of Famer Peyton Manning. Ultimately, the Colts chose Manning, and Leaf was selected second to the San Diego Chargers.
In 1998, Leaf was a Week 1 starter, like Ward. He won his first two starts over the Bills and Titans before getting benched in Week 10 due to a sour performance against the Broncos.
Leaf would appear in one more game in Week 15 as a backup; he finished his rookie season 3-9 as a starter.
Over the next two seasons, Leaf would only make nine more starts before flaming out with the Dallas Cowboys in 2001. Although Leaf was one start shy of 22 career starts, he still earned one more win than Ward.
Across his three seasons as a pro, Leaf went 4-17 as a starter and had a horrendous 14-36 touchdown-to-interception ratio. He was out of the NFL by the age of 25.
Today, Leaf is widely regarded as one of the biggest busts in recent NFL history.

title: Grading Every Titans Position Group After Week 5 Loss vs. Texans
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans produced another lifeless effort on Sunday, falling 26-3 to the Houston Texans in a lopsided battle between two winless teams.
Even the most optimistic Titans fan can’t help but feel dejected after a performance like that . Things started badly, and they only got worse as the game progressed.
This Titans team is simply broken in many ways, and until things get fixed, you’re going to continue seeing the type of poor grades you’re about to sees
QB Cam Ward struggled mightily in this one, completing just 23 of his 36 passes for 170 yards and one interception.
The second-year quarterback continues to be erratic with his ball placement. Ward has a knack for making catches harder than they have to be, which leads to drops or missed opportunities after the catch.
Another area where he continues to struggle is his ability to process what he’s seeing both pre- and post-snap. His inability to diagnose the moving puzzle often gets him in trouble and/or prevents him from hitting the big plays that are there to be made.
All of these issues showed up early and often in what was arguably Ward’s worst outing of the season. But considering the performance of the offensive line (we’ll touch on that later), I’ll at least spare him from the F.
Things got off to a rocky start and never get much better. RB Tyjae Spears fumbled in the first quarter and failed to record a single rushing yard, while RB Tony Pollard averaged less than four yards per carry.
It was a putrid afternoon all around, and the inability to get anything going on the ground was a big reason why.
The receiver group of Carnell Tate, Wan’Dale Robinson, Elic Ayomanor, Calvin Ridley, and Chimere Dike combined for just 137 yards on 13 catches.
There were a couple of big plays left on the table, most notably a couple of missed opportunities to Tate that failed to connect because of poor execution and/or penalties. But aside from that, it was a rather lifeless performance by the entire passing attack.
Where do we even begin with this one?
I would say this was an absolutely atrocious performance by the offensive line, but that would somehow be downplaying how bad it really was. The offensive line allowed a combined 20 pressures, three sacks, and two hits on the day.
LT Dan Moore was the biggest culprit, allowing eight of those pressures for an absurd pressure rate of 19.5 percent.
Watching this play in slow-motion with this music is *chefs kiss* pic.twitter.com/OvC0NYFbzI
It was a long afternoon for the group upfront, and the point total on the scoreboard directly reflects that.
It was another largely irrelevant day for a group that hasn’t contributed much. The group of Gunnar Helm, Daniel Bellinger, and Kylen Granson combined for just five yards.
The latter of whom had the opportunity for a big play early in the game, but he was unable to reel in the pass, and it became another missed opportunity for a team that’s had more than its fair share.
It was a rather mediocre outing for a group that has actually played well for most of the year. The group combined for eight pressures and six run stops. DT Jeffery Simmons led the way with three pressures, while DL Jordan Elliott topped the group with two run stops.
But for the Titans to win, they need their defensive line to be a dominant front, and that just wasn’t the case here.
Cody Barton, Cedric Gray, and Anthony Hill Jr. had a solid game for the most part. The three of them were credited with 17 combined tackles, multiple pressures, and half a sack (Gray).
They also helped play a key role in holding the Texans’ ground game to under three yards per carry.
The Titans’ secondary entered the game very thin on the backend, and it only got worse. S Amani Hooker was ruled out with a concussion, while S Kevin Winston Jr. left early with a quadriceps injury, and their absence was felt throughout the contest.
The Texans’ group of pass catchers combined for 261 yards and one touchdown on 26 catches.

title: Postgame Quotes That Matter From Robert Saleh After Titans' Lifeless Week 5 Loss to Texans
full_text:
Another Sunday means another Tennessee Titans loss. This time, head coach Robert Saleh's group fell to the Houston Texans 26-3 at home, dropping to 0-5 in the 2026 season.
Not much went right for Tennessee against Houston. The offense managed just 187 total yards and didn't find the end zone, while the defense allowed Houston quarterback C.J. Stroud to get too comfortable in the pocket, leading to an efficient outing for the 2023 No. 2 overall pick.
The Titans are arguably the worst team in the NFL and have shown no improvement from last season's 3-14 performance. Saleh spoke to the media after his team's latest embarrassing loss, and it's clear that he is running out of answers.
Though he isn't the sole reason for Sunday's loss to the Texans, quarterback Cam Ward still didn't play very well . The 2025 No. 1 overall pick completed 23 of 36 passes for 170 yards and threw an interception.
After another uninspiring performance from his young signal-caller, Saleh was asked about the possibility of benching Ward for veteran Mitchell Trubisky, and the Titans head coach made it known that Ward is still Tennessee's No. 1 quarterback.
"Cam's our starting quarterback," Saleh said. "We're going to give him every opportunity to be successful this year, and we're going to continue working with him, grinding with him and trying to help him get better."
Ward was also asked why he should remain the Titans' QB1, and the Miami product said he is more than capable of handling the responsibilities of being an NFL starting quarterback.
"I just think my process, what I'm willing to sacrifice every week to get to the player that I want to be," Ward said on remaining as the Titans starting quarterback. "Also the player that the team needs and the organization needs to win games. I love the criticism and everything that comes with the quarterback territory. It's the best position in the world. Stuff goes the right way, you take all the credit. Stuff goes the wrong way, you take all the blame."
He hasn't lived up to expectations so far this year, but it is still too early to bench Ward. Tennessee must give Ward an ample sample size before making a decision on whether he is the answer at the most pivotal position in the sport.
Despite a 0-5 start to his tenure as head coach, Saleh isn't losing any confidence. The defensive-minded coach stated that he will turn the Titans around and bring the franchise back into the sun as a winning organization.
"We are going to flip this thing, and eventually this organization is going to have its day in the sun," Saleh said.
Tennessee has won six games since the start of the 2024 season, and hasn't tallied a victory since Week 16 of the 2025 season. There may not be a franchise in a darker place than the Titans right now, and we'll see whether Saleh can turn the tide and be the coach who brings winning football back to Nashville.
The most impactful quote from Saleh's press conference was his message to his guys about the next 12 games. Saleh said that the final 12 games of the year will decide who will stick around in Tennessee and be a part of the franchise turnaround.
"The next 12 games will determine which of you will be here when we turn this thing around."
The Titans were one of the most active franchises in the league on the player acquisition front this past offseason. So far, none of those additions have paid off and made major contributions. We could see another roster turnover period for Tennessee as soon as next spring.
A road contest against the 2-3 Indianapolis Colts is next for the Titans. A loss would drop Tennessee to 0-6 for the first time since 2009, and could officially kickstart draft talk.

title: Titans QB Cam Ward's Promising Progress Stalls In 26-3 Loss vs. Texans
full_text:
All of the optimism surrounding QB Cam Ward went out the window on Sunday. The Titans' signal caller had arguably his worst outing of the season, completing 23 of his 36 passes for 170 yards and one interception. It certainly wasn't all his fault that the team only produced three points.
Ward was sacked four times and was under duress throughout the contest, largely due to LT Dan Moore Jr. having a horrendous performance on Sunday. Truthfully, the entire offense looked overmatched on a day where a fellow 0-4 team stood across from them.
Look at my franchise’s left tackle… pic.twitter.com/mhBxrYeMWW
The Titans shot themselves in the foot far too many times to have a realistic chance in this one. This team doesn’t have the talent or experience to overcome those types of mistakes.
At one point, they had four straight drives in the first half that resulted in a three-and-out, a fumble, an interception, and another three-and-out.
To take their struggles a step further, Tennessee only produced 108 total yards of offense through the first three quarters, ultimately ending the game with just 187 in total.
While things haven’t necessarily been as bad as they were on Sunday, they haven’t exactly been much better. The former first overall pick is now 3-19 as a starter and has just five total touchdowns and four turnovers through the first five games.
Now that another lifeless loss is in the rearview mirror, Ward was bluntly asked why he deserves to continue being the Titans’ quarterback long term.
“ I just think my process. What I’m willing to sacrifice each and every week to get to the player that I want to be, but also the player that the team needs, and the organization needs to win games. I love the criticism. I love everything that comes with the quarterback territory. At the end of the day, it’s the best position in the world. ( When ) stuff goes the right way, you take all the credit, and when stuff goes the wrong way, you take all the blame. I know I’m capable of this position. I have the right guys around me to uplift me, and myself to uplift them. And we’ll eventually put it together .”
Coaches and teammates continue to rave about Ward behind the scenes and the amount of work he puts in. However, It’s clear that Ward’s effort inside the building isn’t carrying over to the games. The second-year quarterback was asked why he thinks that is.
“ We just gotta continue to have urgency. I think we have that each and every week, but at the end of the day, we just gotta make plays. I have to make plays. The whole team has to make plays. That’s what it comes down to — making plays. ”
Ward was then asked what this team could do to start fixing these seemingly never-ending problems and how much blame he puts on himself for the issues at hand
“ I just try to continue to do my job. At the end of the day, I have a lot of stuff to continue to get better at. I think that’s gonna put us in position to win games… But everyone in the building knows it’s going to take all 11 of us on offense to get things how we want it. But as far as my job, there’s still a lot of things I have to clean up. I have to continue to motivate my guys the way they need to be motivated. I have to continue to lead with my style. I think if we keep doing that, if we keep on making progress forward, the wins will eventually come .”
One thing is for certain, Tennessee needs better production from their young quarterback they invested so much in. If Ward starts to figure things out and he starts to play well, the wins will follow.
But if they don’t, the Titans might need to have some uncomfortable conversations this offseason.

title: What’s Next For The Robert Saleh-Led Titans After Falling to 0-5
full_text:
The Robert Saleh era in Tennessee hasn’t exactly gotten off to the start many hoped for when he was hired.
After another lopsided loss, his team now sits at 0-5 on the year, which is a low not even former coaches Brian Callahan and Ken Whisenhunt can relate to. This is now the Titans’ worst start to a season since starting 0-6 back in 2009.
Now, if you want to remain optimistic, the Titans drastically turned that season around. They went on to win their next five in a row and nearly snuck into the playoffs at 8-8.
Unfortunately, this team doesn’t have anything close to what former RB Chris Johnson was doing that year. To put it bluntly: realistic chances of a turnaround for this Titans team are slim to none.
The Titans have now lost 44 of their last 56 games dating back to 2023. And to make matters worse, second-year QB Cam Ward has regressed to the point where many have become skeptical about his long-term future with the franchise.
The Miami product was supposed to be the savior for a Titans team that desperately needed one. Instead, he looks like a quarterback who is completely in over his head at the moment. That certainly doesn’t mean things can’t improve over time, but considering the product this fanbase has been forced to watch the last few years, nobody can blame them for growing impatient.
The real question is how patient this franchise — a franchise that’s infamously lacked patience of late — is willing to be with their former first overall pick?
I do think there’s a world where the Titans try to go the ‘Bryce Young route’ by sitting him for a few weeks, but someone like Ward needs to play. The only way he’s going to reach his full potential is by getting the reps he needs.
Therefore, I have a hard time believing Ward will be benched any time soon, but if these types of ugly performances continue to stack up, then anything is possible.
Now that the playoffs appear to be an unrealistic goal, what happens to veteran players such as DT Jeffery Simmons, RB Tony Pollard, and WR Calvin Ridley?
Let’s start with the obvious blockbuster. Trading Simmons would undoubtedly net to a massive return that would surely include a first-round pick in the upcoming draft.
But for them to trade the one true star they have on this team, the return would have to be an offer they simply couldn’t refuse. And maybe they do get that from a desperate team that's willing to do anything to get over the hump.
But trading Simmons would undoubtedly be another crushing blow for a franchise that’s suffered far too many of them as of late. Without a king's ransom in return, I think he ends up staying in Tennessee as the face of the franchise heading into their fancy new stadium next year.
Every other veteran should be on the table. Rumors of Pollard drawing interest elsewhere should only grow as we get closer to the trade deadline. If/when they get a respectable offer for the veteran running back, that’s one deal they should make without hesitation.
Pollard is likely gone after this year either way, so it would be wise to get something in return while they still can. Someone with his production and resume could yield an early-to-mid-day three pick in return.
As for Ridley, the divorce between both parties is inevitable at the end of this year, so I have a hard time not envisioning Tennessee picking up the phone if someone calls about the veteran receiver.
With that said, given the age and recent production (or lack thereof) out of the Alabama product, don’t expect anything more than a late-round pick in return should somebody call.
Nonetheless, the fact that we’re talking about all this before Halloween is extremely disappointing. The Titans are clearly in the midst of another long season that has some fans already shifting their focus toward next year’s draft.
Many Titans fans are already salivating over the possibility of reuniting the former Buckeye tandem of Jeremiah Smith and Carnell Tate in Tennessee. However, that’s way down the line and they’ll need to do a lot more losing to make that happen.
But at the end of the day, that’s something for the fans to focus on. This team has to focus on blocking out the noise and continue trying to put their best foot forward regardless of the outcome on Sunday’s.
Only time will tell how all this plays out, but it’s clear that Saleh and his staff have a lot of work to do to get this team where they need to be.

title: Where to Watch and 2 Things to Expect: Titans Host 0-4 Texans in Battle for First Victory
full_text:
Neither the Tennessee Titans nor the Houston Texans have pulled out a win this season. Both teams sit in that bottom-of-the-barrel level of NFL teams who simply haven't figured it out yet.
Today, the division rivals will butt heads at Nissan Stadium. It's Cam Ward vs. C.J. Stroud. JC Latham vs. Will Anderson Jr. Robert Saleh vs. DeMeco Ryans - we'll touch on that matchup specifically.
Here's our weekly guide on where to watch the Titans, as well as what to expect from Tennessee's team in Week 5 at home.
The Titans take on the Texans at 12:00 PM CT on Sunday, October 11, in Nashville. You can catch the contest live on CBS and streaming on NFL+ and Paramount+. Locally, Nashville affiliate WTVF NewsChannel 5 will have the game.
There are a handful of ways to watch this one, Titans fans, but we're bringing you just two major wrinkles to expect.
Cam Ward set his season high in passing yards in Week 4, throwing for 222 through the air againt the Baltimore Ravens. We should be in for a similar performance, if not one more focused on the deep ball.
Ward has been criticized time and time again this season for failing to connect on explosive plays, along with OC Brian Daboll. Even in losing to the Ravens, however, Tennessee's offense finally opened up the passing game. Carnell Tate had 145 yards all by himself.
Against a so-far lackluster Texans secondary, the Titans are facing a must-win scenario coming off their best passing performance of the year. It'd be shocking for Ward and Daboll not to lean into that apparent advantage today.
With head coach DeMeco Ryans taking over play-calling duties for Houston's defense, two of the league's most storied DCs will coach against one another today. Saleh and Ryans have met one time prior as HCs, back in 2023.
The Jets beat the Texans all that time ago, and now, Saleh will look to repeat. Both coaches looking for their first win in a divisional matchup certainly raises the stakes of this bittersweet reunion.
Expect varied looks on either side of the ball, and even potentially turnovers both ways. The Texans certainly have the better offense on paper, but at least prior to Ryans taking over, the Titans' defense could easily be granted an edge here.
It'll be a real clash of the defensive titans on the sidelines, no pun intended. The victor in this duel could end up being the overall victor as a direct result.

title: Commanders' Sonny Styles Just Made the Defensive Rookie of the Year Race More Interesting
full_text:
Say what you will about the Washington Commanders; there's plenty worth airing out considering their 1-3-1 record , but they're not talentless.
Even if their recent draft history and fuzzy team-building ambitions have clouded the squad's attempts at recapturing the magic of their 2024 run, they can only fail so often with the few prospect gems they've chosen. That sentiment doesn't apply only to prized centerpiece Jayden Daniels , either; just as they found their quarterback with that No. 2 draft pick back in 2024, they seem to have similarly nabbed their defensive star of the future by signing up for the Sonny Styles experience this past offseason.
He wasted no time looking like a premium prospect, having already tallied 33 tackles through his first five professional outings. That mark is tied for second on Washington, indicating just how valuable he's been as a do-it-all defender who can generate pressure, stop the run, and defend in coverage whenever he's asked to pick up an assignment.
Be still my beating heart. A Commanders LB just ran down the field with a speedy RB step for step and broke the pass up. Sonny Styles is an absolute freak. pic.twitter.com/TCUnAdmAqg
He had the chance to build on his still-lagging reputation in the Commanders' Week 5 duel against the New York Giants, a game that left a sour taste in most Washington fans' mouths following a 27-27 tie. They may have blown their chance to make early divisional noise by falling winless to each of their three NFC East rivals , but Styles showed up when tasked with rising to the occasion against Arvell Reese.
The former Ohio State Buckeyes had to transition from a set of defensive NCAA Championship-winning stars to opponents with two top-10 selections in the past NFL Draft, and they both backed up their early Defensive Rookie of the Year cases with statistically proficient outings. While Styles led all players with 13 total tackles, his highest in-game mark yet, Reese tied for his own squad’s lead with nine, and a Daniels sack to boot.
Big sack by Arvell Reese, the Giants have forced OT. pic.twitter.com/kBXWLw03U6
He still couldn't catch Daniels in a footrace, but who can?
Conversely, Styles did his best work blowing up numerous Giants attempts at beating Washington's defense on the ground, further flexing his defense's greatest strength. They're among the league's better run defenses in total rushing yards allowed, rushing yards per carry, rushing touchdowns, and total rushing attempts, having scared most opponents off from beating the Commanders through the dogpile.
The tradeoff has, of course, shown up in the Commanders' porous aerial defense , but that's not on Styles. He can't do everything, but he can come close to seamlessly transitioning between defensive duties. Reese also looks incredible as a mammoth disruptor, as the two commemorate their joint early greatness with a postgame jersey swap.
WHOLESOME: #Giants LB Arvell Reese and #Commanders LB Sonny Styles shared an awesome moment postgame swapping jerseys. The two helped each other take off their jerseys before exchanging words of encouragement: “Keep ballin’, baby.” “Love you too, bro.” pic.twitter.com/KKxDzypgPL
Washington's brass faces tough decisions in the coming weeks, after a disappointing season following a summer of opportunity, but they can at least appreciate the one unadulterated long-term franchise swing that's emerged through the first month-plus of the season. Styles is the truth, and management ought to build around his talents far more efficiently than it has around Daniels.

title: Commanders Are 1-3-1, but the NFC East Has Left Them an Opening
full_text:
The Washington Commanders are 1-3-1. Things look bleak: injuries are already ravaging the lineup, the team isn't playing where it needs to be , and it sits in last place in the NFC East. It's a lonely place: the basement. The only solace is that Philadelphia and Dallas are both 2-3, just half a game ahead of Washington. With 12 games left, the NFC East is still very much wide open. New York leads the division at 3-1-1; Washington is two games back, but not very far behind the Giants in terms of where they are on the field. In fact, a strong argument could be made that if they'd gotten out of their own way for a bit, this conversation would be very different right now. The NFL’s tiebreaking procedures state that : "Tie games count as one-half win and one-half loss for both clubs." So there's that.
vs Saints (W6), at Texans (W7), at Eagles (W9)
vs Panthers (W6), vs Cowboys (W7), at Washington (W8)
at Packers (W6), at Eagles (W7), vs Cardinals (W8)
at 49ers (W6), vs Eagles (W8), vs Rams (W9)
Even though Washington started the season losing to both the Eagles and Cowboys, Philadelphia has now lost three straight and sits at 2-3, while Dallas now has the same record after losing to Tampa Bay last week. New York is the only team in the division with a winning record, and they looked horrible in the first half against Washington before the Commanders found a way to tie. So, while Washington visits San Francisco Monday night (Oct. 19), a place they haven't won since 2004, and then has the Week 7 bye, the Giants will host the Saints on October 18 and visit Houston on the 25th. The very first game after the bye is in Week 8 against the Eagles. From there, Washington will play host to the Rams on November 8, then visit the Giants on November 12. That means two of their first three post-bye games are against NFC East opponents, where wins can turn the season around. With the team 0-2-1 against their rivals, the rematches become the season's most important games. Washington can split the season series with a victory over the depleted Eagles, but can still win the season series with the Giants. Victories in both would set up a game with the Cowboys, who return to Washington in Week 18. Winning all three remaining division games would move Washington to 3-2-1 against the NFC East. If Philly and Dallas also split their series and take wins off New York, that could put the Commanders in prime position. That can change quickly, though. If Washington loses Monday and New York wins both games before the Commanders return from the bye, the gap grows to 3½ games. Dallas and Philadelphia play each other during that break, so only one can win, but the Giants still have a chance to pull away.
The timing matters for Adam Peters, too. I know it's easy to get mad at the guy getting the groceries, but the trade deadline is November 10, two days before the Giants rematch. That leaves San Francisco, Philadelphia, and the Rams as Washington's last three games before the deadline. For me, those games need to give Peters a reason to add help. Being within reach in the standings is one consideration; whether this team can do something with that help is another. Always remember, Peters is not in Washington with a golden ticket to serve Daniel Snyder's every whim; this is a different era of ownership with a group making decisions, not a tiny dictator on a perch he built to stand taller than others. The pressure is on Peters to put a winning product on the field yesterday, not next year. Make no mistake, he's feeling the heat just as much as Quinn, although he probably has a longer leash.
This team is beaten and battered, but it's not down and out yet, with 12 games remaining on the schedule. Don't get me wrong, they've already burned through any mistakes that come with a normal season and added a few more. I thought Washington showed enough against New York to make a run at this division possible. I also thought it should have won that game. That's the frustrating part: Washington has already let at least one division win slip away . Add in how things ended in Philly, and this season has turned on the smallest of margins. The bye gives them time to address what's costing them games, but that work has to show up against Philadelphia. They've already lost to the Eagles once; they can't keep counting on everyone else's losses to make up for their own. Still, Washington has pulled off this kind of Monday night upset before, beating the unbeaten Eagles 32-21 in 2022, even if their all-time record in the Bay Area is 3-10-1. title: Tress Way Reached a Milestone No Washington Punter Had Before — Commanders Daily
full_text:
One franchise milestone was overshadowed by the 27-27 tie this past weekend as punter Tress Way surpassed 40,000 career punting yards. Way became the first punter in franchise history and the 36th in NFL history to reach that mark. Officially, Way and Bryan Anger are the only two active punters above that threshold. Earlier this year, Way played in his 200th game for the Washington Football franchise (Commanders, Redskins, WFT), joining Washington Legends Darrell Green, Monte Coleman, Art Monk , and Dave Butz as the only players to reach that mark in the Burgundy & Gold. Way was highly active and effective Sunday, punting six times for 312 yards, for a 52-yard gross average and a 43.3-yard net average. His longest punt traveled 59 yards from Washington’s own seven-yard line in the first quarter.
Way first became a Redskins player back during the 2014 preseason after Chicago cut him and Washington claimed him . Way became the franchise’s career punting-yardage leader by passing Mike Bragg during the 2024 season, and he is currently the longest-tenured player on the roster. The Commanders describe him as an emotional team leader and mentor who was voted captain for the fifth time before this season. Way has been to the Pro Bowl three times, after the 2019, 2022, and 2025 seasons, and signed a contract extension in February 2026, though he said on September 10 that this will likely be his last season. "I've felt wanted here my whole career. I didn't want to play anywhere else," Way said.
Tress Way says he thinks this will be his last season pic.twitter.com/l4nLJA1CMF
This isn't some random free agent the team signed during free agency; he's played his entire regular-season career in Washington and remains a key contributor. Maybe it was always in the cards for him to be here after playing kicker and punter for the Union Redskins back at his high school in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Those returns meant some other players saw their roles diminish as they got fewer opportunities. The Commanders also worked out TE Quentin Moore, an UDFA signed by Washington after this year's draft. https://t.co/ol9gY3Vb5r
The Washington Commanders had a tough week, falling from up 14 in the fourth quarter, letting the game slip away, and ending in a 27-27 overtime tie. That performance didn't do Washington any favors with the national media, either, as eight of the nine power rankings we track each week have the Commanders sitting between No. 25 and No. 28.
"First name Sonny, last name Styles!" @SonnyStyles_ was EVERYWHERE on Sunday for the @Commanders pic.twitter.com/gAX3YSm9Ir
"Jayden Daniels probably cost my man Dan Quinn his job, to be honest with you," Parsons said on his podcast, "The Edge with Micah Parsons." "I'm a defensive player, and this s---'s programmed to me. I even know what to do in those situations," Parsons said, adding that Daniels, who is in his third NFL season, has no excuse not to know how to operate in that scenario. "And mind you, it'd be different if Jayden Daniels was a rookie. This is your third year. This is your third year. You've been to the NFC Championship Game. You've been in big moments before."
The Washington Commanders entered Week 5 knowing they needed to get their tight ends more involved in the offense , especially Chig Okonkwo, who returned in Week 4. Okonkwo caught four passes for 21 yards in two appearances before Sunday, then caught four passes for 60 yards against the New York Giants.
. @Giants @Commanders @DAR0NPAYNE Daron with the "peanut punch" and @KingTut_90 with the FR...Defense did their job to give the Commanders a chance in OT. #BaldysBreakdowns pic.twitter.com/VuKx9ScnyK
Daniels was all of that against the Giants, accounting for 302 total yards and two touchdowns. His first pass of the day was an 11-yard completion to Chig Okonkwo, and he found the tight end again two plays later for a 23-yard gain, setting up Jacory Croskey-Merritt's 33-yard rushing score. Daniels was most impactful on the ground, and the Giants had few answers for him when he got into the open field. He went untouched up the middle of the Giants' defense, outrunning every defender on his way to a 38-yard rushing touchdown -- his first of the season and the longest of his career. He did it again on the Commanders' following drive, turning a third-and-2 into a 26-yard score. Daniels is now tied with Sammy Baugh for most all-time rushing touchdowns by a quarterback in franchise history and the first Washington quarterback to rush for nine rushing touchdowns within the first three seasons of their career.
The most critical/important play of the 4th quarter was Isaiah Likely's TD. Never in my life have I seen the most important player on an opposing team's offense get 13 free yards!! On a 4th and 7!! Never in my life bruh, I swear. pic.twitter.com/Pofpz18NcV
After effectively limiting Jameis Winston to 7-of-16 for 72 passing yards and 0 TDs in the first half, Daronte Jones’ defense came apart in the second half once again, as Winston went 13-for-17 for 141 passing yards and 2 TDs in the fourth quarter. At one point, Daronte Jones had Daron Payne dropping into coverage. Fans will also note how far off the line of scrimmage the secondary was on the play, and Isiah Likely is given ten free yards in the red zone. title: Commanders Stock Report: Jayden Daniels' Playmaking Shines While Dan Quinn’s Stock Keeps Falling
full_text:
The Washington Commanders got several key players back, including Jayden Daniels, Terry McLaurin, Sam Cosmi, and Rachaad White, for their game against the New York Giants this past weekend. Those returns meant some other players saw their roles diminish as they got fewer opportunities. Keep in mind this post is about players moving in a better or worse direction this season, not just what happened in Sunday's game. Washington had one of the most disappointing game endings in recent memory, but that doesn't mean everyone's stock went down with it.
Antonio Williams’ role With the Commanders' number one receiver returning against the Giants, some wondered about what Antonio Williams' role might look like moving forward. Put that worry aside: his snap share jumped from 37% in Week 1 to 49% in Week 2, then rose to 69% in London, when McLaurin sat, and then 68% against New York this past Sunday. The season-long opportunity he's been getting has grown, and this week's snap count shows his workload held steady. He caught all three passes thrown his way for 31 receiving yards against New York. While McLaurin didn't play 100% of the snaps, Williams' role isn't diminishing, which is a good sign; Diggs' eventual return will be the next test. Chig Okonkwo’s impact If there was one name I wanted to see with more snaps next to it in Week 5, it was Chig Okonkwo. His offensive share increased from 58% in London to 71% against New York. His production jumped: he caught four passes for 60 yards, all in the first half. Looking back at what the entire room had coming into this game, 10 catches for 65 yards, Okonkwo almost eclipsed that yardage total by himself. Sonny Styles/Starting LB Pair Sonny Styles and Frankie Luvu each played all 89 defensive snaps against the Giants, with Styles finishing with 13 tackles (one for loss) and one pass defensed. Luvu added nine tackles and a quarterback hit.
"First name Sonny, last name Styles!" @SonnyStyles_ was EVERYWHERE on Sunday for the @Commanders pic.twitter.com/gAX3YSm9Ir
Jayden Daniels’ playmaking With Jayden Daniels back at the helm, the offense moved the ball as he completed 17-of-25 passes for 199 yards and added 103 rushing yards, with touchdown runs of 38 and 26 yards. Jacory Croskey-Merritt’s rushing production On Sunday, Bill Croskey-Merritt had 11 carries for 82 yards and a 33-yard touchdown, for 7.5 yards per carry as his production took a clear step forward even if his snaps took a step back . Josh Conerly Jr.’s development Josh Conerly Jr. is an offensive lineman who has clearly improved from last year. Conerly played all 62 offensive snaps Sunday against the Giants and has seen his Pro Football Focus pass-blocking grade improve from 57.8 last season to 66.3 this year, and he's yet to give up a sack.
#Commanders RT Josh Conerly Jr through 5 weeks • 207 pass block snaps • 0 sacks allowed • 89% pass-block win rate pic.twitter.com/JGeBgkfEBl
Kain Medrano’s defensive opportunity Against Seattle, Kain Medrano played 44 defensive snaps, got the 50-yard pick-6, and made a huge impression. Last week, that dropped to 21 snaps in London, then one against the Giants Sunday. The London drop came because Frankie Luvu returned to the lineup; this week, it was because the staff had tons of confidence in their starting pair of Styles and Luvu. Austin Ekeler’s backfield role The staff hoped Austin Ekeler, a veteran presence, would spark the backfield, but his snaps dropped from 17 in London (27%) to six snaps (10%) against New York, mainly because Rachaad White returned and played 37 snaps (60%). The defense’s ability to finish In a nasty trend that keeps showing its face, Washington allowed just three first-half points, then 24 after halftime. The Giants scored touchdowns on their final three regulation possessions. The offense and coaching staff’s situational awareness The entire offense, including the coaching staff, is to blame for the end of the game against the Giants.  The situation began on White's final run with 55 seconds remaining, moving Washington to the Giants' 24, comfortably within rookie kicker Drew Stevens' range. The next snap didn't occur until 12 seconds remained—43 seconds between snaps. Daniels was then sacked, and the time expired before Washington could spike it or get a kicker on the field. The issue is that the plan, substitutions, and communication are all on the coaching staff; Quinn has acknowledged this in both of his press conferences since. At the same time, Daniels and the offense needed to execute with urgency in that situation, and they didn't. Daniels should have known they didn't have any timeouts, but ultimately that falls back on coaching to keep him informed when they're in communication with him through the speaker inside the quarterback’s helmet until the audio cuts off when the play clock reaches 15 seconds. "With about 56 seconds, we hand it off to Rachaad White, and it took entirely too long from there on to execute our strategy from subbing to clock awareness to clocking the ball," Quinn said Monday.
you can talk about the late game botch, but Dan Quinn screwed up the game for the Commanders well before that first half, Quinn went 22% man coverage & 50% 2-high (#5 highest) held Jameis Winston 4.5 YPA, 44% comp & -0.58 EPA/att it worked but in the second half, despite… pic.twitter.com/vTLi6aSRPh

title: Commanders Power Rankings Show a Troubling Consensus After Giants Tie
full_text:
Each week during the regular season, we'll look at what the national media is saying about the Washington Commanders via various publications' NFL Power Polls. With it being Week 6, things are starting to get clearer for several teams. We didn't have a poll in Week 5, so the last polls shown are still from Week 4... The Washington Commanders had a tough week, falling from up 14 in the fourth quarter, letting the game slip away, and ending in a 27-27 overtime tie. That performance didn't do Washington any favors with the national media, either, as eight of the nine power rankings we track each week have the Commanders sitting between No. 25 and No. 28. * Side note: Many have asked whether these polls are helpful, which is a fair question. One way to look at them is as a way to broaden your perspective on what others believe. Not to mention, sometimes it's fun to see the national media guys bump around in the dark, chasing their tails, clueless.
Commanders Power Rankings - Week 4 (Average of 25)
Commanders Power Rankings - Week 6 (Average of 27)
Sports Illustrated - No. 26
Sports Illustrated - No. 28
Note : The table above links each poll to the corresponding publication name. Last week’s Power Ranking Index : No. 25 HIGHEST Ranking: No. 20 LOWEST Ranking: No. 28 Last week’s result : tied the New York Giants 27-27 This week : @ San Francisco 49ers on MNF ESPN had this to say (28th): The Commanders are last in second-half points allowed per game (19) and 28th in second-half yards allowed per game (151.2). They have given up 20 or more points after halftime in each of the past four games, which includes a blown two-touchdown lead Sunday. One big issue has been a lack of pressure. Washington ranks 28th in sacks per dropback in the second half. Their secondary has played better, but it lacks playmakers. That issue, combined with little pressure, is why the Commanders are allowing a 53.1 third-down conversion rate after halftime. -- John Keim
CBS Sports had this to say (28th) The tie they got against the Giants should have been a victory. They choked at the end. That has to sting to not win it.  — Pete Prisco NFL.com had this to say (28th) Jayden Daniels returned and injected life into Washington’s offense, which was nice. The Commanders’ defense acquitted itself well, too, until the fourth-quarter collapse that saw Jameis Winston lead two touchdown drives to send the game to overtime. The ending wiped everything else away in the general football consciousness, which is understandable, but I liked what I saw from the Commanders for most of this game. That chaotic, disastrous finish was too fitting for this team, though, which is why it lands here after giving away a gift-wrapped win to take a painful tie. — Nick Shook
Fox Sports had this to say (27th): What the hell was that? There’s really not much more to say than that after the way the Commanders lost (OK, tied) the Giants on Sunday. It was bad enough that they wasted a triumphant return performance by QB Jayden Daniels that was giving them hope for the rest of their season. It was worse that head coach Dan Quinn ’s defense forgot how to play in the second half and let the Giants shove them down the field and almost win the game. Letting the clock run out in overtime when you’re staring at a short, game-winning field goal? It’s inexcusable. And it’s on the coach — or more accurately, their soon-to-be-former coach. — Ralph Vacchiano Sports Illustrated had this to say (28th): Commanders and a moment both completely inexplicable and completely familiar for any human. — Conor Orr
Yahoo Sports had this to say (25th): Let's wait a moment to pile on Dan Quinn, Jayden Daniels and whoever else was responsible for the fiasco at the end of Sunday's tie. There were other issues. The Commanders allowed a field goal and three touchdowns on the Giants' first four possessions of the second half. They had a 27-13 lead with just over 11 minutes left and couldn't win. The Commanders couldn't make a play against Jameis Winston to clinch a victory. And with a chance to ice the game with a 27-20 lead or win the game in the final 1:43 of regulation or after a missed Giants field goal in overtime, the Commanders punted three times. Those were failures too and can't be forgotten. And obviously the end of the game was inexcusable. The Commanders were rudderless as the clock ran out, and that's alarming. Quinn doesn't call offensive or defensive plays so a stupefying failure in clock management at the end is a really bad look for him. Daniels has to be more aware as well. It's not impossible for the Commanders to rebound from blowing a shot at a win Sunday, but it was embarrassing and will affect them all season in the NFC East race, if they ever get back in it.  — Frank Schwab Pro Football Talk had this to say (28th) The clock is still ticking on Dan Quinn. In more ways than one. — Mike Florio The Athletic had this to say (27th) Has a tie ever felt like more of a loss? There are so many questions coming out of this one. How did Jayden Daniels not understand the situation? How did Dan Quinn not have his team better prepared for that late-game moment? In a way, that sums up where the Commanders sit after a promising 2024 season: just a lot of questions with no great results. — Chad Graff and Josh Kendall Walter Football had this to say (20th) I think we've seen enough from Dan Quinn as a head coach. There's no reason the Redskins should have run a play when they could have just kicked the field goal. Quinn is a brilliant defensive coordinator, but he has now failed twice as a head coach, and the Redskins need to go in a different direction next year.
At the end of the day, the Commanders enter Week 6 with an average ranking of No. 26.55. Washington dipped a bit this week, but the tie against the Giants suggests the team is probably better than its ranking and needs to get back to situational football. title: Chig Okonkwo Can’t Be a Second-Half Afterthought for Washington — Commanders Daily
full_text:
The Washington Commanders entered Week 5 knowing they needed to get their tight ends more involved in the offense , especially Chig Okonkwo, who returned in Week 4. Okonkwo caught four passes for 21 yards in two appearances before Sunday, then caught four passes for 60 yards against the New York Giants. On the opening drive, Okonkwo made catches of 11 and 23 yards as the offense moved downfield for a 69-yard drive that ended with a touchdown from Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt . His 25-yard reception in the second quarter was part of the drive that ended in Drew Stevens' 28-yard field goal. Clearly, the offense does better when they build it around the play-action, but that's not always an option or isn't always utilized correctly. Now that both Daniels and Okonkwo are back , the Commanders need to make the Chig-Jayden connection a top priority, especially when their top receivers are dinged up. Chig Okonkwo missed Weeks 2 and 3 with a hamstring injury he suffered during Week 1's game in Philadelphia. In London last week, several factors clouded Chig's return to action, leaving him with only two catches for five yards despite being open multiple times on the game film. So, needing to build on that connection, Chig was targeted five times in the first half against New York and caught four of those passes for 60 yards. The problem is, Washington targeted him only once in the second half, on an incompletion late in the fourth quarter, and none in overtime.
Chig Okonkwo breakout game? He's got 3 catches for 59 yards so far and it's early in the 2nd quarter. #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/c3MxBe8kMk
To be clear, Daniels attempted 11 passes in the first half, five to Okonkwo. He had eight attempts in the second and another six in overtime. One target was erased in the third because of a defensive holding call on Deonte Banks. Okonkwo doesn't need to see every single target, but when something works, take advantage of it. How the Commanders get that first half from Chig and finish with only one official target the rest of the game is beyond me. This needs to be a growth moment for Blough if he wants to be a head coach, as the failed offensive coordinator world is full of guys who lose track of personnel and need the head coach to regulate that for them, a job Quinn isn't that good at either. Quinn's comments on Monday seemed aimed at the entire setup: "I don’t catastrophize things, but I do want to make sure that I don’t minimize things either, and there are plenty of things for us to improve upon in this game, and not just the last play," Quinn said. With Washington traveling to play the undefeated 49ers in San Francisco on Monday Night Football in Week 6, they'd better make dependable receiving roles that work a priority moving forward. title: Commanders Got 7.5 Yards Per Carry From Jacory Croskey-Merritt. Then His Carries Stopped
full_text:
Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt led all Commanders running backs with 82 yards on 11 carries in Washington's 27-27 tie with the New York Giants on Sunday . That doesn't sound odd, but the snap count makes it seem off. Despite the 7.5 yards per carry, Bill didn't see the ball over the final 14:20 of regulation or during overtime.
The interesting part about the running back usage in this game is that Bill led the team with 82 rushing yards despite playing 15 fewer offensive snaps than Rachaad White, the team's alleged third-down back. Now, I already know what you're thinking about White and his receiving ability, but he had one catch for two yards, while Austin Ekeler also had one catch for 15 yards.
Jacory Croskey-Merritt breaks free for a 33-yard TD run! 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/9wfDhRQB9V
The Commanders were driving late in the third quarter (:39) when Bill took off for a 22-yard run. The problem is, his next carry, a one-yard gain at the 14:20 mark in the fourth, would be his last. Washington would go up 27-13 with 11:05 remaining. After Bill's final carry, the running back usage shifted , and the process favored White. From that point on, White got all five remaining running back carries and finished with seven rushes for 18 yards, making the move a highly questionable head-scratcher. Those opportunities included early-down situations, not the obvious passing downs White normally plays. After New York cut the lead to 27-20, White took the first-down carry at Washington's 37 with 7:15 remaining, gaining one yard; after that, the second-down play gave them one more yard, Daniels was sacked on third down, and then Washington punted. So basically, with a seven-point lead, the team moved away from what had been working and tried to get White going, but not in a way that highlighted his abilities that outshine Bill in the passing game, making this running back usage confusing. A guy averaging 7.5 yards per carry shouldn't be put on the shelf after breaking off a 22-yard run.
Then came overtime; White took a first-and-10 handoff at the 7:20 mark, gaining three yards on a possession that ended in a punt. After the Cam Skattebo fumble, Washington drove into scoring territory, and White took his last carry at the 55-second mark, gaining two yards. That was the moment the team should have spiked it and sent the kicking team out. Of course, as the entire sporting world knows, that didn't happen. Now, Dan Quinn has talked about whether they even need one featured running back, instead of using different players depending on what the offense needs. I get the thinking, especially since White brings more experience in pass protection and the receiving game, two areas where Bill is still developing . The problem with that explanation is that Washington wasn't asking White to protect Daniels or catch passes on those late carries. They were handing him the ball, mostly on first down, while the guy averaging 7.5 yards per carry wasn't getting another opportunity. Maybe David Blough saw something in the Giants' defense that he liked with White on the field, or maybe something went down with Croskey-Merritt that we don't know about. Both are possible, but until someone from the coaching staff explains the decision, we're left guessing why Washington went away from its most productive running back. I'm not suggesting Bill needs 25 carries every week, and White and Austin Ekeler certainly have a place in Washington's offense. What I have a hard time understanding is how a running back can be having that much success, get into a situation where a couple of first downs could make all the difference, and then never touch the ball again. Would giving Bill another carry have changed the outcome? Maybe not, but I'd certainly rather find out than watch him standing on the sideline. With San Francisco coming up, it'll be interesting to see whether Blough continues using the same rotation or starts giving more opportunities to the guy who's actually producing. title: Commanders Report Card: A 14-Point Lead Vanishes in Disastrous Giants Tie
full_text:
Washington Commanders fans know a low point when they see one. They'd already had plenty of practice through this regular season's first four weeks in watching a near-endless slew of untimely penalties and called-back highlights, occasionally broken up by the occasional devastating quarterback injury , and that's to say nothing of last year's regression to the mean or the two decades of unimpressive football that preceded the Jayden Daniels era.
Their Week 5 tie to the New York Giants may not go down as the most embarrassing moment in the history of the historic and proud Washington football franchise, but it certainly feels as look-in-the-mirror-worthy as any moment since Daniels took over the on-field ship. Even if they didn't have to walk away with a fourth defeat in five matchups, the key Commanders are already acknowledging how much this draw feels like a blown chance at disrupting the divisional standings.
Dan Quinn says the tie feels like a loss. Says he hasn’t talked to Jayden yet but that the coach needs to “make life easier” for his QB pic.twitter.com/Dq4yreEKjG
This 27-27 finish was the sort of matchup that leaves plenty to ponder in choosing the best path forward, even if a few position groups held up their end of the bargain in spurts. Balancing those meteoric early-game highs with the humiliating lows is tough, but we'll try our best.
How do you evaluate Daniels' first day back? He did everything he was asked and more while adjusting to football with a brace protecting his recently dislocated elbow, but he deserves a fair share of the blame pie for his lack of urgency and awareness in that final tie-clinching disaster.
The Commanders can't get the play off in time and this game ends in a tie pic.twitter.com/WmPp6q5hU0
It's also fair to counter that they never would have been in position to keep their five-game win streak against the Giants going without him, with his 300+ all-purpose yards and two rushing touchdowns pushing Washington to an early 14-point lead. The five sacks didn't help, though he may have shown how tough it'll be to win behind a thrown-together offensive line and battered receiving corps when the defense loses steam.
Anyone attempting to look up Daniels' highlights on X will be instead greeted by a flood of angry Washingtonians and befuddled outsiders reacting to the final 12 seconds as opposed to anything that occurred over the nearly-75 minute sequence that preceded that lapse, and understandably so. Daniels wasn't alone in calling it a rollercoaster finish, but more on the coaching staff's performance later.
After weeks of diminishing returns, Jacory ‘Bill’ Croskey-Merritt re-took the reins as Washington's lead back, rushing for 82 yards on 11 carries to lead all rushers not named Daniels. 7.5 yards per carry is the highest per-game mark he's posted through five weeks, and he was sure to enjoy his first red zone return trip since Week 1 in Philadelphia.
Rachaad White wasn't quite so lucky in his own return to the lineup alongside Daniels, attracting just one target to couple with his eight so-so attempts on the ground. At the very least, Washington's coaching staff remains comfortable leaving it up to the backs to control the occasional series on their own, a strategy that couldn't have worked with some of the running back rotations from the last month.
The receivers were there for Daniels when he needed them, but not as much as they have been in other matchups. With the rushing attack holding its weight against New York's solid front seven, the quarterback's platoon of dynamic, Stefon Diggs-less downfield options successfully leveraged their athleticism and hands to meet Daniels where he needed them.
Though none of the recently returned Terry McLaurin, the still-ascending Antonio Williams , or big play-magnet Treylon Burks scored a touchdown, they remained effective in the clutch, keeping the offense chugging downfield whenever called upon. That threesome converted on nine of the 11 passes thrown their way for 119 yards, clearly separating themselves from the rest of the error-prone wideout reserve pack.
Finally, after weeks of minimal impact from Chig Okonkwo's understudies , the starter drew eyes back to Washington's tight end assortment with his first fully healthy outing as a Commander. He finished with 60 yards, nearly tripling his season total of 21 yards through the first four weeks, when injuries and ineffective usage had bogged him down.
Jayden Daniels and Chig Okonkwo are cooking early. #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/dRA9FpRpCi
He glided through defenders, repeatedly opening up the middle of the field and giving Daniels a reliable intermediate threat to dish to, with the legs to continue creating after the catch. That's all that's been asked of him since moving to D.C. over the offseason, and it had to feel cathartic for Okonkwo to finally factor into an early scoring wave.
Besides the pass-catcher, few of Okonkwo's fellow targets attracted much attention downfield. John Bates tried his darndest to get his teammates in position during that soon-to-be-infamous clock expiration, while Ben Sinnott drew a pass-interference call on one of his few routes, so they at least have those memories to cherish, with chances at a win having slipped through the Commanders' fingers.
As handy as it was to welcome Sam Cosmi back into the fold, further sparing Daniels from having to get blocked for by another unproven reserve or unwanted journeyman lineman, their quarterback really could have used better protection in his season debut at home.
Brandon Coleman struggled against the admittedly imposing Giants pass rush, giving up several of the five sacks that Daniels took while holding little ground one-on-one. The false starts and holding penalties didn't help, either.
Josh Conerly Jr., Chris Paul, and center Lucas Patrick didn't allow those same routine pressures, but the offensive line is one of those units that's only as strong as its weakest link. As always, Laremy Tunsil is missed.
That vaunted Commanders defense, courtesy of first-year coordinator Daronte Jones , was nowhere to be found as Washington succumbed to a Jameis Winston-led attack and saw its 14-point lead evaporate. Frankie Luvu's energy and instincts were much appreciated, though usual quarterback pressure accumulators Odafe Oweh and K'Lavon Chaisson disappeared when the going got tough.
Winston, a quarterback known for erratic play, shouldn't have played so smoothly against a unit that is disproportionately solid against the run as they are. If nothing else, up-and-coming star Sonny Styles recorded a game-high 13 tackles along with another deflected pass, continuing his reign of terror as Washington's do-it-all rookie disruptor. If only his unit had the consistency (or legs?) to keep that same momentum up whenever the offense failed to score.
Despite the highlights Rasul Douglas and Amik Robertson totaled, a growing trend amidst the Commanders' new-look cornerbacks, 326 yards against the famously interception-happy Winston, is an indictment . Sure, the pick Robertson snagged went down as an immediately questionable refereeing decision, but soft coverage and a lack of that same aggression on those short-yardage completions let the Giants march back in the fourth quarter.
It was good to see Jeremy Reaves, as aware as he was, flying cross-field to make tackles with Nick Cross still out of commission, as he almost netted an interception of his own late in the game. But to fans' disbelief, Mike Sainristil still squeezed in a few snaps in a limited role and somehow allowed a late touchdown to Malik Nabers in single coverage.
MALIK NABERS COMES UP CLUTCH @NYGvsWAS on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/FF9Fws8i2n
It seems that every time this unit shows life with their veteran disruptors, they reveal just how far away they are from achieving any series-to-series consistency.
White stepped up as a primary kick returner alongside Luke McCaffrey, with…
